Commerce Platform calculates a cart total through a Checkout Pipeline. Customer Context identifies a region, loyalty tier, and active campaign, and these attributes can change between requests. The Pricing Engine currently contains conditionals for standard prices, member discounts, employee discounts, campaign pricing, tax handling, and fallback behavior. Each pricing variant must be selected at run time and must implement the same operation for producing a quote. The Checkout Pipeline must remain unaware of pricing details, and adding a campaign rule must not require recompiling or replacing the checkout workflow. The selected rule must receive an immutable pricing context, return line-level adjustments and a total, and participate in existing audit and metrics collection. Rule selection happens before quote calculation, with an explicit fallback used when no campaign rule matches. The team must choose how to organize the interchangeable pricing computations and how selection should be separated from the checkout flow.

Decision: Choose the structure that lets the Pricing Engine invoke interchangeable pricing computations selected from each Customer Context while keeping the Checkout Pipeline independent of rule details.
proposition: Pattern 'strategy' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: strategy: Define a family of algorithms, encapsulate each one behind a common operation, and make them interchangeable, so the algorithm a context executes can vary independently of the context and its clients - including at run time. Problem: One class supports several variants of the same computation - sort orders, pricing or tax rules, routing and backoff policies, compression codecs - and the variant has to be selected at run time. Hard-wiring the variants into the class (or into one subclass per variant) mixes algorithm detail with the class's own logic, forces recompilation for every new variant, and turns selection into a growing conditional that runs on every call.

proposition: Pattern 'model-view-intent' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: model-view-intent: Structure one UI feature as a single loop in which every user interaction becomes an intent value, a pure reduce step derives the next immutable state from the previous state and that intent, and the view renders only that state - so the screen's behaviour is determined by data instead of by scattered event handlers. proposition: Pattern 'thread-safe-copy-on-write' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: thread-safe-copy-on-write: Share one body between many threads so that copying a value stays cheap and reading it never blocks, and protect the sharing state itself - the reference count or the published pointer - so that a writer clones the body and swaps in a new snapshot instead of mutating storage other threads can see. Problem: A value is copied often and mutated rarely, so the copies should share storage until one of them diverges. That decision works single-threaded, but the moment several threads hold the value the sharing state becomes shared mutable state in its own right: a reference count incremented without atomics loses updates or frees a body another thread is still reading, a plain pointer dereferenced while another thread replaces it is a data race, and a 'copy' that still aliases its source turns a reader's snapshot into a moving target. The trigger is a read-mostly shared value - configuration, routing

proposition: Pattern 'row-data-gateway' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: row-data-gateway: Give each database row its own in-memory object that mirrors the row's columns and carries the row's own find, insert, update and delete operations, so all data-access code for a table lives in one place instead of being duplicated across the scripts that use it. Problem: SQL text, parameter binding and result-set mapping are re-derived inside every transaction script that touches a table, while the in-memory objects those scripts work with know nothing about the database. No single place knows how one row is read, written and deleted, so a schema change ripples through every script and every new query is another chance to get parameterisation and type conversion wrong.

proposition: Pattern 'monitor-object' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: monitor-object: Serialise concurrent method invocations on a shared object by giving the object its own lock and condition variables, so that only one method executes inside it at a time and methods that cannot proceed wait cooperatively instead of polling. Problem: Objects shared by several threads expose their state through ordinary methods, and nothing stops concurrent callers from interleaving inside those methods, corrupting the invariants they were written to maintain. The race is then papered over with ad-hoc locking, sleeps and busy-wait loops scattered through client code. The recurring decision is whether the object itself should own the serialisation (and the scheduling) of its methods instead of leaving that discipline to every caller.

proposition: Pattern 'pipeline' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: pipeline: Decompose a transformation into an ordered sequence of named stages that each consume the previous stage's output and produce the next stage's input, so the workflow reads top to bottom and every step can be tested, instrumented, reordered or replaced on its own. proposition: Pattern 'request-reply' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: request-reply: Let a sender obtain a result or a domain error from an asynchronous or remote receiver by pairing each request with a correlated reply, and give the missing reply a defined outcome: timeout, cancellation and disposal of late replies. Problem: Messaging is one-way, but the sender frequently needs a return value or a domain error from the receiver before it can continue. Without an agreed reply destination, a way to match replies to requests, and a rule for what happens when no reply arrives, the caller either blocks forever, mis-associates the next reply with the wrong request, or accumulates pending state it never cleans up.

proposition: Pattern 'functional-options' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: functional-options: Keep a constructor's required parameter list fixed while optional settings arrive as named configuration functions that are applied in order over built-in defaults, so the API can grow without breaking callers and without exposing a mutable configuration object. Problem: A constructor accumulates optional settings: every new setting changes the signature for all callers, zero values and booleans cannot be distinguished from 'not supplied', and a configuration struct has to be handed out (often by pointer, with nil meaning 'default') so callers can retain and mutate the very state the library depends on. The recurring decision is how to let an option set grow across the life of a public API while keeping meaningful defaults, source compatibility and a documented resolution rule for conflicting options.

Candidate: newtype: Give a single primitive its own distinct type so that values with different meanings cannot be substituted for one another, and the raw representation is reachable only through the wrapper's own construction and accessors. proposition: Pattern 'deadline-propagation' is relevant to this decision. proposition: Pattern 'cancellation-token' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: cancellation-token: Give a caller-owned operation tree a one-way request to stop: pass a read-only cancellation signal through every cancellable call, observe it at safe points, clean up what was acquired, and report a distinct cancelled outcome without pretending that cooperative cancellation is forced termination. Orbital Tactics runs a fixed-step simulation where Bullet, Missile, Drone, Hull, Shield, and Asteroid objects can collide. CollisionResolver receives two independently selected participants and must choose the result: a missile striking a shield may deactivate the shield, a drone touching a hull may apply impact damage, and a bullet meeting an asteroid may ricochet. Some combinations have no interaction. The rules team owns the entity classes, while the physics team owns effect calculations, and either side may add concrete entity kinds over time. CollisionResolver must not contain a growing ladder of concrete-type checks, and callers that collect candidate pairs must not know the applicable interaction rule. At runtime, selection must account for both participants' concrete types, not merely the first argument or a numeric category attached by the caller. The engine also needs to register and log each pair-specific handler so that an unsupported combination can be reported explicitly rather than silently treated as a generic collision.

Decision: Whether interaction selection should be resolved from the runtime types of both participants, with pair-specific rules kept out of the collision caller.
proposition: Pattern 'double-dispatch' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: double-dispatch: Select the operation to execute from the runtime types of two collaborating objects, so behaviour can vary along two independent type axes instead of being resolved by hand-written type tests in the caller. Problem: Behaviour depends on the runtime type of *two* objects - element and visitor, shape and surface, left operand and right operand - but an ordinary call resolves on the receiver only (or, in dynamic languages, on no argument at all). Every operation then grows its own type-test ladder, knowledge of the concrete classes leaks into callers, and adding a class silently breaks the cases nobody remembered to extend.

proposition: Pattern 'protected-system' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: protected-system: Give a resource exactly one owning object whose published operations are the only way to touch it, so that every access is decided by an authorization check before the resource is used. Problem: A resource - a credential store, a file tree, a socket, a connection pool, a device handle - is referenced from many places. When each use site performs its own permission check, the checks drift, new code paths forget them, and the resource remains reachable as a raw handle, so a missing check cannot even be detected. The recurring trigger: one object can own the resource and clients can be made to hold only that object, so ownership itself can carry the enforcement.

proposition: Pattern 'update-method' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: update-method: Give every live object one self-contained per-frame step and let a single driver call each object's step every frame, so behaviour advances one frame at a time while input and rendering stay responsive. Problem: A running world is full of objects that each have to keep doing their own thing - guards patrolling, statues charging, agents acting - and the recurring decision is where one object's per-frame behaviour lives and how all those behaviours get driven. Coding a behaviour as a loop that runs to completion blocks input and rendering (the skeleton walks, but nobody sees it); coding it inline in the game loop turns the loop into a switchboard over every kind of object, so every new behaviour edits central code; and there is no way for two actors to evolve independently and simultaneously.

Candidate: durable-subscriber: Keep a publish-subscribe consumer's place while it is offline: the broker binds a stable subscription identity to retained messages or a committed position, then resumes delivery after reconnect until retention, expiry, or quota says the backlog is no longer available. proposition: Pattern 'assertion' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: assertion: Express a model object's preconditions, postconditions and class invariants as executable, side-effect-free predicates at the operations that must uphold them, so a broken contract fails at its boundary instead of remaining a comment or surfacing later as corrupt state. This pattern is for design-by-contract correctness checks, not routine validation of untrusted input or test-only assertions. Problem: Model rules - a balance never below its floor, a period whose end follows its start, a status that cannot move backwards - are left in comments, documents and team memory while constructors and mutators check nothing. proposition: Pattern 'implicit-lock' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: implicit-lock: Make the framework or layer-supertype code that every business operation must pass through acquire and release the locks, so no application method can forget an acquisition and silently invalidate the concurrency policy. IroncladBuffer is a reusable C++ storage class whose design currently combines several independent decisions: ownership of memory, bounds-check strength, allocation behavior, and whether internal access is serialized. Development builds need exhaustive checks, production builds need low overhead, embedded deployments need a fixed arena, and threaded deployments need locking. Each combination must remain type-safe, inlineable, and fixed before execution begins; a configuration read in a constructor is not acceptable because changing it would alter the class's structure or thread contract. Users should be able to instantiate only coherent combinations and should see incompatible combinations as compile errors. The buffer also needs to expose a stable public API and support value semantics where appropriate. The implementation must avoid copying a single implementation into several specialized classes and must not add a virtual layer to each buffer operation merely to select behavior. The decision is where the ownership, checking, allocation, and synchronization variations should be bound and selected during type construction.

Decision: Decide how IroncladBuffer should bind its independent ownership, checking, allocation, and synchronization decisions at compile time so each instantiation is fixed, type-safe, and inlineable.
proposition: Pattern 'policy-based-design' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: policy-based-design: Assemble a class's behaviour, structure and defaults from small interchangeable policy units bound when the host type is instantiated, so that each orthogonal design decision can be varied independently instead of being frozen in the class's code. Problem: A reusable class hard-codes several independent design decisions - allocation, ownership, storage, threading, validation, error handling - inside its implementation, so a different combination is only reachable by editing or copying the class, while the runtime Strategy alternative costs a virtual call per use and gives up the guarantee that the choice is fixed, inlineable and checked before the program runs.

proposition: Pattern 'crtp' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: crtp: Give a base class template access to the concrete type that derives from it - passed as the base's own template argument - so that shared behaviour and interface methods are generated and resolved at compile time, with no virtual dispatch, no vtable and no runtime indirection. Problem: A family of related types must share behaviour or an interface, but the shared code has to call members of the concrete type, and that type is already known at compile time. Virtual functions would answer the call, yet they add a per-object pointer, an indirect call that defeats inlining, and they force the participating types to become runtime-polymorphic - which costs size and speed for value types and is impossible where the operation itself is static (per-class counters, nested types) or must run in constexpr contexts.

Candidate: guarded-suspension: Suspend a state-dependent method call inside the object that owns the state until another thread makes its guard predicate true, so callers neither poll nor get refused while the object is temporarily not ready. proposition: Pattern 'cursor-pagination' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: cursor-pagination: Bound what a read boundary returns for a large or changing ordered collection by sending one page plus an opaque continuation token that pins the filter and ordering, so clients advance deterministically without offsets and without watching rows move under them. OrderGateway exposes a shared CommandMailbox to several HTTP request threads, a scheduler thread, and a command-processing worker. Request handlers submit CompleteOrder and CancelOrder commands and await their individual results. The worker removes commands one at a time, so when the mailbox is empty it cannot execute another command immediately and later discover one. A command submitted while the worker is idle must eventually be processed rather than being rejected, because the HTTP request remains outstanding until the business operation completes. Incoming commands may also need to wait for a per-order authorization record to appear, which another component supplies after a database callback. The mailbox must preserve FIFO ordering, wake the worker exactly when work arrives, avoid lost notifications, and ensure that a worker stopping does not strand a producer. Callers are not permitted to spin while waiting, and a timeout must report failure without corrupting command state.

Decision: What should a mailbox operation do when the worker cannot currently proceed, given that the submitted command must eventually be processed?
proposition: Pattern 'guarded-suspension' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: guarded-suspension: Suspend a state-dependent method call inside the object that owns the state until another thread makes its guard predicate true, so callers neither poll nor get refused while the object is temporarily not ready. Problem: A method may only proceed while a precondition over shared state holds - a buffer is non-empty, a pool still has a free lease, a session is authenticated, a worker has a task - and that state is produced by another thread at an unknown time. The recurring decision is what the caller should do while the guard is false: refusing the request would drop work the application still needs, forcing the transition would break the object's invariants, and polling wastes a core and still races. Guarded suspension answers it by waiting on a condition the object itself owns, and by making that wait atomic

The Payments API accepts authorization requests from merchant webhooks while the Settlement Service processes them asynchronously. HTTP handlers must return an acknowledgement quickly, but a burst of retries can exceed settlement throughput. Introduce a hand-off channel with a hard capacity of 5,000 messages: producers enqueue without waiting for processing, consumers remove messages independently, and producers block for at most 50 ms when the channel is full before returning HTTP 429. Twenty settlement workers share the channel, and each message carries an idempotency key so retries remain safe. During shutdown, producers stop accepting work, consumers finish already queued messages for up to 30 seconds, and unfinished messages are moved to durable storage. The key decision is how to decouple request arrival from processing rate while ensuring overload creates visible backpressure rather than an unbounded memory backlog.

Decision: Choose the bounded handoff and overload behavior that decouple request producers from settlement consumers without allowing the backlog to grow without limit.
proposition: Pattern 'producer-consumer' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: producer-consumer: Insert a bounded buffer between producers and consumers of work items so the two sides run concurrently at their own rates, the buffer absorbs bursts and slack, and its bound turns overload into backpressure, queueing or an explicit drop policy instead of unbounded growth. Problem: Production and consumption proceed at different rates: a fast producer outruns its consumer and either drops items or grows a backlog until memory runs out, a slow producer leaves consumers idle, and bursts arrive faster than they can be processed. Wiring the two sides together directly also couples their lifetimes and schedules - a synchronous hand-off makes the faster side wait for the slower - so neither side can be scaled, restarted or tested on its own.

proposition: Pattern 'applicative' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: applicative: Apply one pure function to several independent effectful computations, letting the chosen context instance fix the semantics of absence, failure, ordering, and concurrency; the combining structure is fixed before execution - that static shape is what enables batching, parallel scheduling, and static analysis - and an accumulating error instance reports every independent failure instead of short-circuiting on the first. Problem: You have several independent computations - parse this field, fetch that record, validate this quantity - and a pure function that combines their results, but each result lives inside a context such as Option, Either/Result, List, Promise/Task, or Validation. state:
Product API has a 1,500 millisecond end-to-end latency objective. A page request fans out concurrently to Catalog, Pricing, Reviews, and Recommendation services. Each client currently has an independent 1,200 millisecond limit, and a request can also wait 300 milliseconds in the fan-out coordinator. If Pricing is slow, Product API continues running the other calls, and the server may complete them after the browser has disconnected. Catalog also forwards the request to Inventory with another fresh limit. The desired behavior is for one end-to-end time budget to remain authoritative across the whole call tree: each hop must limit outgoing work to the remaining time, pass the remaining budget and cancellation downstream, and avoid starting calls that cannot finish within it. Responses arriving after expiry must be discarded rather than included.

Decision: Choose how Product API should carry and enforce one end-to-end time budget across its concurrent downstream call tree so work stops when the original request can no longer succeed.
proposition: Pattern 'deadline-propagation' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: deadline-propagation: Bound the total time and work of a logical request by carrying one deadline through its whole call tree: every hop forwards the remaining budget and the cancellation signal instead of inventing a fresh timeout, so work that can no longer succeed is abandoned at every level. Problem: A request fans out into a chain or tree of downstream calls and each hop applies its own timeout: the end-to-end latency budget becomes the sum of N independent timeouts, servers keep working after the originating client has given up, and cancellation never reaches the deeper work - resources are consumed producing answers nobody will read.

Product API has a 1,500 millisecond end-to-end latency objective. A page request fans out concurrently to Catalog, Pricing, Reviews, and Recommendation services. Each client currently has an independent 1,200 millisecond limit, and a request can also wait 300 milliseconds in the fan-out coordinator. If Pricing is slow, Product API continues running the other calls, and the server may complete them after the browser has disconnected. Catalog also forwards the request to Inventory with another fresh limit. The desired behavior is for one end-to-end time budget to remain authoritative across the whole call tree: each hop must limit outgoing work to the remaining time, pass the remaining budget and cancellation downstream, and avoid starting calls that cannot finish within it. Responses arriving after expiry must be discarded rather than included.

Decision: Choose how Product API should carry and enforce one end-to-end time budget across its concurrent downstream call tree so work stops when the original request can no longer succeed.
proposition: Pattern 'side-effect-free-function' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: side-effect-free-function: Put the model's logic into operations that compute a result from their inputs alone, so that a caller - and a test - can predict the result without knowing any state the operation might secretly touch. Problem: Reasoning about a design becomes guesswork when operations do more than return a result: the caller must read the implementation and every delegation to know which state a call changes, and no result can be reproduced in a test without recreating the state around it. As rules compose, the number of hidden interactions grows faster than the behaviour being built, so the model stops being safely predictable.

state:
The Edge Gateway maintains a routing configuration containing 20,000 routes and is read by 48 request-handling threads on every request. An administrative reload may replace the configuration several times per minute, but readers must never wait behind a reload and a request must continue seeing one internally consistent version even if another thread publishes a replacement. RoutingSnapshot values are copied into request contexts, so allocating and filling 20,000 routes for every copy would create unacceptable latency and allocation pressure. The implementation needs cheap copies, safe publication of a new version, and retirement of an old version only after its remaining users are finished. The key choice is how to protect both the shared payload and the state that tracks which version is current while keeping the read path nonblocking.

Decision: Choose the internal representation and publication mechanism that provide cheap version copies, nonblocking reads, isolated reloads, and safe reclamation of retired configurations.
proposition: Pattern 'thread-safe-copy-on-write' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: thread-safe-copy-on-write: Share one body between many threads so that copying a value stays cheap and reading it never blocks, and protect the sharing state itself - the reference count or the published pointer - so that a writer clones the body and swaps in a new snapshot instead of mutating storage other threads can see. Problem: A value is copied often and mutated rarely, so the copies should share storage until one of them diverges. That decision works single-threaded, but the moment several threads hold the value the sharing state becomes shared mutable state in its own right: a reference count incremented without atomics loses updates or frees a body another thread is still reading, a plain pointer dereferenced while another thread replaces it is a data race, and a 'copy' that still aliases its source turns a reader's snapshot into a moving target. The trigger is a read-mostly shared value - configuration, routing

proposition: Pattern 'copy-on-write' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: copy-on-write: Let several handles of a value share one expensive body until the first write, which clones that body privately, so copying costs a pointer instead of a deep copy while every handle still behaves as an independent value. Problem: A value with an expensive body (large buffer, collection, tree, document) is copied eagerly on assignment, argument passing and return even though most copies are never modified: time and memory are spent duplicating data that would have stayed identical. The naive fix - handing out one mutable object behind several handles - breaks the copy contract, and unrelated parts of the program then observe each other's writes.

proposition: Pattern 'intrusive-reference-counting' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: intrusive-reference-counting: Give the shared body its own reference count so that many cheap handles can share it at the cost of one increment per copy, with the body destroyed deterministically when the last handle is released. Without a count owned by the object itself, either bodies are copied gratuitously or nobody can tell when the last user is finished with them.

proposition: Pattern 'option-maybe' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: option-maybe: Make the possible absence of a result part of the value and of the signature, so every caller has to decide what happens when nothing is there instead of meeting a null, a sentinel or a silently defaulted value at run time. Problem: A function has something to return for some inputs and nothing for others, but the signature does not say so: it returns a null reference, a sentinel (-1, empty string, NULL), an out-parameter, or a value that quietly means 'not found'. Callers forget the check, dereference the null or treat the sentinel as data, and the 'this case does not exist' path is discovered in production rather than at the call site.

proposition: Pattern 'anti-corruption-layer' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: anti-corruption-layer: Protect a downstream bounded context from a foreign model by making one explicitly owned boundary translate calls, data and failure semantics into the downstream language; unlike a mere wrapper, an anti-corruption layer prevents foreign concepts from becoming domain concepts. Problem: A bounded context must use a legacy application, packaged product, partner API or another context whose model it cannot control, and the same words carry different meanings on each side. Reusing the foreign SDK types and status codes directly makes its names, optionality, units, errors and version churn load-bearing parts of the local domain; translation then drifts across callers and every upstream change becomes a core-model change. Without an explicit boundary, the contexts become accidental conformists and neither can evolve independently.

proposition: Pattern 'entity' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: entity: Give a domain concept a stable identity that survives attribute changes, representation changes and time, and define its equality, lifecycle and lookup in terms of that identity instead of in terms of its attributes. Problem: A model that compares objects by their attributes cannot answer whether two instances are the same thing: a customer whose e-mail and plan changed looks like a different customer, while two distinct people who share a name look like one. References held by other objects, caches and audit records break silently, and every state change forces callers to re-identify the object.

Candidate: active-record: Make a domain object the record for one database row: keep the row's state, row-local behavior, and the methods that find and persist it together, so a small domain does not pay for a separate mapping layer. Candidate: applicative: Apply one pure function to several independent effectful computations, letting the chosen context instance fix the semantics of absence, failure, ordering, and concurrency; the combining structure is fixed before execution - that static shape is what enables batching, parallel scheduling, and static analysis - and an accumulating error instance reports every independent failure instead of short-circuiting on the first. A media-import service runs three worker threads that block on a shared in-memory work queue. Each item is a batch that must be fully written to a staging directory and recorded in the database before the worker asks for another item. During deployment, the service receives a termination request while the producer may still be enqueueing files. The system must stop accepting new work, ensure every item already in the queue is processed exactly once, and then let all three workers leave their blocking wait. Killing the process is not acceptable because it can leave half-written batches and incomplete database records. A separate control connection to each worker would complicate deployment and require every worker to implement a second waiting mechanism. The queue has no native close operation, so the shutdown design must use only ordinary item messages and must deliver one unambiguous end-of-stream indication to each worker.

Decision: How should the service tell all blocked workers to finish the queued batches and exit without interrupting work already in progress?
proposition: Pattern 'poison-pill' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: poison-pill: Terminate queue consumers cooperatively by sending a reserved sentinel message that each consumer recognises as "no more work", so consumers drain the backlog and exit without a separate control channel or forced cancellation. Problem: A producer-consumer system must shut down, but its consumers block on an empty queue and the queue has no built-in "no more items" signal: callers either kill the workers mid-work and drop buffered items, or leave them blocked forever. Production has ended - how do the consumers learn that while still processing everything already queued?

proposition: Pattern 'structured-concurrency' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: structured-concurrency: Confine the lifetimes of related concurrent subtasks to the dynamic extent of the operation that started them, so the parent cannot complete before its children do and failure or cancellation in either direction tears down the whole task tree in a controlled way. Problem: With raw spawn primitives (go, Thread.new, create_task, Task.Run, std::async, pthread_create) a child runs independently of the code that started it: when the parent fails, is cancelled or returns early, its children keep running, their failures are never observed, and shutdown must be coordinated by hand. The task-subtask relationships exist only in the developer's head, so leaked tasks, delayed cancellation and orphaned work become normal.

proposition: Pattern 'cancellation-token' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: cancellation-token: Give a caller-owned operation tree a one-way request to stop: pass a read-only cancellation signal through every cancellable call, observe it at safe points, clean up what was acquired, and report a distinct cancelled outcome without pretending that cooperative cancellation is forced termination. Problem: A request handler, background job or UI action starts work that fans out into nested calls, tasks or threads. When the caller disconnects, a deadline expires, the user presses stop or a sibling fails, merely abandoning the result leaves already-started work burning CPU, holding connections and calling dependencies. Force-killing a thread or process can interrupt a critical section and corrupt shared state, while a signal that is not propagated or observed cannot stop the call tree or make its cleanup visible to the joiner.

Each item is a batch that must be fully written to a staging directory and recorded in the database before the worker asks for another item. During deployment, the service receives a termination request while the producer may still be enqueueing files. Both the HTTP CheckoutController and the command-line checkout command currently coordinate the same set of collaborators: OrderValidator, PricingService, InventoryReservation, TaxCalculator, PaymentGateway, LedgerRepository, and OutboxPublisher. Each entry point knows the required order of calls, which operations must share a database transaction, how compensation works when payment succeeds but ledger persistence fails, and how domain errors become its own response format. Changes to checkout sequencing therefore require edits in multiple clients, and the two clients already disagree about whether inventory is reserved before or after tax calculation. The application team wants one application-owned operation for completing checkout that returns a stable receipt or a stable failure reason, while the underlying collaborators remain independently testable. The new entry point must expose no catalog, payment, ledger, or messaging details to callers, and existing direct orchestration must not remain in the controllers.

Decision: Choose the single application-owned entry point that hides checkout's required collaboration and ordering from controllers while preserving one coherent result contract.

Each entry point knows the required order of calls, which operations must share a database transaction, how compensation works when payment succeeds but ledger persistence fails, and how domain errors become its own response format. Changes to checkout sequencing therefore require edits in multiple clients, and the two clients already disagree about whether inventory is reserved before or after tax calculation. The application team wants one application-owned operation for completing checkout that returns a stable receipt or a stable failure reason, while the underlying collaborators remain independently testable. The new entry point must expose no catalog, payment, ledger, or messaging details to callers, and existing direct orchestration must not remain in the controllers.

Decision: Choose the single application-owned entry point that hides checkout's required collaboration and ordering from controllers while preserving one coherent result contract.
proposition: Pattern 'pattern-matching' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: pattern-matching: Eliminate a value drawn from a closed set of variants by matching its structure and binding the payload, so the compiler proves that every variant is handled before the program runs. Problem: Code that inspects which variant of a tagged value it received - a result type, a domain event, an AST node, a protocol frame, a state - drifts into chains of type tests, casts and accessor calls, and nothing guarantees that a variant added later is handled: the missing branch is found in production rather than by the compiler.

proposition: Pattern 'anti-corruption-layer' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: anti-corruption-layer: Protect a downstream bounded context from a foreign model by making one explicitly owned boundary translate calls, data and failure semantics into the downstream language; unlike a mere wrapper, an anti-corruption layer prevents foreign concepts from becoming domain concepts. Problem: A bounded context must use a legacy application, packaged product, partner API or another context whose model it cannot control, and the same words carry different meanings on each side. Reusing the foreign SDK types and status codes directly makes its names, optionality, units, errors and version churn load-bearing parts of the local domain; translation then drifts across callers and every upstream change becomes a core-model change. Without an explicit boundary, the contexts become accidental conformists and neither can evolve independently.

proposition: Pattern 'strategy' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: strategy: Define a family of algorithms, encapsulate each one behind a common operation, and make them interchangeable, so the algorithm a context executes can vary independently of the context and its clients - including at run time. Problem: One class supports several variants of the same computation - sort orders, pricing or tax rules, routing and backoff policies, compression codecs - and the variant has to be selected at run time. Hard-wiring the variants into the class (or into one subclass per variant) mixes algorithm detail with the class's own logic, forces recompilation for every new variant, and turns selection into a growing conditional that runs on every call.

proposition: Pattern 'consumer-driven-contract-test' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: consumer-driven-contract-test: Capture, from each consumer's own tests, the concrete provider interactions that consumer depends on, and verify the provider against that contract inside the provider's own build, so consumer and provider can be released independently without a shared end-to-end environment. proposition: Pattern 'revocable-forwarder' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: revocable-forwarder: Let a collaborator use an object through a forwarding wrapper that the grantor can switch off at any time through a separate control, so authority already handed out can be withdrawn without destroying the target and without the collaborator's cooperation. proposition: Pattern 'characterization-test' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: characterization-test: Pin the actual, currently deployed behaviour of existing code in committed reference artefacts (golden masters) so that a later edit can be distinguished from an accidental regression even when nobody can say what the code is supposed to do. Problem: You must change code whose behaviour is undocumented, surprising or only known to production: there is no specification to test against, and tests written from intended behaviour would take too long and silently encode guesses as fact. The safety net therefore has to be built from observed behaviour: replay a corpus of real inputs through the untouched subject, capture everything observable, commit the result as the reference, and let every later run diff against it - pinning what the code does today before changing how it does it.

Candidate: double-dispatch: Select the operation to execute from the runtime types of two collaborating objects, so behaviour can vary along two independent type axes instead of being resolved by hand-written type tests in the caller. Candidate: page-controller: Give each logical page or form its own input controller that handles the requests addressed to it — reading the request, invoking domain logic and choosing the view — instead of routing every request through one shared handler. proposition: Pattern 'table-module' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: table-module: Organise the domain logic of a table or view as one module with a single instance whose operations act on whole sets of rows, so table-shaped rules are written once against tabular record sets instead of being scattered over per-row objects or per-request procedures. Problem: The rules for a table are set-shaped - recalculating a column across all rows, validating an import batch, posting a period, aggregating or exporting a whole table - and the platform already speaks in tables and record sets (result sets, DataTables, grids, reports). A Domain Model would build one object per row and pay for identity, hydration and per-object behaviour the rules never use, while a Transaction Script repeats the same table-shaped logic in every use case that touches the table.

Candidate: mock: Replace a collaborator of the system under test with a test-specific object that is programmed with the expected calls and verifies them as they happen, so the interaction itself - not the resulting state - is what the test asserts. proposition: Pattern 'request-reply' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: request-reply: Let a sender obtain a result or a domain error from an asynchronous or remote receiver by pairing each request with a correlated reply, and give the missing reply a defined outcome: timeout, cancellation and disposal of late replies. Problem: Messaging is one-way, but the sender frequently needs a return value or a domain error from the receiver before it can continue. Without an agreed reply destination, a way to match replies to requests, and a rule for what happens when no reply arrives, the caller either blocks forever, mis-associates the next reply with the wrong request, or accumulates pending state it never cleans up.

The public TelemetryClient constructor currently requires an endpoint and project key, and released clients also need optional credentials, request timeouts, retry counts, tracing exporters, and keep-alive settings. The endpoint and project must remain positional, but new optional settings will be added every few releases. Existing callers must continue compiling unchanged, and the library must distinguish an omitted boolean or zero-valued setting from an explicit false or zero. Callers should be able to combine only the settings they care about, with later overrides replacing earlier ones. The resulting client must use an immutable configuration snapshot so a caller cannot mutate settings after construction. Passing a mutable configuration record is undesirable because tenants commonly retain it, while repeatedly expanding the constructor would break source compatibility. The decision is specifically how optional constructor settings are represented and applied while the required parameters and existing call sites remain stable.

Decision: Choose how optional client settings are supplied as named, composable overrides over defaults without changing the required constructor signature or exposing mutable configuration.
proposition: Pattern 'functional-options' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: functional-options: Keep a constructor's required parameter list fixed while optional settings arrive as named configuration functions that are applied in order over built-in defaults, so the API can grow without breaking callers and without exposing a mutable configuration object. Problem: A constructor accumulates optional settings: every new setting changes the signature for all callers, zero values and booleans cannot be distinguished from 'not supplied', and a configuration struct has to be handed out (often by pointer, with nil meaning 'default') so callers can retain and mutate the very state the library depends on. The recurring decision is how to let an option set grow across the life of a public API while keeping meaningful defaults, source compatibility and a documented resolution rule for conflicting options.

The Checkout API has an OrderController, OrderRepository, PaymentGateway, Clock, and Mailer. The controller creates orders and sends confirmation messages, while the repository and payment gateway differ between production, local development, and automated tests. Production uses PostgreSQL, a Stripe-backed gateway, UTC system time, and SMTP; tests need in-memory persistence, a deterministic clock, a fake gateway, and captured mail. The deployment process must choose these implementations once during startup, and route tests must be able to construct a controller with substitutes without invoking deployment configuration. The controller should expose only operations for creating and querying orders, and the payment, persistence, time, and notification collaborators must be visible in its public construction contract. A separate startup component is responsible for creating the implementation objects and connecting them to the controller, while the controller must not read environment variables or select concrete classes itself.

Decision: Choose how the Checkout API receives its repository, payment gateway, clock, and mailer so implementations are selected once and remain replaceable in tests.
proposition: Pattern 'dependency-injection' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: dependency-injection: Supply an object with the collaborators it needs from the outside — through its constructor, its setters/properties, or a dedicated injection interface — so it never constructs or looks a dependency up itself and every wiring decision is made once, in a composition root or container. Problem: An object that creates its own collaborators hard-wires a concrete class, a construction recipe and often a lifetime into itself: swapping the implementation for a test double, a second deployment or a new platform means editing the class, and the dependency graph stays invisible in the API. The recurring trigger is exactly the catalog's rule: an object should not create what it depends on — the caller, the framework or the composition root decides, and hands the dependency in.

The controller creates orders and sends confirmation messages, while the repository and payment gateway differ between production, local development, and automated tests. Candidate: transaction-script: Organizes the business logic of a single request as one procedure - read the data it needs, validate and calculate, write the results and complete in one database transaction - trading object-model structure for a straight-line implementation that can be read top to bottom. Problem: A request-scoped use case (book a room, place an order, recognize revenue, import a file) has to be implemented, and its logic mixes input validation, calculation and persistence. Candidate: stub: Replace a collaborator with a test-specific stand-in that returns canned answers, so the component under test can be driven down paths - success, empty, error, timeout - that the real collaborator cannot be made to produce on demand. The InventoryMessageAdapter and InventoryHttpImporter both convert external payloads into an InventoryItem. Their implementations duplicate the same ordered changes: trim text fields, parse numeric and date values, convert country codes to a canonical form, reject missing identifiers, and produce a domain value. The two entry points receive slightly different envelopes, but after envelope removal they must apply identical validation and normalization. Each change is pure, takes one value, and returns the next value; none may access the database, clock, or network. The team wants the order declared once, the individual changes to remain independently testable, and the resulting transformation to be passed to both adapters and reused by a scheduled CSV importer. A failed change should identify itself in tests without requiring either adapter to run. Avoid a shared mutable normalization object because adapters may execute concurrently.

Decision: How should the shared pure normalization sequence be represented so its order is declared once and the complete transformation can be reused across the three adapters?
proposition: Pattern 'function-composition' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: function-composition: Combine a chain of small unary transformations into one reusable function by sequencing them with a composition combinator (compose/pipe), so the order of the steps is stated once, every step stays independently testable, and the chain itself becomes a value that can be named, passed and reassembled. Problem: A transformation that is naturally a sequence of small pure steps gets written as nested calls or as repeated imperative assignment (`h(g(f(x)))`, or `y = f(x); y = g(y); ...; return y`) at every call site. The order is duplicated wherever the chain is used, the intermediate values need throwaway names, steps cannot be reused in a different order, and changing one stage means editing every copy.

DocumentIndex owns a heap-backed character buffer and a cached word offset table. Its assignment operator currently releases the existing buffer, allocates storage for the replacement text, and then copies the characters. An allocation failure during that copy leaves the object with invalid ownership metadata, while an exception during offset-table reconstruction leaves the buffer and index mutually inconsistent. DocumentIndex is copied by value and may be assigned to objects already referenced by readers, so assignment must provide a strong guarantee: after success all owned state must correspond to the source, and after failure the destination must remain unchanged and usable. Implement the ownership transfer so all fallible allocation and copying happens in a separate replacement object, followed by a commit that exchanges ownership handles without allocation, copying, or user callbacks. Destruction of the displaced state may then occur after the commit, and self-assignment must have no observable effect.

Decision: Choose the assignment implementation that preserves DocumentIndex validity and unchanged state when replacement allocation or copying fails.
proposition: Pattern 'copy-and-swap' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: copy-and-swap: Implement assignment (and any in-place state replacement) so that a failure while producing the new state leaves the target untouched: build the complete replacement off to the side, commit it with operations that cannot fail, and let the temporary's destructor or the garbage collector release the old state. Problem: A hand-written assignment has to tear down the old state and build a copy of the new one, but only the build can fail: destroying before allocating exposes a half-updated object when the allocation or the element copy throws, and the usual repair -- a self-assignment check plus manual rollback -- duplicates the per-member copying that already lives in the copy constructor. The trigger is an assignment (or, in a garbage-collected language, an in-place state replacement) that must satisfy the strong exception guarantee: either it completes, or the target still holds its previous value.

Candidate: recursive-descent-parser: Parse a small grammar by translating every rule directly into a function that consumes the tokens the rule matches and calls the functions of the rules it references, so the parser's control flow is the grammar itself and stays readable, debuggable and free of a code-generation step. Candidate: composite-entity: Represent a cluster of related, dependent objects through one coarse-grained entity that owns them and persists and synchronises the whole graph as a single unit of work, so clients never reference, sequence, or save the parts themselves. proposition: Pattern 'cancellation-token' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: cancellation-token: Give a caller-owned operation tree a one-way request to stop: pass a read-only cancellation signal through every cancellable call, observe it at safe points, clean up what was acquired, and report a distinct cancelled outcome without pretending that cooperative cancellation is forced termination. proposition: Pattern 'producer-consumer' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: producer-consumer: Insert a bounded buffer between producers and consumers of work items so the two sides run concurrently at their own rates, the buffer absorbs bursts and slack, and its bound turns overload into backpressure, queueing or an explicit drop policy instead of unbounded growth. The ImportController reads a CSV file, the ShipmentRow module holds normalized staging records, and a CarrierReference table maps external codes to destination zones and service levels. Every row in the batch must be checked against carrier-code validity, postal-format rules, maximum weight, and duplicate shipment identifiers within the same file. Candidate: version-number: Store a version token alongside each persistent record and make every write assert the token it read, so a write computed from stale data fails as a detectable conflict instead of silently overwriting a newer value. proposition: Pattern 'update-method' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: update-method: Give every live object one self-contained per-frame step and let a single driver call each object's step every frame, so behaviour advances one frame at a time while input and rendering stay responsive. Candidate: extensible-visitor: Keep the visitor open on both axes at once - new element kinds and new operations arrive without editing or recompiling any visitor that already exists - by giving every visitor a default method that catches element kinds it was not written for, introducing extended element kinds under an intermediate base whose accept hooks overload (not override) accept, and extending an operation by subclassing the existing concrete visitor so it inherits every case it already handled. The Expression Compiler evaluates a fixed grammar for numeric literals, variable references, addition, multiplication, and negation. The parser currently returns an open node hierarchy, and the evaluator discovers node kinds through repeated runtime type checks and casts. Each new grammar case requires edits in the evaluator, formatter, optimizer, and diagnostics mapper; a forgotten branch causes a runtime failure or an incorrect default result. The compiler team requires one total analysis operation for every node kind, with payload fields bound directly during analysis so the optimizer can distinguish literal values from variable identifiers without accessing unrelated properties. Because the grammar is owned by this compiler and additions are reviewed together, the complete node vocabulary can be enforced in the type system. Decide how the node representation and evaluation flow should ensure that every supported expression is handled and that adding a grammar case forces all relevant analyses to be revisited.

proposition: Pattern 'pattern-matching' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: pattern-matching: Eliminate a value drawn from a closed set of variants by matching its structure and binding the payload, so the compiler proves that every variant is handled before the program runs. Problem: Code that inspects which variant of a tagged value it received - a result type, a domain event, an AST node, a protocol frame, a state - drifts into chains of type tests, casts and accessor calls, and nothing guarantees that a variant added later is handled: the missing branch is found in production rather than by the compiler.

proposition: Pattern 'algebraic-data-type' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: algebraic-data-type: Model a closed sum of product-shaped alternatives: each value is exactly one constructor or case, and each case carries only its own fields, so legal states are explicit and eliminators can be checked exhaustively. Problem: Code often encodes mutually exclusive shapes as a tag beside optional or nullable fields, or as an open hierarchy. That representation admits tag/payload mismatches, forces callers to rediscover legal combinations, and lets a newly added case fall through silently; a sum-of-products type ties each case to its product payload and lets matchers be checked.

The Treasury platform transfers funds between LedgerAccount, PostingBatch, and CurrencyAccount. Every debit must be positive, use the account currency, preserve the minimum balance, and be represented by postings whose signed amounts sum to zero. A credit above the account ceiling or a posting batch that does not balance must be rejected before invalid ledger state is stored; otherwise an unrelated report may later discover the corruption. TransferRequest values are produced by an internal authorization component, while malformed commands from HTTP clients are rejected earlier by request validation. The account operations and batch finalization therefore need executable checks for their required inputs and for the guarantees they establish, including the balance after a debit and the final equality of postings. A failed operation must leave the account and batch unchanged, and the checks must remain part of production builds rather than appearing only in tests. The team must decide where these guarantees are evaluated so that all callers receive the same immediate failure and the ledger never contains a partially applied transfer.

Decision: Place executable preconditions, postconditions, and ledger invariants at the account and posting operations that must establish them, distinct from ordinary rejection of malformed external input.

Customers may change all of these attributes, while invoices, subscriptions, audit entries, and cached account references must continue to point to the same person. proposition: Pattern 'version-number' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: version-number: Store a version token alongside each persistent record and make every write assert the token it read, so a write computed from stale data fails as a detectable conflict instead of silently overwriting a newer value. Problem: Two sessions read the same record, both edit it, and the later write wins: the earlier update vanishes without any error (the lost update). Once the read-modify-write spans more than one system transaction the database cannot tell 'this is the record I read' from 'this record changed under me', so no code path can notice in time - unless the record itself carries a per-row token that changes on every write and the write tests that token before committing.

A Room Booking service manages reservations for hotel rooms and meeting rooms. The Reservation Repository stores a start instant and an end instant for each booking, and the Availability component must determine whether a proposed reservation overlaps an existing one. The rules permit one checkout at noon followed by another check-in at noon, so touching endpoints do not conflict, but a reservation from 14:00 to 16:00 conflicts with either neighboring booking. Some availability rules apply for the entire day, whereas others have no upper or lower limit because they represent agreements that have not yet been scheduled. Today, callers implement these checks independently using different strict and non-strict comparisons, and several use Long.MAX_VALUE or a distant date to mean an open end. This has produced both false conflicts for back-to-back reservations and false availability when an unbounded rule is clipped accidentally. The model must make endpoint inclusion, open ends, overlap, enclosure, and adjacency explicit and reusable without changing the persistent representation of timestamps.

Decision: Choose the value model that centralizes endpoint inclusion, unbounded ends, containment, overlap, and adjacency for reservation windows.
proposition: Pattern 'range' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: range: Represent a span of values as a single interval value whose bound inclusivity and open ends are explicit, so containment and interval-to-interval comparisons live in one place instead of repeated ad-hoc endpoint tests. Problem: Start and end travel together through the code but every caller re-derives what they mean: containment is written as scattered <= / < comparisons that drift apart, "unbounded" is smuggled in as a sentinel value (Long.MAX_VALUE, 9999-12-31), and interval-to-interval questions - do these two overlap, does one enclose the other, what is the gap between them - have no home at all.

proposition: Pattern 'effectivity' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: effectivity: Attach an explicit validity period - a Range of dates - to a fact or relationship, so every reader can ask "is this true on date D?" and get a defined answer instead of inferring history from insertion and modification timestamps. Candidate: coarse-grained-lock: Give a cluster of objects that must change together one shared lock — held on the cluster's root object, on a lock entry keyed by that root, or on a version token the root carries — so a caller locks one thing instead of discovering and locking every member. proposition: Pattern 'cancellation-token' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: cancellation-token: Give a caller-owned operation tree a one-way request to stop: pass a read-only cancellation signal through every cancellable call, observe it at safe points, clean up what was acquired, and report a distinct cancelled outcome without pretending that cooperative cancellation is forced termination. Problem: A request handler, background job or UI action starts work that fans out into nested calls, tasks or threads. When the caller disconnects, a deadline expires, the user presses stop or a sibling fails, merely abandoning the result leaves already-started work burning CPU, holding connections and calling dependencies. Force-killing a thread or process can interrupt a critical section and corrupt shared state, while a signal that is not propagated or observed cannot stop the call tree or make its cleanup visible to the joiner.

BillingService, ShipmentRepository, TenantCache, and AuditLog currently represent customer, order, shipment, tenant, and session identifiers as plain strings, even though all are generated as UUIDs. Public methods such as findOrder(String), attachShipment(String, String), and routeByTenant(String, String) therefore accept interchangeable arguments. A recent release routed a shipment through a customer lookup and the incorrect record was retrieved without a runtime conversion error. The raw UUID must remain available only at infrastructure boundaries, while domain APIs should reject swapping identifier families before code runs. Every repository must still be able to persist and query its existing UUID column without separate lookup tables, and equality, serialization, and logging must remain predictable. The key decision is whether these semantically different identifiers receive separate static identities despite sharing the same underlying representation.

An Order Service commits a new purchase and then announces that fact to several independently deployed systems. The Billing Service charges the customer, the Search Projector refreshes its catalog, the Loyalty Service awards points, and an Audit Service stores the record. None of these consumers may depend on another consumer, and adding a new consumer must not require the Order Service to change. The announcement has no intended recipient and requires no response; delivery may occur more than once, so each record carries a stable event identity and occurrence time. A consumer may reject an unknown future record kind without causing the producer to wait or retry against it. The design must clearly distinguish an immutable statement about a completed change from an instruction addressed to a particular worker, while preserving enough metadata for broker-side subscription filtering.

Decision: Choose one-way, recipient-independent publication for a completed order change, with no required response and no producer coupling to downstream consumers.

The trigger is open-ended interest: something changed, and the set of parties wanting to know is neither closed nor known at compile time.

An Order Service commits a new purchase and then announces that fact to several independently deployed systems. The Billing Service charges the customer, the Search Projector refreshes its catalog, the Loyalty Service awards points, and an Audit Service stores the record. None of these consumers may depend on another consumer, and adding a new consumer must not require the Order Service to change. The announcement has no intended recipient and requires no response; delivery may occur more than once, so each record carries a stable event identity and occurrence time. A consumer may reject an unknown future record kind without causing the producer to wait or retry against it. The design must clearly distinguish an immutable statement about a completed change from an instruction addressed to a particular worker, while preserving enough metadata for broker-side subscription filtering.

Decision: Choose one-way, recipient-independent publication for a completed order change, with no required response and no producer coupling to downstream consumers.

OrderProjection subscribes to an order-events topic and updates a reporting database. OrderEventProcessor is deployed continuously but may be scaled to zero during a nightly maintenance window while orders continue to be published. The broker supports stable consumer-group identities, retained events for seven days, and committed delivery positions. The deployment configuration must use a fixed group identifier so OrderEventProcessor resumes from its last committed position after a restart rather than creating a fresh subscription that misses the outage. Processing is at least once, so duplicate OrderApproved and OrderRefunded events may arrive; the database update must be idempotent. Events older than the retention window are a recovery incident and must raise an operational alert. The team must choose whether downtime should preserve a replayable backlog or whether the projection may intentionally remain incomplete and be rebuilt separately.

proposition: Pattern 'durable-subscriber' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: durable-subscriber: Keep a publish-subscribe consumer's place while it is offline: the broker binds a stable subscription identity to retained messages or a committed position, then resumes delivery after reconnect until retention, expiry, or quota says the backlog is no longer available. Problem: A subscriber on a publish-subscribe channel can be unavailable during redeployment, maintenance, device disconnects, or scheduled batch work. A non-durable subscription drops messages published during that gap, so the design must choose a stable identity and broker-side state, then make finite retention, replay pressure, and at-least-once redelivery explicit; durable state prevents a gap only while that state remains available.

Regal's compliance clients need to export every matching audit event from a rapidly growing, continuously changing event table. The current endpoint accepts an offset and page size, so deep exports repeatedly scan earlier rows, while concurrent inserts can shift records across page boundaries and cause the client to export duplicates or omit events. The service must keep responses bounded, preserve the requested tenant, event type, date range, and ordering throughout an export, and allow a client to resume after a disconnect without restarting from the beginning. Replace numeric offsets with a one-page response containing an opaque continuation value. The server must validate that the value represents the same query scope and resolve the next position from a stable unique ordering key rather than from a row count. The external representation should contain only the event summary fields needed by export consumers and must not leak the internal event entity or persistence query implementation.

proposition: Pattern 'cursor-pagination' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: cursor-pagination: Bound what a read boundary returns for a large or changing ordered collection by sending one page plus an opaque continuation token that pins the filter and ordering, so clients advance deterministically without offsets and without watching rows move under them. Problem: A boundary must expose a collection that is too large to return at once and keeps changing while clients read it. Offset or page-number requests make the store count or scan everything up to the requested page, and concurrent inserts or deletes shift rows across page boundaries so consumers see duplicates or miss items; the server has no way to state where the sequence should resume.

Candidate: applicative: Apply one pure function to several independent effectful computations, letting the chosen context instance fix the semantics of absence, failure, ordering, and concurrency; the combining structure is fixed before execution - that static shape is what enables batching, parallel scheduling, and static analysis - and an accumulating error instance reports every independent failure instead of short-circuiting on the first. Billstream generates customer invoices that are delivered through three channels: an HTML portal page, a printable PDF, and a plain-text email. All three contain the same customer, line items, discounts, tax summary, due date, and payment instructions, but their visual conventions and output rules differ. The current implementation has three separate generation paths, so adding a discount field or changing invoice wording requires coordinated edits and the email version sometimes disagrees with the portal version. Domain code already owns monetary calculations, but it returns channel-specific formatting structures. The team wants the invoice's content and structure to be represented independently of any output format, with format-specific components responsible for layout, typography, escaping, pagination, and transport packaging. Changes to business content should propagate to every channel, while a visual redesign of the portal or email must not require rewriting invoice calculations. A machine-readable invoice API also exists, but it exposes typed fields rather than reproducing the customer-facing invoice layout, so it should not be forced into the same presentation pipeline.

Decision: Should invoice structure be produced independently and then rendered for HTML, PDF, and email, or should each channel duplicate its own invoice-building and formatting logic?
proposition: Pattern 'two-step-view' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: two-step-view: Split presentation into two transformations - first turn domain data into a channel-neutral logical page, then render that logical page into a concrete output format - so page structure is defined once while look-and-feel and output channel live entirely in the renderer. Problem: Every page owns its own presentation decisions: with one template or one transform per page, a global look-and-feel change means editing every file, and serving a second channel (print/PDF, e-mail, plain text, a machine-readable feed) means duplicating the page's structure. Nothing in the codebase represents 'the page' independently of the markup it currently happens to be rendered as.

Candidate: copy-on-write: Let several handles of a value share one expensive body until the first write, which clones that body privately, so copying costs a pointer instead of a deep copy while every handle still behaves as an independent value. Candidate: deadline-propagation: Bound the total time and work of a logical request by carrying one deadline through its whole call tree: every hop forwards the remaining budget and the cancellation signal instead of inventing a fresh timeout, so work that can no longer succeed is abandoned at every level. ClaimsPortal loads a claim into CaseEditor, where a caseworker may change severity, notes, and assigned queue over several minutes. The portal is deployed in two instances, and both instances can display the same claim revision. When the first caseworker saves, the second caseworker's later save currently overwrites the first change because the update contains only the editable columns. The ClaimRepository must make a stale save detectable and return a conflict response containing the current revision, without holding a database lock while the form is open. Every claim row needs a durable, opaque revision value that changes whenever the row is stored; the value presented in the editor must be checked against the stored value during the update, and an atomic compare-and-set operation must ensure that only one competing save succeeds. This concurrency rule applies independently to each claim and must also cover saves made by the background ClaimAutomationWorker, even when that worker uses a different application service.

Decision: Whether each claim update should be conditioned on the opaque revision supplied when the editor loaded the row, rejecting stale edits instead of overwriting newer data.
proposition: Pattern 'version-number' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: version-number: Store a version token alongside each persistent record and make every write assert the token it read, so a write computed from stale data fails as a detectable conflict instead of silently overwriting a newer value. Problem: Two sessions read the same record, both edit it, and the later write wins: the earlier update vanishes without any error (the lost update). Once the read-modify-write spans more than one system transaction the database cannot tell 'this is the record I read' from 'this record changed under me', so no code path can notice in time - unless the record itself carries a per-row token that changes on every write and the write tests that token before committing.

proposition: Pattern 'unit-of-work' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: unit-of-work: Maintain a list of the objects affected by one business transaction and write their changes to the database in a single ordered flush, so that each business operation commits exactly once and in a consistent state. The portal is deployed in two instances, and both instances can display the same claim revision. When the first caseworker saves, the second caseworker's later save currently overwrites the first change because the update contains only the editable columns. proposition: Pattern 'recursive-descent-parser' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: recursive-descent-parser: Parse a small grammar by translating every rule directly into a function that consumes the tokens the rule matches and calls the functions of the rules it references, so the parser's control flow is the grammar itself and stays readable, debuggable and free of a code-generation step. Problem: A hand-written parser is the only option - no generator in the toolchain, or the grammar is a small DSL - yet the grammar is not a flat token sequence: alternatives must be chosen from lookahead, repetition must become a loop, and the natural grammar for expressions is left-recursive, which a top-down parser cannot translate directly. The Billing Workshop is a transaction-script application used by warehouse staff and scheduled billing jobs. CustomerRepository contains a query that loads customers, BillingJob repeats a customer lookup with different filtering, and CustomerMaintenance embeds inserts and updates. Each location independently handles parameter binding, result mapping, and persistence errors. Customer records are passed between scripts as arrays of values, so a script can reorder columns without an immediate failure. Create one CustomerRow type that mirrors the customer table and exposes the row's read, save, update, and remove operations. Scripts should obtain rows through a shared customer-table component and retain the row behavior during a transaction. The database mapping must remain explicit because the schema is owned by another system and cannot be reshaped into a richer business model. Existing reports may continue returning tabular records, but the row type is the only object permitted to contain persistence details for individual customers.

Decision: Should each database row be represented by an object that owns its own read and write operations, rather than repeating row mapping and SQL in transaction scripts?
proposition: Pattern 'row-data-gateway' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: row-data-gateway: Give each database row its own in-memory object that mirrors the row's columns and carries the row's own find, insert, update and delete operations, so all data-access code for a table lives in one place instead of being duplicated across the scripts that use it. Problem: SQL text, parameter binding and result-set mapping are re-derived inside every transaction script that touches a table, while the in-memory objects those scripts work with know nothing about the database. No single place knows how one row is read, written and deleted, so a schema change ripples through every script and every new query is another chance to get parameterisation and type conversion wrong.

Candidate: dao-factory: Hand out a coherent family of data access objects bound to the store this deployment actually runs on: one factory object per store (the Factory Method form when there is a single store, the Abstract Factory form when stores vary) owns driver, dialect, connection and pooling policy, so the store choice is made once at the composition root and business components never name a vendor. proposition: Pattern 'producer-consumer' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: producer-consumer: Insert a bounded buffer between producers and consumers of work items so the two sides run concurrently at their own rates, the buffer absorbs bursts and slack, and its bound turns overload into backpressure, queueing or an explicit drop policy instead of unbounded growth. Problem: Production and consumption proceed at different rates: a fast producer outruns its consumer and either drops items or grows a backlog until memory runs out, a slow producer leaves consumers idle, and bursts arrive faster than they can be processed.
