The team wants product domain behavior, validation, and persistence access to remain in one compact component because there is no meaningful object graph or multi-row invariant. Database transactions may still be controlled by the application service, but the chosen persistence arrangement should keep SQL and table details out of HTTP handlers and presentation code. A recent incident saw a deactivation endpoint bypass the shared sort-order check with its own inline SQL, leaving gaps in the public listing until editors re-saved each row by hand.

Decision: Choose where row state, row-local behavior, and CRUD operations belong for a simple catalog category.
proposition: Pattern 'deadline-propagation' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: deadline-propagation: Bound the total time and work of a logical request by carrying one deadline through its whole call tree: every hop forwards the remaining budget and the cancellation signal instead of inventing a fresh timeout, so work that can no longer succeed is abandoned at every level. Problem: A request fans out into a chain or tree of downstream calls and each hop applies its own timeout: the end-to-end latency budget becomes the sum of N independent timeouts, servers keep working after the originating client has given up, and cancellation never reaches the deeper work - resources are consumed producing answers nobody will read.

The Policy Administration system edits claims across several repositories and service methods. Every request must acquire the relevant data protection before reading or changing it and release it only after the request completes. Today, controllers and repository helpers acquire guards inconsistently: some report paths acquire them, scheduled jobs do not, and a newly added endpoint can forget the required step. Unit tests pass because they exercise methods sequentially, while concurrent users occasionally observe a protected record during an unfinished operation or trigger a late conflict after expensive work. The design must make it impossible for an application method to omit the acquisition, and it must keep the guard active across all database calls made during the business operation. A central request pipeline or shared application supertype is being considered so that acquisition and release are enforced uniformly, including for non-HTTP entry points.

Decision: Place acquisition and release of required data protection in a mandatory framework or shared supertype boundary so every business operation follows the same policy.
proposition: Pattern 'implicit-lock' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: implicit-lock: Make the framework or layer-supertype code that every business operation must pass through acquire and release the locks, so no application method can forget an acquisition and silently invalidate the concurrency policy. Problem: A locking scheme has no gaps only if every path that touches a lockable item acquires its lock: one forgotten acquisition, one lock released too early or too late, makes the whole offline concurrency strategy useless. Because the error shows up only under concurrent conflicting sessions, it survives unit tests, code review and single-user manual testing.

proposition: Pattern 'pessimistic-offline-lock' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: pessimistic-offline-lock: Prevent conflicts between concurrent business transactions by making each one acquire an explicit, persisted lock on the data before it starts to use it, so that once work begins it is almost certain to complete without a concurrency conflict. Candidate: coarse-grained-lock: Give a cluster of objects that must change together one shared lock — held on the cluster's root object, on a lock entry keyed by that root, or on a version token the root carries — so a caller locks one thing instead of discovering and locking every member. proposition: Pattern 'optimistic-offline-lock' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: optimistic-offline-lock: Let a business transaction span several system transactions without holding a database lock by validating at commit that the records it read are still unchanged - and aborting or retrying the business transaction when they are not. Holding a database lock for the whole session is not acceptable because the session lasts minutes or hours while a conflict is unlikely.

proposition: Pattern 'aggregate' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: aggregate: Define a transactional consistency boundary around domain objects: one root entity is the sole externally reachable entry point, owns internal entities and value objects, and is the only object application code modifies directly; each command loads and commits one root instance, while other roots are referenced by identity and coordinated separately. Problem: Business rules relate several objects at once - an order total that must stay within a credit limit, allocations that must never exceed stock - but if every object is writable on its own, no single place can enforce the rule at commit time. Concurrent callers interleave, persistence updates parts separately, and the invariant survives only while every caller remembers to check it; the model needs one owner and one atomic persistence boundary.

proposition: Pattern 'cancellation-token' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: cancellation-token: Give a caller-owned operation tree a one-way request to stop: pass a read-only cancellation signal through every cancellable call, observe it at safe points, clean up what was acquired, and report a distinct cancelled outcome without pretending that cooperative cancellation is forced termination. Problem: A request handler, background job or UI action starts work that fans out into nested calls, tasks or threads. When the caller disconnects, a deadline expires, the user presses stop or a sibling fails, merely abandoning the result leaves already-started work burning CPU, holding connections and calling dependencies. Force-killing a thread or process can interrupt a critical section and corrupt shared state, while a signal that is not propagated or observed cannot stop the call tree or make its cleanup visible to the joiner.

proposition: Pattern 'watchman' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: watchman: Detect that a message flow has gone silent - not that a message failed - and tell a responsible person or system within a bounded time by comparing each flow's arrivals against the cadence its business deadline implies. The Policy Administration system edits claims across several repositories and service methods. Every request must acquire the relevant data protection before reading or changing it and release it only after the request completes. Today, controllers and repository helpers acquire guards inconsistently: some report paths acquire them, scheduled jobs do not, and a newly added endpoint can forget the required step. Unit tests pass because they exercise methods sequentially, while concurrent users occasionally observe a protected record during an unfinished operation or trigger a late conflict after expensive work. The design must make it impossible for an application method to omit the acquisition, and it must keep the guard active across all database calls made during the business operation. A central request pipeline or shared application supertype is being considered so that acquisition and release are enforced uniformly, including for non-HTTP entry points.

Decision: Place acquisition and release of required data protection in a mandatory framework or shared supertype boundary so every business operation follows the same policy.

Problem: Inbound data - HTTP requests, RPC messages, queue events, protocol frames - is validated inside each handler: every new endpoint re-implements parsing, range and encoding checks, rules drift between handlers, and some paths end up with no validation at all. proposition: Pattern 'composed-method' is relevant to this decision. proposition: Pattern 'state-colocation' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: state-colocation: Keep each piece of presentation state in the component closest to where it is used — down to the single component that owns and reads it — instead of hoisting it to a common ancestor or a global store, so that a change touches only the smallest part of the view that can observe it. Problem: State gets hoisted 'just in case': a value only one component reads is lifted to the screen or application root, or pushed into one global store, because someone may want it later. The consequences are components that receive props they never read, updates that invalidate far more of the UI than the value's actual consumers, an unclear owner for each value, and tests that must assemble the whole state container to exercise one field. The recurring decision is where a new piece of state should live: keep it at the smallest scope that actually needs it.

The Inventory platform persists more than sixty domain classes, including Product, Warehouse, StockMovement, Supplier, and PurchaseOrder. Each class contains state and business behavior but no SQL, save methods, or storage-related annotations. Field-to-column declarations live in externally supplied YAML files that identify tables, columns, generated identifiers, null handling, and enum conversions; a single MappingEngine reads and writes every class from those declarations. The build also generates descriptor files from an existing PostgreSQL schema so that production can remain schema-first, and deployment-specific descriptor sets may target different column layouts without recompiling domain code. A schema change must require editing a declaration or regenerating descriptors, not editing every affected class, and domain unit tests must be able to construct entities without the mapping engine or a database.

Decision: Should field-to-column correspondence and conversion rules be held in external declarations consumed by one generic engine, keeping persistence details out of the domain classes?
proposition: Pattern 'metadata-mapping' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: metadata-mapping: Holds the correspondence between object fields and database columns in metadata - annotations, mapping files, table objects, struct tags or a schema definition - so that one generic mapping engine performs the reads, inserts and updates instead of hand-written per-class mapper code. Problem: Every class that is persisted needs the same tedious, repetitive code: which field maps to which column, which key is generated, how nulls and types convert, what the table is called. Written per class it is duplicated everywhere and drifts from the schema; the catalogue's trigger is that the mapping knowledge belongs in metadata or configuration, duplicated in no class.

proposition: Pattern 'lightweight-entity' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: lightweight-entity: Keep domain entity classes free of persistence logic - no queries, no save/delete, no table knowledge - so that all knowledge of how the object maps to the store lives in metadata (annotations, mapping files, tags, descriptor tables) that a generic mapper consumes. Problem: When each entity class carries its own mapping code (table name, column list, SQL, load/save methods) the same schema knowledge is duplicated in every class, the domain model is welded to the store, and a schema change becomes an edit inside the model. Moving the mapping out then raises the reverse problem: the entities must be dumb enough for a generic mapper to drive them, i.e. they may carry state and domain behaviour but no persistence behaviour.

proposition: Pattern 'extensible-visitor' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: extensible-visitor: Keep the visitor open on both axes at once - new element kinds and new operations arrive without editing or recompiling any visitor that already exists - by giving every visitor a default method that catches element kinds it was not written for, introducing extended element kinds under an intermediate base whose accept hooks overload (not override) accept, and extending an operation by subclassing the existing concrete visitor so it inherits every case it already handled. Problem: A classic Visitor is cheap in one direction only: a new operation is a new visitor, but a new element kind forces every visitor to grow one more method, so shipped visitors must be edited and redeployed. The trigger is an element hierarchy that is extended by parties who do not own the operations - language dialects, plugin node types, versioned grammars, third-party message formats - where the existing operations must keep working unchanged on the extended structure.

proposition: Pattern 'characterization-test' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: characterization-test: Pin the actual, currently deployed behaviour of existing code in committed reference artefacts (golden masters) so that a later edit can be distinguished from an accidental regression even when nobody can say what the code is supposed to do. Problem: You must change code whose behaviour is undocumented, surprising or only known to production: there is no specification to test against, and tests written from intended behaviour would take too long and silently encode guesses as fact. The safety net therefore has to be built from observed behaviour: replay a corpus of real inputs through the untouched subject, capture everything observable, commit the result as the reference, and let every later run diff against it - pinning what the code does today before changing how it does it.

Candidate: stub: Replace a collaborator with a test-specific stand-in that returns canned answers, so the component under test can be driven down paths - success, empty, error, timeout - that the real collaborator cannot be made to produce on demand. proposition: Pattern 'copy-and-swap' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: copy-and-swap: Implement assignment (and any in-place state replacement) so that a failure while producing the new state leaves the target untouched: build the complete replacement off to the side, commit it with operations that cannot fail, and let the temporary's destructor or the garbage collector release the old state. Problem: A hand-written assignment has to tear down the old state and build a copy of the new one, but only the build can fail: destroying before allocating exposes a half-updated object when the allocation or the element copy throws, and the usual repair -- a self-assignment check plus manual rollback -- duplicates the per-member copying that already lives in the copy constructor. The trigger is an assignment (or, in a garbage-collected language, an in-place state replacement) that must satisfy the strong exception guarantee: either it completes, or the target still holds its previous value.

WorkforceRegistry manages Employee, Engineer, Manager, and Contractor records from a stable domain hierarchy. Every worker shares common details such as name, hire date, department, and status, while each kind has mandatory additional details: engineers require a technical grade, managers require a team size, and contractors require a supplier and contract end date. The registry must frequently load workers across all kinds for directory searches, reporting, and authorization, and callers commonly request all workers of a particular kind. The hierarchy changes infrequently, but additions within a kind are routine. Decide the relational layout that preserves mandatory subtype-specific constraints, avoids duplicating shared attributes, and supports efficient polymorphic retrieval without requiring application code to merge records from several tables.

Decision: Decide how to persist a small, stable worker hierarchy with mostly shared attributes, mandatory kind-specific fields, and frequent retrieval across all kinds.
proposition: Pattern 'single-table-inheritance' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: single-table-inheritance: Map an inheritance hierarchy of classes onto one shared table whose columns are the union of all classes' fields, using a type code (discriminator) column to decide which class each row instantiates, so polymorphic reads need no joins. Problem: A class hierarchy must be persisted, the hierarchy is small and its classes share most fields, and cross-class queries or polymorphic loads are frequent: mapping each class to its own table would force a join per level on almost every read, while the subtypes differ by only a few columns.

proposition: Pattern 'class-table-inheritance' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: class-table-inheritance: Represent an inheritance hierarchy relationally with one table per class: each table stores only the attributes the class itself declares, and each subclass table's primary key doubles as a foreign key to its superclass table, so every attribute is stored exactly once and the schema itself enforces that every subtype row is also a base-class row. AttachmentService is one of several services in a document-processing platform. Every request may include a tenant document identifier, but only about five percent request an archived attachment. AttachmentService currently creates a GatewaySession during construction, validates remote credentials, and reserves a channel from the archive gateway. Session establishment takes roughly 1.5 seconds, the shared gateway permits only twelve channels, and each service instance currently consumes one even when no attachment is ever requested. Credential problems in the archive subsystem also prevent otherwise healthy instances from passing startup checks. The public call to retrieveAttachment must remain unchanged for callers. The service should establish at most one session when the first archive request arrives, reuse it for later requests, synchronize concurrent first calls, and release it during controlled shutdown. Creating the session after a request arrives is acceptable even though the first such request becomes slower. The metadata service must remain operational when the archive gateway is unavailable, and a one-shot command that definitely reads one attachment should not retain a channel longer than necessary.

Decision: Decide whether the archive gateway session should be acquired during service construction or only when an attachment is first requested, while preventing duplicate concurrent acquisitions and preserving shutdown behavior.

AttachmentService is one of several services in a document-processing platform. Every request may include a tenant document identifier, but only about five percent request an archived attachment. AttachmentService currently creates a GatewaySession during construction, validates remote credentials, and reserves a channel from the archive gateway. Session establishment takes roughly 1.5 seconds, the shared gateway permits only twelve channels, and each service instance currently consumes one even when no attachment is ever requested. Credential problems in the archive subsystem also prevent otherwise healthy instances from passing startup checks. The public call to retrieveAttachment must remain unchanged for callers. The service should establish at most one session when the first archive request arrives, reuse it for later requests, synchronize concurrent first calls, and release it during controlled shutdown. Creating the session after a request arrives is acceptable even though the first such request becomes slower. The metadata service must remain operational when the archive gateway is unavailable, and a one-shot command that definitely reads one attachment should not retain a channel longer than necessary.

The Admin Control Plane performs role grants, policy changes, and signing-key rotations through the Configuration Service. The current workers append JSON lines to a local file, can rotate that file, and run with enough permission to rewrite or remove earlier records. Security and Internal Audit must be able to prove after an incident that privileged activity was attributable and that no event was silently deleted, reordered, or truncated. The records must include denied and failed attempts as well as successful changes. A separate Verification Service must be able to validate the history without trusting the worker that produced it, and the key used to authenticate records must not be stored beside the writable event file. A managed evidence store is not available, so the design must define how records are written, linked, and independently checked across multiple files and rotations.

Decision: Choose whether to replace privileged-activity files with a verifiable event sequence whose integrity can be checked independently by a party that cannot rewrite the source records.

proposition: Pattern 'poison-pill' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: poison-pill: Terminate queue consumers cooperatively by sending a reserved sentinel message that each consumer recognises as "no more work", so consumers drain the backlog and exit without a separate control channel or forced cancellation. Problem: A producer-consumer system must shut down, but its consumers block on an empty queue and the queue has no built-in "no more items" signal: callers either kill the workers mid-work and drop buffered items, or leave them blocked forever. Production has ended - how do the consumers learn that while still processing everything already queued?

Candidate: bulkhead: Partition finite shared capacity at the failure domain (dependency, tenant, priority class, or cell) into independently bounded pools or permits, with an explicit queue and saturation policy, so one slow, saturated, or failing participant cannot consume capacity reserved for others. Candidate: durable-subscriber: Keep a publish-subscribe consumer's place while it is offline: the broker binds a stable subscription identity to retained messages or a committed position, then resumes delivery after reconnect until retention, expiry, or quota says the backlog is no longer available. Candidate: request-reply: Let a sender obtain a result or a domain error from an asynchronous or remote receiver by pairing each request with a correlated reply, and give the missing reply a defined outcome: timeout, cancellation and disposal of late replies. Candidate: copy-and-swap: Implement assignment (and any in-place state replacement) so that a failure while producing the new state leaves the target untouched: build the complete replacement off to the side, commit it with operations that cannot fail, and let the temporary's destructor or the garbage collector release the old state. The Admin Control Plane performs role grants, policy changes, and signing-key rotations through the Configuration Service. The current workers append JSON lines to a local file, can rotate that file, and run with enough permission to rewrite or remove earlier records. Security and Internal Audit must be able to prove after an incident that privileged activity was attributable and that no event was silently deleted, reordered, or truncated. The records must include denied and failed attempts as well as successful changes. A separate Verification Service must be able to validate the history without trusting the worker that produced it, and the key used to authenticate records must not be stored beside the writable event file. A managed evidence store is not available, so the design must define how records are written, linked, and independently checked across multiple files and rotations.

Decision: Choose whether to replace privileged-activity files with a verifiable event sequence whose integrity can be checked independently by a party that cannot rewrite the source records.
proposition: Pattern 'dependency-injection' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: dependency-injection: Supply an object with the collaborators it needs from the outside — through its constructor, its setters/properties, or a dedicated injection interface — so it never constructs or looks a dependency up itself and every wiring decision is made once, in a composition root or container. Problem: An object that creates its own collaborators hard-wires a concrete class, a construction recipe and often a lifetime into itself: swapping the implementation for a test double, a second deployment or a new platform means editing the class, and the dependency graph stays invisible in the API. The recurring trigger is exactly the catalog's rule: an object should not create what it depends on — the caller, the framework or the composition root decides, and hands the dependency in.

proposition: Pattern 'producer-consumer' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: producer-consumer: Insert a bounded buffer between producers and consumers of work items so the two sides run concurrently at their own rates, the buffer absorbs bursts and slack, and its bound turns overload into backpressure, queueing or an explicit drop policy instead of unbounded growth. Problem: Production and consumption proceed at different rates: a fast producer outruns its consumer and either drops items or grows a backlog until memory runs out, a slow producer leaves consumers idle, and bursts arrive faster than they can be processed. Wiring the two sides together directly also couples their lifetimes and schedules - a synchronous hand-off makes the faster side wait for the slower - so neither side can be scaled, restarted or tested on its own.

Candidate: composed-method: Divide the work into methods that each perform one identifiable task, written as a short outline of invocations in which every operation sits at the same level of abstraction, so a reader grasps the task top-down and every change lands on one small, named step. Candidate: extensible-visitor: Keep the visitor open on both axes at once - new element kinds and new operations arrive without editing or recompiling any visitor that already exists - by giving every visitor a default method that catches element kinds it was not written for, introducing extended element kinds under an intermediate base whose accept hooks overload (not override) accept, and extending an operation by subclassing the existing concrete visitor so it inherits every case it already handled. Problem: A classic Visitor is cheap in one direction only: a new operation is a new visitor, but a new element kind forces every visitor to grow one more method, so shipped visitors must be edited and redeployed. Candidate: cursor-pagination: Bound what a read boundary returns for a large or changing ordered collection by sending one page plus an opaque continuation token that pins the filter and ordering, so clients advance deterministically without offsets and without watching rows move under them. The Extension Runtime gives an untrusted Code Review Plugin access to a workspace file, a diagnostic client, and a small configuration service. The plugin receives live objects rather than copied data, and it may retain those references for the lifetime of its process. The Plugin Supervisor must be able to disable the plugin's access when the extension is unloaded or violates policy, without asking the plugin to release anything. Other extensions must continue using the same underlying workspace and services after that action, so those targets cannot be destroyed. Existing operations may finish, but every later call made through the plugin's access must fail. The control must reside with the supervisor and take effect even if the plugin ignores an unload event or continues running in a background thread.

Decision: Select the mechanism that lets the Extension Supervisor terminate all future access held by an untrusted plugin while preserving the underlying workspace and services for everyone else.
proposition: Pattern 'revocable-forwarder' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: revocable-forwarder: Let a collaborator use an object through a forwarding wrapper that the grantor can switch off at any time through a separate control, so authority already handed out can be withdrawn without destroying the target and without the collaborator's cooperation. Problem: A capability is just a reference, so once a collaborator has been given access to an object there is no built-in way to take it back: the grantor can destroy the object, ask the collaborator to stop, or leave the access standing. The recurring decision is how to grant access that is bounded in time - temporary use of a file, a service object, a session, an account - while keeping a control that only the grantor holds.

proposition: Pattern 'membrane' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: membrane: Wrap every capability that crosses a subsystem boundary - arguments passed in and objects, callbacks or results handed back out - so a restriction on the interface applies transitively instead of guarding only the first reference, and the whole wrapped set can be revoked at once. Problem: An interface hands out a reference that carries a restriction - a read-only view, a tenant-scoped directory, a sandboxed plugin API - but the objects exchanged through it stay raw: a callee that returns a capability to itself, or stores a capability the caller passed in, gives one side an unguarded route around the restriction. Guarding only the initial reference (an attenuated or revocable forwarder) therefore fails exactly when the far side cannot be trusted to respect the attenuation.

proposition: Pattern 'deadline-propagation' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: deadline-propagation: Bound the total time and work of a logical request by carrying one deadline through its whole call tree: every hop forwards the remaining budget and the cancellation signal instead of inventing a fresh timeout, so work that can no longer succeed is abandoned at every level. Problem: A request fans out into a chain or tree of downstream calls and each hop applies its own timeout: the end-to-end latency budget becomes the sum of N independent timeouts, servers keep working after the originating client has given up, and cancellation never reaches the deeper work - resources are consumed producing answers nobody will read.

Login currently establishes a role claim that many controllers trust for the remainder of the request, and several methods repeat slightly different ownership checks. The Platform Security team will separate business authorization from the resource services. proposition: Pattern 'version-number' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: version-number: Store a version token alongside each persistent record and make every write assert the token it read, so a write computed from stale data fails as a detectable conflict instead of silently overwriting a newer value. Problem: Two sessions read the same record, both edit it, and the later write wins: the earlier update vanishes without any error (the lost update). Once the read-modify-write spans more than one system transaction the database cannot tell 'this is the record I read' from 'this record changed under me', so no code path can notice in time - unless the record itself carries a per-row token that changes on every write and the write tests that token before committing.

proposition: Pattern 'copy-on-write' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: copy-on-write: Let several handles of a value share one expensive body until the first write, which clones that body privately, so copying costs a pointer instead of a deep copy while every handle still behaves as an independent value. Northstar operates a browser application, a mobile API, and a service-to-service endpoint behind one gateway. Browser requests carry a server-side session cookie, mobile requests carry a signed OIDC token, and service requests use mTLS client certificates. The gateway's Edge Security component validates each credential, while controllers, tenant filters, and audit interceptors must consume the same stable user identifier, tenant identifier, roles, and authentication time. None of those downstream components may parse tokens, read certificate fields, or depend on the credential format. Expired, malformed, incorrectly addressed, and untrusted credentials must all produce a consistent denial without exposing which verification step failed to the caller. A contractor who appears in both the corporate directory and the customer identity provider must still resolve to one acting account. The engineering decision is where to establish this credential-independent identity representation and how to ensure every entry path produces it before request handling begins.

Decision: Decide whether to establish one normalized acting-user representation at the trust boundary so all downstream authorization, tenant filtering, and audit code consume identical identity attributes regardless of credential format.
proposition: Pattern 'subject-descriptor' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: subject-descriptor: Give every part of a system one credential-independent representation of the entity on whose behalf an operation is performed, so authorization, audit and domain code can ask who is acting and read that subject's security-relevant attributes without knowing which credential format proved it. Problem: Authentication arrives in many formats - password plus session cookie, OIDC/JWT, mTLS certificate, API key, Kerberos ticket, signed assertion - while every decision downstream only needs the same few facts: a stable identifier for the acting subject and its roles or attributes. Without a common representation each consumer parses the credential itself, or a raw token or user-record type is threaded through the layers: consumers are coupled to one mechanism, two layers can disagree about who the caller is, attributes are re-derived per component, and values that were never verified get treated

proposition: Pattern 'guarded-suspension' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: guarded-suspension: Suspend a state-dependent method call inside the object that owns the state until another thread makes its guard predicate true, so callers neither poll nor get refused while the object is temporarily not ready. Problem: A method may only proceed while a precondition over shared state holds - a buffer is non-empty, a pool still has a free lease, a session is authenticated, a worker has a task - and that state is produced by another thread at an unknown time. The recurring decision is what the caller should do while the guard is false: refusing the request would drop work the application still needs, forcing the transition would break the object's invariants, and polling wastes a core and still races. Guarded suspension answers it by waiting on a condition the object itself owns, and by making that wait atomic

Candidate: functional-options: Keep a constructor's required parameter list fixed while optional settings arrive as named configuration functions that are applied in order over built-in defaults, so the API can grow without breaking callers and without exposing a mutable configuration object. proposition: Pattern 'monitor-object' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: monitor-object: Serialise concurrent method invocations on a shared object by giving the object its own lock and condition variables, so that only one method executes inside it at a time and methods that cannot proceed wait cooperatively instead of polling. Problem: Objects shared by several threads expose their state through ordinary methods, and nothing stops concurrent callers from interleaving inside those methods, corrupting the invariants they were written to maintain. The race is then papered over with ad-hoc locking, sleeps and busy-wait loops scattered through client code. Candidate: table-data-gateway: Confine every SQL statement that touches one table or view inside a single gateway object whose methods take and return plain record structures, so that no other code contains SQL for that table and rows cross the boundary as data rather than as domain objects. Candidate: implicit-lock: Make the framework or layer-supertype code that every business operation must pass through acquire and release the locks, so no application method can forget an acquisition and silently invalidate the concurrency policy. The Claims mobile application and ClaimsProvider service are built and released by separate teams. The mobile client relies on specific interactions that are not obvious from the service documentation: it sends a GET /claims/{id} request with an X-Tenant-ID header, expects a particular status when a claim has no settlement, and depends on the exact field names and value types in the response. The provider team wants to replace its database access layer without requiring a shared staging system or coordinating releases with the mobile team. The mobile team's existing request-level tests already exercise these expectations. The provider must run those concrete interaction checks inside its own build before merging an internal change, and the mobile release pipeline must not need access to a live provider deployment. A shared end-to-end environment is unavailable, while the provider can expose the relevant endpoint in a local verification process.

Decision: Decide how the ClaimsProvider build will verify the concrete API interactions relied upon by the independently released Claims client.

Candidate: cancellation-token: Give a caller-owned operation tree a one-way request to stop: pass a read-only cancellation signal through every cancellable call, observe it at safe points, clean up what was acquired, and report a distinct cancelled outcome without pretending that cooperative cancellation is forced termination. Candidate: anti-corruption-layer: Protect a downstream bounded context from a foreign model by making one explicitly owned boundary translate calls, data and failure semantics into the downstream language; unlike a mere wrapper, an anti-corruption layer prevents foreign concepts from becoming domain concepts. Candidate: update-method: Give every live object one self-contained per-frame step and let a single driver call each object's step every frame, so behaviour advances one frame at a time while input and rendering stay responsive. Every route except login and health must accept either a browser session cookie or a mobile JWT, and token issuers are expected to change independently of business code. Candidate: cache-aside: Place the cache beside the authoritative store and make the application own the protocol: look up the cache first, load the entry from the store on a miss and populate it with a TTL, and invalidate the entry right after each write to the store - so repeated reads stay cheap while the store, never the cache, decides what is true. The API gateway currently passes requests directly to Spring controllers, so each controller checks credentials differently and several exceptional routes bypass checks. A GatewaySecurityComponent must verify credentials through replaceable SessionCredentialVerifier and JwtCredentialVerifier components, reject invalid or absent credentials, and place an immutable customer identifier and tenant identifier into request-scoped context before routing. The gateway must also preserve public-route exceptions without allowing controllers to override a failed decision. Operations wants one auditable place to observe every authentication attempt and rotate credential mechanisms without modifying controllers. The decision is where identity verification and request-context population should occur while keeping controllers unaware of credential formats.

Decision: Choose the request-processing location and component boundary that verify credentials for every protected route and populate request-scoped identity before controller dispatch, while preserving explicit public-route exceptions.
proposition: Pattern 'bulkhead' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: bulkhead: Partition finite shared capacity at the failure domain (dependency, tenant, priority class, or cell) into independently bounded pools or permits, with an explicit queue and saturation policy, so one slow, saturated, or failing participant cannot consume capacity reserved for others. Problem: Several dependencies or tenants share thread, connection, worker, or permit pools. When one becomes slow, leaky, or overloaded, its calls hold shared slots and fill shared queues, so unrelated work queues and fails behind it; the design needs a boundary that contains resource exhaustion without pretending to isolate CPU, network, or server-side limits that remain shared.

Candidate: assertion: Express a model object's preconditions, postconditions and class invariants as executable, side-effect-free predicates at the operations that must uphold them, so a broken contract fails at its boundary instead of remaining a comment or surfacing later as corrupt state. proposition: Pattern 'version-number' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: version-number: Store a version token alongside each persistent record and make every write assert the token it read, so a write computed from stale data fails as a detectable conflict instead of silently overwriting a newer value. Problem: Two sessions read the same record, both edit it, and the later write wins: the earlier update vanishes without any error (the lost update). Once the read-modify-write spans more than one system transaction the database cannot tell 'this is the record I read' from 'this record changed under me', so no code path can notice in time - unless the record itself carries a per-row token that changes on every write and the write tests that token before committing.

HarborPay lets treasury specialists create wire disbursements above 25,000 USD, but releasing those wires is a separate sensitive action. A specialist who creates a payment must not be able to approve or release that same payment, even by signing in through another browser or using an administrator account. The Payments Console records the creator, the approver, and the releaser separately; the Workflow Service rejects a release when the approving identity equals the creating identity, and a second authorized treasury specialist must approve before the Release Adapter can contact the banking partner. Service accounts used by the console and release adapter are not permitted to stand in for either human reviewer, and automated reconciliation cannot release a pending payment. If the approval record cannot be retrieved or its signer cannot be verified, the payment remains pending. The ledger keeps the full history of both human actions and prevents either reviewer from editing the other reviewer's decision.

Decision: Should a wire above the threshold require approval and release by different treasury specialists before any funds can be sent?

Candidate: fail-safe-defaults: Make denial the default outcome of every access decision, so that access exists only where it has been explicitly granted and no missing rule, missing identity or failed check can silently permit an operation. Candidate: make-illegal-states-unrepresentable: Encode each domain rule in the shape of the data type so that values violating the rule cannot be constructed at all, replacing scattered run-time validation and defensive checks with a model in which only legal states exist. proposition: Pattern 'applicative' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: applicative: Apply one pure function to several independent effectful computations, letting the chosen context instance fix the semantics of absence, failure, ordering, and concurrency; the combining structure is fixed before execution - that static shape is what enables batching, parallel scheduling, and static analysis - and an accumulating error instance reports every independent failure instead of short-circuiting on the first. Problem: You have several independent computations - parse this field, fetch that record, validate this quantity - and a pure function that combines their results, but each result lives inside a context such as Option, Either/Result, List, Promise/Task, or Validation. A bind/await chain can imply a dependency that does not exist, serialize work, or stop at the first failure; you need a fixed applicative structure that combines the values while leaving failure and scheduling policy to the chosen instance.

HarborPay lets treasury specialists create wire disbursements above 25,000 USD, but releasing those wires is a separate sensitive action. A specialist who creates a payment must not be able to approve or release that same payment, even by signing in through another browser or using an administrator account. The Payments Console records the creator, the approver, and the releaser separately; the Workflow Service rejects a release when the approving identity equals the creating identity, and a second authorized treasury specialist must approve before the Release Adapter can contact the banking partner. If the approval record cannot be retrieved or its signer cannot be verified, the payment remains pending. Candidate: recursive-descent-parser: Parse a small grammar by translating every rule directly into a function that consumes the tokens the rule matches and calls the functions of the rules it references, so the parser's control flow is the grammar itself and stays readable, debuggable and free of a code-generation step. AdminCredentialClient verifies an administrative challenge through a DeviceSession interface. Its verify method must open a session, write the exact challenge bytes, read a six-byte response, and close the session, in that order and exactly once each. The method exposes only a boolean result to its caller, while the actual device commands and their ordering have no other observable effect. Compliance requires the test to reject an open after write, a missing read, duplicate writes, or failure to close. Hardware is unavailable in the test environment, so the production device cannot be used. Decide how to provide a DeviceSession implementation that permits the client to complete its flow while making every protocol violation immediately visible to the test.

Candidate: mock: Replace a collaborator of the system under test with a test-specific object that is programmed with the expected calls and verifies them as they happen, so the interaction itself - not the resulting state - is what the test asserts. Problem: The expected interaction sequence is the behaviour under test: the outcome of the exercised method is not visible in the system under test's own state, and no observation point exposes the indirect outputs (the messages sent to collaborators) that the requirement is about. Candidate: cache-aside: Place the cache beside the authoritative store and make the application own the protocol: look up the cache first, load the entry from the store on a miss and populate it with a TTL, and invalidate the entry right after each write to the store - so repeated reads stay cheap while the store, never the cache, decides what is true. The administrative console exposes account review, session revocation, and role assignment screens through Selenium tests. Dozens of security regression tests currently locate labels and buttons, wait for status text, and interpret banner messages directly in each test body. A markup redesign therefore breaks the entire suite and obscures which user action each test performs. Create one wrapper for the account review screen and another for the session administration screen. Each wrapper owns all selectors, waits, and driver interactions, and exposes operations such as searchByEmail, openReview, assignLeastPrivilegeRole, and readOutcome. Tests should call those operations and assert on observable review results, while the wrappers remain responsible for synchronization and page-specific mechanics. The console has no reusable component already hiding these details, and the wrappers must not contain authorization policy decisions.

Decision: Choose whether to isolate console locators and interactions behind screen-specific test wrappers instead of embedding them in security regression tests.
proposition: Pattern 'page-object' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: page-object: Wrap each UI surface a test drives - a page or a significant component - in an object that exposes the services the surface offers and hides every locator, driver call and wait, so a UI change is absorbed by one class instead of by every test that touched the markup. Problem: A UI test that drives the automation API directly - find an element, type, click, wait, read text - keeps the page's locators and interaction mechanics in the test body: the same selector is repeated across dozens of tests, a markup change breaks them all at once, and a reader must reconstruct the page's structure to understand what the test does. The catalog's trigger: a UI change should touch one class, not fifty assertions.

The administrative console exposes account review, session revocation, and role assignment screens through Selenium tests. Dozens of security regression tests currently locate labels and buttons, wait for status text, and interpret banner messages directly in each test body. A markup redesign therefore breaks the entire suite and obscures which user action each test performs. Create one wrapper for the account review screen and another for the session administration screen. Each wrapper owns all selectors, waits, and driver interactions, and exposes operations such as searchByEmail, openReview, assignLeastPrivilegeRole, and readOutcome. Tests should call those operations and assert on observable review results, while the wrappers remain responsible for synchronization and page-specific mechanics. The console has no reusable component already hiding these details, and the wrappers must not contain authorization policy decisions.

Candidate: arrange-act-assert: Structure a behaviour-focused test as an explicit arrange phase that establishes only its preconditions, one act interaction with the system under test, and an assert phase that checks the resulting observable outcome, so a failure localises to one behaviour without pretending that the runner enforces sequencing. Problem: A test that hides fixture work in hooks, interleaves several actions and assertions, or treats Arrange/Act/Assert labels as enforcement becomes a small workflow that is hard to read and hard to diagnose: the reader cannot tell which state is intentional, which call is under test, or which outcome failed.

proposition: Pattern 'event-message' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: event-message: Announce that something has happened by publishing an immutable, self-describing event message - a past fact that expects no reply - on a channel, so that any number of interested receivers can react without the producer knowing who they are or what they do. Problem: A component has completed a state change that other parts of the system care about, but it must not - and usually cannot - know which ones care. Calling each interested party directly couples the producer to every consumer, to their availability and to their processing order, and every new consumer (search index, audit, notification, analytics) forces a change and a redeploy in the producer. The trigger is open-ended interest: something changed, and the set of parties wanting to know is neither closed nor known at compile time.

proposition: Pattern 'coarse-grained-lock' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: coarse-grained-lock: Give a cluster of objects that must change together one shared lock — held on the cluster's root object, on a lock entry keyed by that root, or on a version token the root carries — so a caller locks one thing instead of discovering and locking every member. Problem: Changing one object really means changing a cluster: an edit that touches any member (a line item, an address, a child entity) has to be atomic with respect to the others, but a separate lock per member forces every caller to find and lock the whole set, makes the amount of locking grow with the object graph, and produces deadlocks whenever two callers acquire member locks in different orders.

proposition: Pattern 'functional-options' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: functional-options: Keep a constructor's required parameter list fixed while optional settings arrive as named configuration functions that are applied in order over built-in defaults, so the API can grow without breaking callers and without exposing a mutable configuration object. Problem: A constructor accumulates optional settings: every new setting changes the signature for all callers, zero values and booleans cannot be distinguished from 'not supplied', and a configuration struct has to be handed out (often by pointer, with nil meaning 'default') so callers can retain and mutate the very state the library depends on. The recurring decision is how to let an option set grow across the life of a public API while keeping meaningful defaults, source compatibility and a documented resolution rule for conflicting options.

proposition: Pattern 'applicative' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: applicative: Apply one pure function to several independent effectful computations, letting the chosen context instance fix the semantics of absence, failure, ordering, and concurrency; the combining structure is fixed before execution - that static shape is what enables batching, parallel scheduling, and static analysis - and an accumulating error instance reports every independent failure instead of short-circuiting on the first. Problem: You have several independent computations - parse this field, fetch that record, validate this quantity - and a pure function that combines their results, but each result lives inside a context such as Option, Either/Result, List, Promise/Task, or Validation. A bind/await chain can imply a dependency that does not exist, serialize work, or stop at the first failure; you need a fixed applicative structure that combines the values while leaving failure and scheduling policy to the chosen instance.

proposition: Pattern 'copy-and-swap' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: copy-and-swap: Implement assignment (and any in-place state replacement) so that a failure while producing the new state leaves the target untouched: build the complete replacement off to the side, commit it with operations that cannot fail, and let the temporary's destructor or the garbage collector release the old state. Problem: A hand-written assignment has to tear down the old state and build a copy of the new one, but only the build can fail: destroying before allocating exposes a half-updated object when the allocation or the element copy throws, and the usual repair -- a self-assignment check plus manual rollback -- duplicates the per-member copying that already lives in the copy constructor. The trigger is an assignment (or, in a garbage-collected language, an in-place state replacement) that must satisfy the strong exception guarantee: either it completes, or the target still holds its previous value.

Candidate: anti-corruption-layer: Protect a downstream bounded context from a foreign model by making one explicitly owned boundary translate calls, data and failure semantics into the downstream language; unlike a mere wrapper, an anti-corruption layer prevents foreign concepts from becoming domain concepts. Candidate: request-reply: Let a sender obtain a result or a domain error from an asynchronous or remote receiver by pairing each request with a correlated reply, and give the missing reply a defined outcome: timeout, cancellation and disposal of late replies. Candidate: cache-aside: Place the cache beside the authoritative store and make the application own the protocol: look up the cache first, load the entry from the store on a miss and populate it with a TTL, and invalidate the entry right after each write to the store - so repeated reads stay cheap while the store, never the cache, decides what is true. The recurring decision is where the read path looks first, when a miss may populate the entry, and what a write must do so the cached copy stops lying.

Candidate: cursor-pagination: Bound what a read boundary returns for a large or changing ordered collection by sending one page plus an opaque continuation token that pins the filter and ordering, so clients advance deterministically without offsets and without watching rows move under them. Dozens of security regression tests currently locate labels and buttons, wait for status text, and interpret banner messages directly in each test body. CertificateGateway is a legacy production class used during service admission. It calls its own protected, non-final currentTimeMillis method to obtain the current instant and then decides whether a certificate is expired. The method is not an injected dependency and is invoked internally rather than supplied by the caller. The deployment has frozen the production source, so adding a constructor parameter, a clock field, or another test hook is not permitted. Existing tests can construct CertificateGateway without any external service, but they cannot reliably test the expiry boundary because the result changes with wall-clock time. The team needs a deterministic test that fixes the instant, exercises both sides of the expiry threshold, and confirms the admission result without changing release behavior. The key decision is how to establish a controllable time boundary around the inherited call while honoring the prohibition on production-source changes.

Decision: Decide how tests can control the internally invoked clock when production code cannot be altered to expose an injection point.
proposition: Pattern 'test-specific-subclass' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: test-specific-subclass: Make an otherwise untestable class testable by defining a test-only subclass that overrides the method reaching the unusable dependency (or exposes the internal state the test needs), so the boundary can be substituted and observed without putting test hooks into production code. Problem: A class that must be tested reaches its dependency through a call on itself - a self-call to a helper method, a field created inside the class, or a singleton/static lookup - so the test has no injection point: the collaborator cannot be replaced from outside, the indirect inputs cannot be controlled and the indirect outputs cannot be observed. Editing the production class to accept the dependency may be impossible (third-party or frozen code) or would introduce test logic into production.

The Payment Gateway receives an authorization request containing a customer identifier, amount, and currency. The Request Parser converts each field, the Account Policy checks whether the account is open, and the Ledger Reserve service enforces available balance and daily limit rules. Any of these stages may reject the request, and the gateway must return a machine-readable failure category, affected field, and diagnostic detail to the API adapter. The API adapter maps unknown-category failures to HTTP 500, but maps known business failures to 400, 409, or 422 responses. It must never infer a category by matching an error message, because downstream clients branch on the category to decide whether to correct the request, refresh an account, or contact support. A request that fails validation must not reach Ledger Reserve, and multiple field errors reported together must retain separate field identities. Design the boundary between Payment Gateway, Account Policy, Ledger Reserve, and API Adapter so every expected rejection reaches the adapter intact while genuine programming faults remain distinguishable from recoverable business failures.

Decision: Choose how each expected payment rejection is represented and propagated so its category and field survive the full parsing, validation, and reservation flow.
proposition: Pattern 'either' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: either: Encode the two outcomes of a fallible operation - a value-carrying success (Right/Ok) and a reason-carrying failure (Left/Err) - in one sum-type value, so a caller must destructure both branches before going further and failures cannot escape as exceptions, sentinel values or undocumented convention. Problem: An operation can fail in ways the caller must handle, but the failure channel is invisible in the signature: exceptions unwind past intermediate callers, where they get swallowed or merely logged, status codes and sentinels are silently ignored, and the reason for failure is flattened into a message string nobody can branch on.

proposition: Pattern 'applicative' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: applicative: Apply one pure function to several independent effectful computations, letting the chosen context instance fix the semantics of absence, failure, ordering, and concurrency; the combining structure is fixed before execution - that static shape is what enables batching, parallel scheduling, and static analysis - and an accumulating error instance reports every independent failure instead of short-circuiting on the first. Problem: You have several independent computations - parse this field, fetch that record, validate this quantity - and a pure function that combines their results, but each result lives inside a context such as Option, Either/Result, List, Promise/Task, or Validation. proposition: Pattern 'guarded-suspension' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: guarded-suspension: Suspend a state-dependent method call inside the object that owns the state until another thread makes its guard predicate true, so callers neither poll nor get refused while the object is temporarily not ready. Problem: A method may only proceed while a precondition over shared state holds - a buffer is non-empty, a pool still has a free lease, a session is authenticated, a worker has a task - and that state is produced by another thread at an unknown time. The recurring decision is what the caller should do while the guard is false: refusing the request would drop work the application still needs, forcing the transition would break the object's invariants, and polling wastes a core and still races. Our design system needs an accessible tab set whose selection rules cannot be bypassed. WorkspaceTabs must own the active tab, coordinate focus and keyboard navigation, and associate each trigger with its panel using stable IDs. A TabTrigger declares its key, label, and disabled state; a TabPanel declares the content associated with that key. Consumers will place these children together in their desired order, and the same selection must be visible to triggers, panels, and automation that checks the active state. Individual children must not keep their own selected flag, because that would allow two panels to appear active. The API also needs to reject duplicate keys, omit disabled triggers from arrow-key navigation, and expose the active key to an onChange callback. We want consumers to compose the family declaratively without passing the current key and update handlers through every descendant.

Decision: Choose how WorkspaceTabs, TabTrigger, and TabPanel share and enforce one active-tab state while allowing consumers to declare the family in ordered JSX.

proposition: Pattern 'producer-consumer' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: producer-consumer: Insert a bounded buffer between producers and consumers of work items so the two sides run concurrently at their own rates, the buffer absorbs bursts and slack, and its bound turns overload into backpressure, queueing or an explicit drop policy instead of unbounded growth. Problem: Production and consumption proceed at different rates: a fast producer outruns its consumer and either drops items or grows a backlog until memory runs out, a slow producer leaves consumers idle, and bursts arrive faster than they can be processed. proposition: Pattern 'table-data-gateway' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: table-data-gateway: Confine every SQL statement that touches one table or view inside a single gateway object whose methods take and return plain record structures, so that no other code contains SQL for that table and rows cross the boundary as data rather than as domain objects. proposition: Pattern 'function-composition' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: function-composition: Combine a chain of small unary transformations into one reusable function by sequencing them with a composition combinator (compose/pipe), so the order of the steps is stated once, every step stays independently testable, and the chain itself becomes a value that can be named, passed and reassembled. Candidate: composite-entity: Represent a cluster of related, dependent objects through one coarse-grained entity that owns them and persists and synchronises the whole graph as a single unit of work, so clients never reference, sequence, or save the parts themselves. Our design system needs an accessible tab set whose selection rules cannot be bypassed. WorkspaceTabs must own the active tab, coordinate focus and keyboard navigation, and associate each trigger with its panel using stable IDs. A TabTrigger declares its key, label, and disabled state; a TabPanel declares the content associated with that key. Consumers will place these children together in their desired order, and the same selection must be visible to triggers, panels, and automation that checks the active state. Individual children must not keep their own selected flag, because that would allow two panels to appear active. The API also needs to reject duplicate keys, omit disabled triggers from arrow-key navigation, and expose the active key to an onChange callback. We want consumers to compose the family declaratively without passing the current key and update handlers through every descendant.

Decision: Choose how WorkspaceTabs, TabTrigger, and TabPanel share and enforce one active-tab state while allowing consumers to declare the family in ordered JSX.

A spreadsheet calculation engine has an ExpressionParser, a FormulaCompiler, and a FormulaEvaluator. Users can define arithmetic, comparison, percentage, logical, assignment, ternary, indexing, and postfix operators, while plug-ins may register new operator tokens. Every operator has a declared precedence and association, and formulas must accept forms such as -value, a + b * c, x = y, flag ? yes : no, and value%. The current implementation contains many nearly identical expression functions, one for each precedence band, and adding an operator often requires changes in several branches. The language team wants all precedence and association information centralized in an operator registry, while still allowing each operator to have its own semantic handler in FormulaCompiler. Diagnostics must identify the operator and operand that failed, and parsing must remain deterministic and forward-only. The decision concerns expression parsing only; statement parsing is limited to assignment wrappers.

proposition: Pattern 'pratt-parser' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: pratt-parser: Parse expressions with many prefix, infix and postfix operators by associating a binding power and a handler with each token type, so precedence and associativity live in one rule table instead of one parsing function per precedence level. Problem: Operator precedence turns expression parsing into a ladder of near-identical functions - one per level - each of which must re-implement associativity, delegate to the next level for its operands, and be edited whenever an operator is added or moves. Grammars with prefix, infix, postfix and mixfix operators (ternary conditionals, assignment, calls, indexing, user-registered operators) make that ladder long, make associativity easy to get subtly wrong, and scatter the grammar across the parser so it cannot be read in one place.

proposition: Pattern 'recursive-descent-parser' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: recursive-descent-parser: Parse a small grammar by translating every rule directly into a function that consumes the tokens the rule matches and calls the functions of the rules it references, so the parser's control flow is the grammar itself and stays readable, debuggable and free of a code-generation step. Problem: A hand-written parser is the only option - no generator in the toolchain, or the grammar is a small DSL - yet the grammar is not a flat token sequence: alternatives must be chosen from lookahead, repetition must become a loop, and the natural grammar for expressions is left-recursive, which a top-down parser cannot translate directly. Without a disciplined mapping from rules to functions the parser degenerates into ad-hoc index arithmetic and exception-driven backtracking, and errors end up without positions.

Candidate: composed-method: Divide the work into methods that each perform one identifiable task, written as a short outline of invocations in which every operation sits at the same level of abstraction, so a reader grasps the task top-down and every change lands on one small, named step. proposition: Pattern 'option-maybe' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: option-maybe: Make the possible absence of a result part of the value and of the signature, so every caller has to decide what happens when nothing is there instead of meeting a null, a sentinel or a silently defaulted value at run time. A city-scale crowd simulation tracks approximately 20,000 pedestrians, 400 bicycles, and moving service vehicles. During each simulation tick, the CollisionBroadphase component asks which participants are within six meters of a pedestrian, the InfluenceField component finds objects inside a circular zone, and the CameraFocus component removes distant pedestrians from view. Each query currently scans every participant, causing millions of irrelevant distance calculations and pushing the tick beyond its 16 millisecond budget. The population is sparse outside dense plazas, so most comparisons involve a small neighborhood, but participants can cross map boundaries and may move substantially between ticks. The chosen organization must support frequent insertions, removals, and position changes while keeping local radius and rectangle queries practical. It must also preserve a stable participant identifier for the simulation state and avoid requiring exact global ordering of query results unless the caller requests it. The main decision is how participants should be stored and maintained so local searches examine nearby entities instead of the entire population.

Decision: Choose the data organization and maintenance strategy for participants that makes position-based neighborhood queries efficient despite frequent movement.
proposition: Pattern 'spatial-partition' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: spatial-partition: Store every object in a structure indexed by its position so that neighbourhood queries visit only the objects near a point or region instead of scanning the whole population. Problem: Queries that ask 'what is near this position?' - collision checks, proximity and aggro radii, culling, spatial analytics - repeatedly scan every object: each query is linear in the population and a whole simulation step becomes quadratic, even though every object interacts only with the few objects next to it.

proposition: Pattern 'data-locality' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: data-locality: Arrange data so the values a loop will process next are already in the cache lines it has fetched - contiguous arrays of values in processing order instead of pointer-linked objects, handles instead of references, hot fields separated from cold - so a hot loop streams through CPU cache instead of stalling on a fresh main-memory access per element. Candidate: update-method: Give every live object one self-contained per-frame step and let a single driver call each object's step every frame, so behaviour advances one frame at a time while input and rendering stay responsive. Candidate: monitor-object: Serialise concurrent method invocations on a shared object by giving the object its own lock and condition variables, so that only one method executes inside it at a time and methods that cannot proceed wait cooperatively instead of polling. A checkout screen in a retail application manages shipping details, payment selection, validation errors, a busy indicator, and retry behavior. Every user action currently updates several controls independently, so a payment timeout can leave the screen showing both a spinner and an editable form. The CheckoutFeature must expose one immutable snapshot containing a discriminated phase, the entered data, field errors, and pending operation details. Gestures such as selecting a shipping method, submitting the address, retrying payment, and returning to review are represented as explicit values. A pure transition function accepts the previous snapshot and one action and returns the next snapshot; rendering cannot write state. Unit tests must replay sequences such as an expired card followed by replacement details without constructing controls, and the action history must support an audit log. The same feature will later be rendered by the mobile application and a headless preview.

Decision: Choose how the checkout screen will represent all user interactions and derive one consistent, immutable screen snapshot through testable transitions.

Every user action currently updates several controls independently, so a payment timeout can leave the screen showing both a spinner and an editable form. The CheckoutFeature must expose one immutable snapshot containing a discriminated phase, the entered data, field errors, and pending operation details. Gestures such as selecting a shipping method, submitting the address, retrying payment, and returning to review are represented as explicit values. A pure transition function accepts the previous snapshot and one action and returns the next snapshot; rendering cannot write state. Unit tests must replay sequences such as an expired card followed by replacement details without constructing controls, and the action history must support an audit log. The same feature will later be rendered by the mobile application and a headless preview.

Decision: Choose how the checkout screen will represent all user interactions and derive one consistent, immutable screen snapshot through testable transitions.
proposition: Pattern 'container-component' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: container-component: Keep presentation state and its access to a data source in an outer wrapper component, so that the components rendering the markup stay stateless functions of the data they are handed. Problem: The same state, or the same data source, is needed by several components below a point in the tree: state ends up duplicated in siblings, intermediate components forward props they never use, and every new field forces edits through components that do not care about it.

proposition: Pattern 'version-number' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: version-number: Store a version token alongside each persistent record and make every write assert the token it read, so a write computed from stale data fails as a detectable conflict instead of silently overwriting a newer value. Problem: Two sessions read the same record, both edit it, and the later write wins: the earlier update vanishes without any error (the lost update). Once the read-modify-write spans more than one system transaction the database cannot tell 'this is the record I read' from 'this record changed under me', so no code path can notice in time - unless the record itself carries a per-row token that changes on every write and the write tests that token before committing.

proposition: Pattern 'request-reply' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: request-reply: Let a sender obtain a result or a domain error from an asynchronous or remote receiver by pairing each request with a correlated reply, and give the missing reply a defined outcome: timeout, cancellation and disposal of late replies. Problem: Messaging is one-way, but the sender frequently needs a return value or a domain error from the receiver before it can continue. Without an agreed reply destination, a way to match replies to requests, and a rule for what happens when no reply arrives, the caller either blocks forever, mis-associates the next reply with the wrong request, or accumulates pending state it never cleans up.

proposition: Pattern 'page-object' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: page-object: Wrap each UI surface a test drives - a page or a significant component - in an object that exposes the services the surface offers and hides every locator, driver call and wait, so a UI change is absorbed by one class instead of by every test that touched the markup. Problem: A UI test that drives the automation API directly - find an element, type, click, wait, read text - keeps the page's locators and interaction mechanics in the test body: the same selector is repeated across dozens of tests, a markup change breaks them all at once, and a reader must reconstruct the page's structure to understand what the test does. The catalog's trigger: a UI change should touch one class, not fifty assertions.

proposition: Pattern 'composite-entity' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: composite-entity: Represent a cluster of related, dependent objects through one coarse-grained entity that owns them and persists and synchronises the whole graph as a single unit of work, so clients never reference, sequence, or save the parts themselves. Coined for coarse-grained EJB business objects; its modern form is the aggregate root with cascading or owned mappings. Problem: A business concept clients treat as one thing (an order with its lines, a customer with addresses) is really a cluster of dependent objects, and persisting each part separately forces callers to know the parts, save them in the right order in the right transaction, delete the ones that left the relationship, and absorb a leaking physical schema. The catalog trigger: a cluster of related objects must persist and synchronise as one unit.

proposition: Pattern 'applicative' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: applicative: Apply one pure function to several independent effectful computations, letting the chosen context instance fix the semantics of absence, failure, ordering, and concurrency; the combining structure is fixed before execution - that static shape is what enables batching, parallel scheduling, and static analysis - and an accumulating error instance reports every independent failure instead of short-circuiting on the first. Problem: You have several independent computations - parse this field, fetch that record, validate this quantity - and a pure function that combines their results, but each result lives inside a context such as Option, Either/Result, List, Promise/Task, or Validation. A bind/await chain can imply a dependency that does not exist, serialize work, or stop at the first failure; you need a fixed applicative structure that combines the values while leaving failure and scheduling policy to the chosen instance.
