proposition: Pattern 'monitor-object' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: monitor-object: Serialise concurrent method invocations on a shared object by giving the object its own lock and condition variables, so that only one method executes inside it at a time and methods that cannot proceed wait cooperatively instead of polling. Problem: Objects shared by several threads expose their state through ordinary methods, and nothing stops concurrent callers from interleaving inside those methods, corrupting the invariants they were written to maintain. The race is then papered over with ad-hoc locking, sleeps and busy-wait loops scattered through client code. The recurring decision is whether the object itself should own the serialisation (and the scheduling) of its methods instead of leaving that discipline to every caller.

proposition: Pattern 'row-data-gateway' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: row-data-gateway: Give each database row its own in-memory object that mirrors the row's columns and carries the row's own find, insert, update and delete operations, so all data-access code for a table lives in one place instead of being duplicated across the scripts that use it. Problem: SQL text, parameter binding and result-set mapping are re-derived inside every transaction script that touches a table, while the in-memory objects those scripts work with know nothing about the database. No single place knows how one row is read, written and deleted, so a schema change ripples through every script and every new query is another chance to get parameterisation and type conversion wrong.

proposition: Pattern 'adapter' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: adapter: Present an existing component through the exact target contract its client already consumes, translating calls, results and boundary semantics without adding responsibilities or pretending a missing capability exists. Problem: An existing or foreign component has useful behaviour but speaks a different protocol: method names and signatures, data shapes, units, lifecycle, error model or sync/async contract do not satisfy the target. If every caller performs ad hoc conversion, semantics drift, vendor types leak and provider replacement becomes a cross-cutting rewrite; changing the adaptee or target may be impossible or too disruptive.

proposition: Pattern 'characterization-test' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: characterization-test: Pin the actual, currently deployed behaviour of existing code in committed reference artefacts (golden masters) so that a later edit can be distinguished from an accidental regression even when nobody can say what the code is supposed to do. Problem: You must change code whose behaviour is undocumented, surprising or only known to production: there is no specification to test against, and tests written from intended behaviour would take too long and silently encode guesses as fact. The safety net therefore has to be built from observed behaviour: replay a corpus of real inputs through the untouched subject, capture everything observable, commit the result as the reference, and let every later run diff against it - pinning what the code does today before changing how it does it.

proposition: Pattern 'revocable-forwarder' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: revocable-forwarder: Let a collaborator use an object through a forwarding wrapper that the grantor can switch off at any time through a separate control, so authority already handed out can be withdrawn without destroying the target and without the collaborator's cooperation. Problem: A capability is just a reference, so once a collaborator has been given access to an object there is no built-in way to take it back: the grantor can destroy the object, ask the collaborator to stop, or leave the access standing. Problem: A value with an expensive body (large buffer, collection, tree, document) is copied eagerly on assignment, argument passing and return even though most copies are never modified: time and memory are spent duplicating data that would have stayed identical. The naive fix - handing out one mutable object behind several handles - breaks the copy contract, and unrelated parts of the program then observe each other's writes.

An operations console combines modules for fleet telemetry, map display, alarm workflows, incident records, and audit reporting. Telemetry sources publish readings, workflow changes publish alarm transitions, and several modules consume both kinds of notifications. Modules are loaded and unloaded independently during rolling deployments. Today, every consumer locates every relevant source, registers separately, and duplicates cleanup logic, so a newly deployed module can begin receiving traffic before its dependencies are ready and shutdown can leave stale subscriptions. The console needs a single registration boundary that accepts source and consumer descriptions, owns the wiring and cleanup, and routes notifications without making telemetry or workflow modules aware of the specific displays and recorders attached to them. Registration failures must be isolated and observable rather than preventing unrelated modules from connecting.

Decision: Choose how notifications from multiple changing sources reach multiple independently deployed consumers without duplicating pairwise registration and cleanup.
proposition: Pattern 'event-aggregator' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: event-aggregator: Funnel the events of many source objects into one hub that owns the subscription wiring, so that subscribers register once with the aggregator instead of tracking down and registering with every publisher. Problem: Many components raise events and many components want to react: if every consumer registers directly with every producer, each consumer has to find the sources and subscribe to each event type separately, each producer accumulates knowledge of who listens, and both sides repeat the same registration and unsubscribe code at every pair. The trigger is a many-publisher / many-subscriber setting in which the wiring itself has become the maintenance problem.

Candidate: observer: Let a subject inform an open-ended set of dependents about its state changes through a one-way subscription, so the subject never has to know which objects react or how many there are. proposition: Pattern 'publisher-subscriber' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: publisher-subscriber: Decouple event producers from their consumers through an event channel — publishers announce events without knowing who receives them — so new consumers can be added, removed or redeployed without changing the producer. Problem: One component's state change or announcement concerns several independent consumers (another module, the UI, a cache, an audit log), the set of consumers is dynamic and changes independently of the producer, and wiring direct calls from producer to consumer would hard-wire identity, ordering and failure behaviour into the producer. The recurring decision is therefore how to broadcast the event to an unknown, changing set of interested parties; the catalog's use-when cell states it as decoupled multi-consumer notification, noting that at part level a Mediator or Observer usually suffices.

Candidate: mediator: Define an object that encapsulates how a set of objects interact, so that colleagues reference only that hub instead of each other and the coordination logic can vary independently of the objects it coordinates. proposition: Pattern 'composite-entity' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: composite-entity: Represent a cluster of related, dependent objects through one coarse-grained entity that owns them and persists and synchronises the whole graph as a single unit of work, so clients never reference, sequence, or save the parts themselves. Coined for coarse-grained EJB business objects; its modern form is the aggregate root with cascading or owned mappings. Problem: A business concept clients treat as one thing (an order with its lines, a customer with addresses) is really a cluster of dependent objects, and persisting each part separately forces callers to know the parts, save them in the right order in the right transaction, delete the ones that left the relationship, and absorb a leaking physical schema. The catalog trigger: a cluster of related objects must persist and synchronise as one unit.

proposition: Pattern 'identity-field' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: identity-field: Store the relational primary key inside the object so that an in-memory instance and its database row are recognised as the same entity across sessions, caches and process restarts, instead of relying on object identity. Problem: Mappers, identity maps and unit-of-work bookkeeping need a stable handle on every object: without a key carried by the object there is no way to tell whether two instances are the same row, which row an UPDATE or DELETE must touch, or what value a referring row should store - and loading the same row twice silently produces two divergent objects.

proposition: Pattern 'cursor-pagination' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: cursor-pagination: Bound what a read boundary returns for a large or changing ordered collection by sending one page plus an opaque continuation token that pins the filter and ordering, so clients advance deterministically without offsets and without watching rows move under them. Problem: A boundary must expose a collection that is too large to return at once and keeps changing while clients read it. Offset or page-number requests make the store count or scan everything up to the requested page, and concurrent inserts or deletes shift rows across page boundaries so consumers see duplicates or miss items; the server has no way to state where the sequence should resume.

proposition: Pattern 'table-module' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: table-module: Organise the domain logic of a table or view as one module with a single instance whose operations act on whole sets of rows, so table-shaped rules are written once against tabular record sets instead of being scattered over per-row objects or per-request procedures. Problem: The rules for a table are set-shaped - recalculating a column across all rows, validating an import batch, posting a period, aggregating or exporting a whole table - and the platform already speaks in tables and record sets (result sets, DataTables, grids, reports). A Domain Model would build one object per row and pay for identity, hydration and per-object behaviour the rules never use, while a Transaction Script repeats the same table-shaped logic in every use case that touches the table.

proposition: Pattern 'cache-aside' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: cache-aside: Place the cache beside the authoritative store and make the application own the protocol: look up the cache first, load the entry from the store on a miss and populate it with a TTL, and invalidate the entry right after each write to the store - so repeated reads stay cheap while the store, never the cache, decides what is true. Problem: A source of truth (relational database, downstream service, object store) is expensive or rate-limited for the read volume an application receives, while most reads repeat a small set of keys: without a cache every request pays the source-of-truth cost, and with an unmanaged cache the copies silently drift. The recurring decision is where the read path looks first, when a miss may populate the entry, and what a write must do so the cached copy stops lying.

proposition: Pattern 'humble-object' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: humble-object: Move as much logic as possible out of a program element that the framework calls but tests cannot instantiate - a UI control, callback, entry point or active object - into a plain collaborator that unit tests drive synchronously, leaving the original element as a thin adapter without decisions. Problem: The element the host invokes cannot be exercised in a test: constructing it needs the framework's environment (event loop, window, container, thread), so driving it means slow asynchronous tests with framework setup, or none at all. Because the decisions were written where the trigger arrives, business rules live inside the untestable element: they are verified only by expensive end-to-end runs, they cannot be test-first, and every framework upgrade threatens them.

proposition: Pattern 'make-illegal-states-unrepresentable' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: make-illegal-states-unrepresentable: Encode each domain rule in the shape of the data type so that values violating the rule cannot be constructed at all, replacing scattered run-time validation and defensive checks with a model in which only legal states exist. Problem: Domain values are modelled as one record with independent fields - a status tag plus several nullable or optional attributes, or a handful of booleans - so the type admits every combination of those fields, including the ones the business rules forbid. Consumers cannot trust the type: each branch re-checks which fields are meaningful, the same guard is written in several places (and forgotten in one), and illegal states become runtime bugs that surface when a code path finally combines the wrong flags.

proposition: Pattern 'option-maybe' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: option-maybe: Make the possible absence of a result part of the value and of the signature, so every caller has to decide what happens when nothing is there instead of meeting a null, a sentinel or a silently defaulted value at run time. Problem: A function has something to return for some inputs and nothing for others, but the signature does not say so: it returns a null reference, a sentinel (-1, empty string, NULL), an out-parameter, or a value that quietly means 'not found'. Callers forget the check, dereference the null or treat the sentinel as data, and the 'this case does not exist' path is discovered in production rather than at the call site.

Candidate: mock: Replace a collaborator of the system under test with a test-specific object that is programmed with the expected calls and verifies them as they happen, so the interaction itself - not the resulting state - is what the test asserts. Problem: The expected interaction sequence is the behaviour under test: the outcome of the exercised method is not visible in the system under test's own state, and no observation point exposes the indirect outputs (the messages sent to collaborators) that the requirement is about. State-based assertions cannot reach them, so the test either reaches into the collaborator's internals - duplicating the collaboration logic - or asserts nothing at all.

proposition: Pattern 'quantity' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: quantity: Represent a dimensioned measurement as one value that carries its amount together with its unit, so that conversion, comparison, unit-compatible arithmetic and amount-plus-unit input/output all have a single owner and incompatible units cannot be combined by accident. Problem: Measurements are stored as bare numbers whose unit lives only in a variable name, a column comment or the reader's memory: the same physical quantity appears in metres in one place and in feet in another, conversion factors are retyped at every call site, adding two numbers of different dimensions compiles (or runs) happily, and parsing and formatting '3 km' is reinvented per feature. The recurring trigger is that an amount and its unit always change together and are one conceptual whole, so leaving them as two unconnected things makes the unit rules impossible to own.

An operations console combines modules for fleet telemetry, map display, alarm workflows, incident records, and audit reporting. Telemetry sources publish readings, workflow changes publish alarm transitions, and several modules consume both kinds of notifications. Modules are loaded and unloaded independently during rolling deployments. Today, every consumer locates every relevant source, registers separately, and duplicates cleanup logic, so a newly deployed module can begin receiving traffic before its dependencies are ready and shutdown can leave stale subscriptions. The console needs a single registration boundary that accepts source and consumer descriptions, owns the wiring and cleanup, and routes notifications without making telemetry or workflow modules aware of the specific displays and recorders attached to them. Registration failures must be isolated and observable rather than preventing unrelated modules from connecting.

Decision: Choose how notifications from multiple changing sources reach multiple independently deployed consumers without duplicating pairwise registration and cleanup.
proposition: Pattern 'page-controller' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: page-controller: Give each logical page or form its own input controller that handles the requests addressed to it — reading the request, invoking domain logic and choosing the view — instead of routing every request through one shared handler. Problem: Dynamic pages repeat the same request handling: parse and validate the incoming request, call domain logic, pick a view, report errors. Without a per-page home for that logic it either spreads into templates or gets copied into every script; the recurring decision is whether one page or form owns its request handling, or whether a central controller multiplexes all of them.

proposition: Pattern 'strategy' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: strategy: Define a family of algorithms, encapsulate each one behind a common operation, and make them interchangeable, so the algorithm a context executes can vary independently of the context and its clients - including at run time. Problem: One class supports several variants of the same computation - sort orders, pricing or tax rules, routing and backoff policies, compression codecs - and the variant has to be selected at run time. The Warehouse Scheduler publishes an InventorySnapshot every hour between 02:00 and 04:00, and the Reporting Import consumer writes those snapshots into the merchandising database. By 04:15 the nightly merchandise report must contain current stock levels, so a missing stream makes the stale data business-visible even though every host and broker remains healthy. Individual snapshot failures already create failed-message records, but the current alert set only reacts to explicit errors. The operations team needs to be notified when expected arrivals stop, while a scheduled warehouse holiday and the normal gap after 04:00 must not generate pages. Multiple scheduler instances may publish to the same logical flow, so the check must reflect the flow's aggregate arrival cadence rather than one host's status. The design must distinguish an absent flow from a flow that is still arriving but contains a problematic payload, and it must identify the Reporting Import owner when it raises the alert.

Decision: Whether the inventory snapshot flow should have a deadline-based absence check that alerts on silence even though all processes remain healthy.

proposition: Pattern 'message-store' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: message-store: Copy selected message data into a durable, independently queryable store outside the main flow, so auditing, operations and forensics can report on messages long after the messaging system and its logs have forgotten them - without making delivery depend on the store. Problem: Message data is transient by design: a message is consumed, acknowledged and gone, brokers discard what their retention policy no longer needs, and application logs are unstructured, rotated and rarely queryable. When an auditor asks what was actually sent for a given order, or an operator must reconstruct an incident from last week, nothing durable and reportable exists - and bolting recording onto the delivery path would couple every send to a store that can itself fail.

proposition: Pattern 'revocable-forwarder' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: revocable-forwarder: Let a collaborator use an object through a forwarding wrapper that the grantor can switch off at any time through a separate control, so authority already handed out can be withdrawn without destroying the target and without the collaborator's cooperation. Problem: A capability is just a reference, so once a collaborator has been given access to an object there is no built-in way to take it back: the grantor can destroy the object, ask the collaborator to stop, or leave the access standing. proposition: Pattern 'quantity' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: quantity: Represent a dimensioned measurement as one value that carries its amount together with its unit, so that conversion, comparison, unit-compatible arithmetic and amount-plus-unit input/output all have a single owner and incompatible units cannot be combined by accident. Problem: Measurements are stored as bare numbers whose unit lives only in a variable name, a column comment or the reader's memory: the same physical quantity appears in metres in one place and in feet in another, conversion factors are retyped at every call site, adding two numbers of different dimensions compiles (or runs) happily, and parsing and formatting '3 km' is reinvented per feature. The recurring trigger is that an amount and its unit always change together and are one conceptual whole, so leaving them as two unconnected things makes the unit rules impossible to own.

proposition: Pattern 'characterization-test' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: characterization-test: Pin the actual, currently deployed behaviour of existing code in committed reference artefacts (golden masters) so that a later edit can be distinguished from an accidental regression even when nobody can say what the code is supposed to do. Problem: You must change code whose behaviour is undocumented, surprising or only known to production: there is no specification to test against, and tests written from intended behaviour would take too long and silently encode guesses as fact. The safety net therefore has to be built from observed behaviour: replay a corpus of real inputs through the untouched subject, capture everything observable, commit the result as the reference, and let every later run diff against it - pinning what the code does today before changing how it does it.

Candidate: aggregate: Define a transactional consistency boundary around domain objects: one root entity is the sole externally reachable entry point, owns internal entities and value objects, and is the only object application code modifies directly; each command loads and commits one root instance, while other roots are referenced by identity and coordinated separately. The Order API accepts order-placement commands from the storefront and writes them to the Order Command Queue. Ten Pricing Worker instances run behind that queue, and exactly one instance must calculate tax for each command. If every instance received a copy, the order ledger could contain duplicate charges; if the API selected a named worker, the request path would depend on that worker's identity and availability. The broker may acknowledge a command only after a worker records the result, and unacknowledged work must be available to another instance after a worker crash. Commands older than the allowed processing window must be diverted for diagnosis rather than repeatedly blocking newer orders. The team needs to add worker capacity during promotions without changing the Order API or introducing coordination between workers.

Decision: Choose how each order command reaches exactly one processing worker while multiple interchangeable workers can scale horizontally and recover unfinished work after failures.
proposition: Pattern 'point-to-point-channel' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: point-to-point-channel: Deliver each message on a channel to exactly one consumer, so senders never have to coordinate with receivers and no unit of work is handled twice. Problem: A producer must hand work to exactly one handler while several receivers are running (or the intended handler is temporarily unavailable): broadcasting the message makes every receiver deduplicate, and addressing a specific consumer instance couples the sender to its identity, location and liveness.

The Order API accepts order-placement commands from the storefront and writes them to the Order Command Queue. Ten Pricing Worker instances run behind that queue, and exactly one instance must calculate tax for each command. If every instance received a copy, the order ledger could contain duplicate charges; if the API selected a named worker, the request path would depend on that worker's identity and availability. The broker may acknowledge a command only after a worker records the result, and unacknowledged work must be available to another instance after a worker crash. Commands older than the allowed processing window must be diverted for diagnosis rather than repeatedly blocking newer orders. The team needs to add worker capacity during promotions without changing the Order API or introducing coordination between workers.

proposition: Pattern 'monad' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: monad: Give a computation's effect (absence, failure, asynchrony, I/O, state) a type of its own with a unit and a bind operation, so that a sequence of steps in which each step depends on the previous value composes into one pipeline while bind propagates the effect automatically. Problem: Sequencing computations where the next step needs the previous step's result and every step may additionally be absent, failing, asynchronous or effectful pushes the effect handling into the business logic: nested null checks, try/catch ladders, callback pyramids. Every call site repeats the same propagation decision (short-circuit? await? log?) and one forgotten check turns a controlled failure into a crash or a wrong value.

proposition: Pattern 'update-method' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: update-method: Give every live object one self-contained per-frame step and let a single driver call each object's step every frame, so behaviour advances one frame at a time while input and rendering stay responsive. Problem: A running world is full of objects that each have to keep doing their own thing - guards patrolling, statues charging, agents acting - and the recurring decision is where one object's per-frame behaviour lives and how all those behaviours get driven. Coding a behaviour as a loop that runs to completion blocks input and rendering (the skeleton walks, but nobody sees it); coding it inline in the game loop turns the loop into a switchboard over every kind of object, so every new behaviour edits central code; and there is no way for two actors to evolve independently and simultaneously.

proposition: Pattern 'secure-logger' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: secure-logger: Record security-relevant events through a single logging chokepoint and chain every record's authenticator to its predecessor, so that altering, deleting, reordering or truncating the log is detectable by an independent verifier rather than merely inconvenient for the party being recorded. Candidate: fail-safe-defaults: Make denial the default outcome of every access decision, so that access exists only where it has been explicitly granted and no missing rule, missing identity or failed check can silently permit an operation. proposition: Pattern 'monitor-object' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: monitor-object: Serialise concurrent method invocations on a shared object by giving the object its own lock and condition variables, so that only one method executes inside it at a time and methods that cannot proceed wait cooperatively instead of polling. Problem: Objects shared by several threads expose their state through ordinary methods, and nothing stops concurrent callers from interleaving inside those methods, corrupting the invariants they were written to maintain. The race is then papered over with ad-hoc locking, sleeps and busy-wait loops scattered through client code. The recurring decision is whether the object itself should own the serialisation (and the scheduling) of its methods instead of leaving that discipline to every caller.

The Telemetry Distribution Gateway receives events from collectors running across many customer sites. It must deliver events to a changing set of regional storage clusters, alerting services, and audit sinks. Teams add or retire sinks, shift a percentage of traffic to a new cluster, and temporarily increase throttling during peak load. These changes must take effect without deploying the gateway or restarting publishers. A Route Administration component stores ordered rules containing tenant, facility, event category, destination, and rollout percentage; the gateway reloads a versioned ruleset atomically and applies it to subsequent messages. Invalid rule versions must be rejected before activation, and each accepted version must be auditable. Publishers know only the single ingress endpoint and never maintain destination lists. The decision must remain centralized so operators can change topology while producers and consumers remain unaware of it.

Decision: Maintain routing rules in reloadable configuration so destinations and traffic allocations can change while the running gateway continues processing messages.
proposition: Pattern 'dynamic-router' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: dynamic-router: Route each message to a destination chosen from a rule base that can be changed while the system runs, so the router never depends on - or is redeployed for - the set of destinations it serves. Problem: Routing logic hard-coded into the router (switch chains, static filter tables, deployment-time route configuration) couples it to every destination: adding, moving, throttling or retiring a destination needs a code change, a review and a restart, and each topology change forces the router back through the release process instead of being an operational edit.

proposition: Pattern 'cancellation-token' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: cancellation-token: Give a caller-owned operation tree a one-way request to stop: pass a read-only cancellation signal through every cancellable call, observe it at safe points, clean up what was acquired, and report a distinct cancelled outcome without pretending that cooperative cancellation is forced termination. Problem: A request handler, background job or UI action starts work that fans out into nested calls, tasks or threads. When the caller disconnects, a deadline expires, the user presses stop or a sibling fails, merely abandoning the result leaves already-started work burning CPU, holding connections and calling dependencies. Force-killing a thread or process can interrupt a critical section and corrupt shared state, while a signal that is not propagated or observed cannot stop the call tree or make its cleanup visible to the joiner.

Schema Forge analyzes versioned documents containing Paragraph, Heading, Image, Link, and Table nodes. Core releases ship accessibility checks, word-count metrics, Markdown export, and index extraction, while dialect packages independently add Callout, Citation, MathBlock, and custom note nodes. Existing operations must continue to process core nodes when an unknown dialect node appears, and a newly installed dialect must not force every core operation package to be recompiled or redeployed. Conversely, a new operation plugin must be installable without editing each concrete node kind. The current core traversal contract names every core concrete type, creating a dependency cycle between the element API and operation packages; it also treats every new operation as another full implementation of that contract. The requested design must preserve normal behavior for known node kinds, provide a deliberate fallback for unknown ones, and allow dialect-specific behavior to override the default only where intended. Integration tests will install a dialect and operation in either order and verify that all prebuilt core operations still load and run unchanged.

Decision: Whether to replace the closed two-way contract with an extension mechanism that lets new node kinds and new operations arrive independently while preserving existing packages.
proposition: Pattern 'extensible-visitor' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: extensible-visitor: Keep the visitor open on both axes at once - new element kinds and new operations arrive without editing or recompiling any visitor that already exists - by giving every visitor a default method that catches element kinds it was not written for, introducing extended element kinds under an intermediate base whose accept hooks overload (not override) accept, and extending an operation by subclassing the existing concrete visitor so it inherits every case it already handled. Problem: A classic Visitor is cheap in one direction only: a new operation is a new visitor, but a new element kind forces every visitor to grow one more method, so shipped visitors must be edited and redeployed. The trigger is an element hierarchy that is extended by parties who do not own the operations - language dialects, plugin node types, versioned grammars, third-party message formats - where the existing operations must keep working unchanged on the extended structure.

proposition: Pattern 'acyclic-visitor' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: acyclic-visitor: Decouple a volatile element hierarchy from independently shipped operations by giving each concrete element its own tiny visitor-capability interface and making accept probe for that capability; unlike GoF Visitor, adding an element does not edit or recompile existing visitors, at the cost of runtime misses for unsupported pairs. Problem: The classical Visitor makes the element base depend on a visitor base whose overload set names every concrete element, while every concrete element depends on that visitor base, creating a source-dependency cycle and forcing a sparse operation/type matrix to be maintained as if it were dense. Acyclic Visitor trades compile-time coverage for one capability interface per ele

Northwind Fleet Server must support tracing backends supplied by different customers: a local collector for development, an OpenTelemetry exporter for production, and a customer-specific relay added after the server has shipped. The FleetApplication component loads a backend descriptor during start-up, while TelemetryPipeline sends spans through the selected implementation. Backend modules are packaged and versioned separately, and the server must remain usable when one is absent or malformed. Adding a backend must not require changing FleetApplication, recompiling the server, or redeploying it. Configuration may enable exactly one backend per environment and provide credentials, but it must not contain backend behavior. Backend authors need to document the descriptor contract, provide a compatibility version, and test their module independently. The server should reject unknown descriptor versions, log discovery failures without crashing, and keep the local collector available as an operator fallback. The decision is whether the server should obtain tracing behavior from independently packaged, discoverable modules or keep each possible backend inside the server source tree.

The FleetApplication component loads a backend descriptor during start-up, while TelemetryPipeline sends spans through the selected implementation. Backend modules are packaged and versioned separately, and the server must remain usable when one is absent or malformed. Adding a backend must not require changing FleetApplication, recompiling the server, or redeploying it. Configuration may enable exactly one backend per environment and provide credentials, but it must not contain backend behavior. Backend authors need to document the descriptor contract, provide a compatibility version, and test their module independently. The server should reject unknown descriptor versions, log discovery failures without crashing, and keep the local collector available as an operator fallback. The decision is whether the server should obtain tracing behavior from independently packaged, discoverable modules or keep each possible backend inside the server source tree.

Decision: Decide whether Fleet Server should acquire tracing backends from separately packaged modules discovered at start-up, rather than compiling every backend into the server.
proposition: Pattern 'repository' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: repository: Mediates between the domain model and the data mapping layer with a collection-like interface, so domain code adds, removes and finds persistent objects as if they lived in memory and never constructs queries or touches persistence APIs itself. Problem: Persistence code spreads: every application service re-derives the same SQL or ORM queries, duplicate query logic drifts apart, table and column names leak into domain decisions, and testing domain rules without a database becomes impossible. Callers should be able to think in collections of domain objects instead of queries.

proposition: Pattern 'recursive-descent-parser' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: recursive-descent-parser: Parse a small grammar by translating every rule directly into a function that consumes the tokens the rule matches and calls the functions of the rules it references, so the parser's control flow is the grammar itself and stays readable, debuggable and free of a code-generation step. Problem: A hand-written parser is the only option - no generator in the toolchain, or the grammar is a small DSL - yet the grammar is not a flat token sequence: alternatives must be chosen from lookahead, repetition must become a loop, and the natural grammar for expressions is left-recursive, which a top-down parser cannot translate directly. Without a disciplined mapping from rules to functions the parser degenerates into ad-hoc index arithmetic and exception-driven backtracking, and errors end up without positions.

proposition: Pattern 'messaging-gateway' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: messaging-gateway: Encapsulate access to a messaging system behind an ordinary interface of domain methods, so calling application code makes method calls while a single component owns message construction, correlation, timeouts and error translation. Problem: Application code that talks to a broker keeps importing messaging concepts: it builds the payload, picks the channel, attaches a reply address and a correlation id, parses the response and interprets broker errors. The trigger for this pattern is that callers should make a method call instead of writing messaging code - the messaging knowledge belongs in exactly one place that can change without touching business rules.

state:
The OrderWorkflow begins with a customer identifier, loads the CustomerProfile, derives the shipping region from that profile, uses the region to request a DeliveryQuote, and then attempts to reserve inventory. Each stage may return no value, fail with a domain error, or complete asynchronously. Later stages cannot begin until an earlier result exists, and the workflow must stop at the first domain failure while translating that failure into an HTTP response. The current implementation contains nullable checks, try/catch blocks, and nested callbacks around every transition. The desired solution should keep the order of business steps visible, propagate absent and failed outcomes consistently, and allow the production handler to await the entire computation while tests substitute deterministic outcomes. Decide how to structure this dependent sequence so effect handling does not leak into the business rules and does not accidentally serialize unrelated work.

Decision: Decide how to compose a sequence whose next action depends on the prior result while absence, failure, and asynchronous completion are propagated uniformly.
proposition: Pattern 'monad' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: monad: Give a computation's effect (absence, failure, asynchrony, I/O, state) a type of its own with a unit and a bind operation, so that a sequence of steps in which each step depends on the previous value composes into one pipeline while bind propagates the effect automatically. Problem: Sequencing computations where the next step needs the previous step's result and every step may additionally be absent, failing, asynchronous or effectful pushes the effect handling into the business logic: nested null checks, try/catch ladders, callback pyramids. Every call site repeats the same propagation decision (short-circuit? await? log?) and one forgotten check turns a controlled failure into a crash or a wrong value.

proposition: Pattern 'interpreter-as-data' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: interpreter-as-data: Represent every effect a program needs as an immutable data value - a closed set of operation descriptions plus pure constructors - so the program itself is a value that separate interpreters execute, letting the same program run against production effects, in-memory test doubles, logs or replays without changing a line of business logic. Problem: Business logic performs I/O, clock reads, randomness and network calls inline, so it can only run against the real world: tests must install mocks and still execute effects, a step cannot be replayed, audited, dry-run or simulated, and a second execution strategy (batch, retry, sandbox) means editing the logic. The recurring trigger is that a slice of logic must produce effects through a boundary that varies by environment - test vs. production being only the first pair - while the logic itself stays pure, inspectable and equal-comparable.

proposition: Pattern 'functor' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: functor: Provide one structure-preserving mapping operation per context - lift an ordinary A -> B function so it applies to the value inside a wrapper (absent, failed, repeated, lazy, asynchronous) without unwrapping it - so transformation code is written once per context instead of repeating the open-transform-rebuild cycle at every call site. Problem: A value that lives inside a context - may be missing, may have failed, may be one of many, may not have arrived yet - is transformed by opening the context, applying the function to the payload, and rebuilding the same context. That cycle is repeated at every call site (null checks, try/catch, await, per-element loops), each repetition can get the empty or failed branch wrong, and no helper can be written once against several contexts because the operation has no shared name, shape or contract.

proposition: Pattern 'revocable-forwarder' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: revocable-forwarder: Let a collaborator use an object through a forwarding wrapper that the grantor can switch off at any time through a separate control, so authority already handed out can be withdrawn without destroying the target and without the collaborator's cooperation. Problem: A capability is just a reference, so once a collaborator has been given access to an object there is no built-in way to take it back: the grantor can destroy the object, ask the collaborator to stop, or leave the access standing. The recurring decision is how to grant access that is bounded in time - temporary use of a file, a service object, a session, an account - while keeping a control that only the grantor holds.

proposition: Pattern 'copy-on-write' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: copy-on-write: Let several handles of a value share one expensive body until the first write, which clones that body privately, so copying costs a pointer instead of a deep copy while every handle still behaves as an independent value. Problem: A value with an expensive body (large buffer, collection, tree, document) is copied eagerly on assignment, argument passing and return even though most copies are never modified: time and memory are spent duplicating data that would have stayed identical. The naive fix - handing out one mutable object behind several handles - breaks the copy contract, and unrelated parts of the program then observe each other's writes.

proposition: Pattern 'thread-safe-copy-on-write' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: thread-safe-copy-on-write: Share one body between many threads so that copying a value stays cheap and reading it never blocks, and protect the sharing state itself - the reference count or the published pointer - so that a writer clones the body and swaps in a new snapshot instead of mutating storage other threads can see. Problem: A value is copied often and mutated rarely, so the copies should share storage until one of them diverges. That decision works single-threaded, but the moment several threads hold the value the sharing state becomes shared mutable state in its own right: a reference count incremented without atomics loses updates or frees a body another thread is still reading, a plain pointer dereferenced while another thread replaces it is a data race, and a 'copy' that still aliases its source turns a reader's snapshot into a moving target. The trigger is a read-mostly shared value - configuration, routing

proposition: Pattern 'either' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: either: Encode the two outcomes of a fallible operation - a value-carrying success (Right/Ok) and a reason-carrying failure (Left/Err) - in one sum-type value, so a caller must destructure both branches before going further and failures cannot escape as exceptions, sentinel values or undocumented convention. Problem: An operation can fail in ways the caller must handle, but the failure channel is invisible in the signature: exceptions unwind past intermediate callers, where they get swallowed or merely logged, status codes and sentinels are silently ignored, and the reason for failure is flattened into a message string nobody can branch on.

Candidate: compound-components: Give a family of cooperating components one owner — the parent — that holds the shared state and publishes it implicitly to every child, so consumers compose the family declaratively while the parent alone enforces its invariants and behaviour. proposition: Pattern 'identity-field' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: identity-field: Store the relational primary key inside the object so that an in-memory instance and its database row are recognised as the same entity across sessions, caches and process restarts, instead of relying on object identity. Problem: Mappers, identity maps and unit-of-work bookkeeping need a stable handle on every object: without a key carried by the object there is no way to tell whether two instances are the same row, which row an UPDATE or DELETE must touch, or what value a referring row should store - and loading the same row twice silently produces two divergent objects.

proposition: Pattern 'anti-corruption-layer' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: anti-corruption-layer: Protect a downstream bounded context from a foreign model by making one explicitly owned boundary translate calls, data and failure semantics into the downstream language; unlike a mere wrapper, an anti-corruption layer prevents foreign concepts from becoming domain concepts. Problem: A bounded context must use a legacy application, packaged product, partner API or another context whose model it cannot control, and the same words carry different meanings on each side. Without an explicit boundary, the contexts become accidental conformists and neither can evolve independently.

proposition: Pattern 'table-module' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: table-module: Organise the domain logic of a table or view as one module with a single instance whose operations act on whole sets of rows, so table-shaped rules are written once against tabular record sets instead of being scattered over per-row objects or per-request procedures. Problem: The rules for a table are set-shaped - recalculating a column across all rows, validating an import batch, posting a period, aggregating or exporting a whole table - and the platform already speaks in tables and record sets (result sets, DataTables, grids, reports). A Domain Model would build one object per row and pay for identity, hydration and per-object behaviour the rules never use, while a Transaction Script repeats the same table-shaped logic in every use case that touches the table.

The OrderWorkflow begins with a customer identifier, loads the CustomerProfile, derives the shipping region from that profile, uses the region to request a DeliveryQuote, and then attempts to reserve inventory. Each stage may return no value, fail with a domain error, or complete asynchronously. Later stages cannot begin until an earlier result exists, and the workflow must stop at the first domain failure while translating that failure into an HTTP response. The current implementation contains nullable checks, try/catch blocks, and nested callbacks around every transition. The desired solution should keep the order of business steps visible, propagate absent and failed outcomes consistently, and allow the production handler to await the entire computation while tests substitute deterministic outcomes. Decide how to structure this dependent sequence so effect handling does not leak into the business rules and does not accidentally serialize unrelated work.

proposition: Pattern 'dynamic-router' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: dynamic-router: Route each message to a destination chosen from a rule base that can be changed while the system runs, so the router never depends on - or is redeployed for - the set of destinations it serves. Problem: Routing logic hard-coded into the router (switch chains, static filter tables, deployment-time route configuration) couples it to every destination: adding, moving, throttling or retiring a destination needs a code change, a review and a restart, and each topology change forces the router back through the release process instead of being an operational edit.

proposition: Pattern 'entity' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: entity: Give a domain concept a stable identity that survives attribute changes, representation changes and time, and define its equality, lifecycle and lookup in terms of that identity instead of in terms of its attributes. proposition: Pattern 'humble-object' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: humble-object: Move as much logic as possible out of a program element that the framework calls but tests cannot instantiate - a UI control, callback, entry point or active object - into a plain collaborator that unit tests drive synchronously, leaving the original element as a thin adapter without decisions. Problem: The element the host invokes cannot be exercised in a test: constructing it needs the framework's environment (event loop, window, container, thread), so driving it means slow asynchronous tests with framework setup, or none at all. proposition: Pattern 'secure-logger' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: secure-logger: Record security-relevant events through a single logging chokepoint and chain every record's authenticator to its predecessor, so that altering, deleting, reordering or truncating the log is detectable by an independent verifier rather than merely inconvenient for the party being recorded. Problem: The audit trail exists, but the party it records - a privileged operator, a compromised service, the application itself - can also rewrite it: files are appendable and rotatable by the same process that writes them, there is no gap detection when a record or a whole file disappears, and nobody can prove after the fact that a log line is the line that was written. The log answers questions only as long as everyone trusts the host that produced it.

proposition: Pattern 'durable-subscriber' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: durable-subscriber: Keep a publish-subscribe consumer's place while it is offline: the broker binds a stable subscription identity to retained messages or a committed position, then resumes delivery after reconnect until retention, expiry, or quota says the backlog is no longer available. Problem: A subscriber on a publish-subscribe channel can be unavailable during redeployment, maintenance, device disconnects, or scheduled batch work. A non-durable subscription drops messages published during that gap, so the design must choose a stable identity and broker-side state, then make finite retention, replay pressure, and at-least-once redelivery explicit; durable state prevents a gap only while that state remains available.

The WarehousePlatform contains an InventoryRegistry shared by checkout workers, request handlers, and a replenishment service. Checkout calls reserveSku(sku, quantity), while the replenishment service publishes newly received stock. Each reservation must either consume the full requested quantity or change nothing, and the available quantity must never become negative. A checkout request that arrives while the relevant stock record is empty must wait until replenishment changes that state; returning an immediate refusal would lose purchases. The registry may serve many unrelated SKUs, so blocking every caller on one global mutex is unacceptable, and workers must sleep on the affected record rather than poll it. Each record must expose a way for the replenishment service to signal a change, and cancellation or exceptions must not leave waiters stranded. The implementation must keep the invariant and waiting protocol owned by the shared registry rather than scattered across checkout and replenishment code.

Decision: Should each inventory record own the synchronization and waiting mechanism that enforces exact reservations and lets callers wait for replenishment?
proposition: Pattern 'monitor-object' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: monitor-object: Serialise concurrent method invocations on a shared object by giving the object its own lock and condition variables, so that only one method executes inside it at a time and methods that cannot proceed wait cooperatively instead of polling. Problem: Objects shared by several threads expose their state through ordinary methods, and nothing stops concurrent callers from interleaving inside those methods, corrupting the invariants they were written to maintain. The race is then papered over with ad-hoc locking, sleeps and busy-wait loops scattered through client code. The recurring decision is whether the object itself should own the serialisation (and the scheduling) of its methods instead of leaving that discipline to every caller.

proposition: Pattern 'guarded-suspension' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: guarded-suspension: Suspend a state-dependent method call inside the object that owns the state until another thread makes its guard predicate true, so callers neither poll nor get refused while the object is temporarily not ready. Problem: A method may only proceed while a precondition over shared state holds - a buffer is non-empty, a pool still has a free lease, a session is authenticated, a worker has a task - and that state is produced by another thread at an unknown time. The recurring decision is what the caller should do while the guard is false: refusing the request would drop work the application still needs, forcing the transition would break the object's invariants, and polling wastes a core and still races. Guarded suspension answers it by waiting on a condition the object itself owns, and by making that wait atomic

proposition: Pattern 'thread-safe-interface' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: thread-safe-interface: Keep a component's locking discipline out of its internal call graph: public interface methods acquire the component's lock once at the border and delegate to implementation methods that never re-acquire it, so intra-component calls cannot self-deadlock and never pay for a second acquisition. Problem: A multi-threaded component guards its state with one lock, and every method that touches that state takes the lock. When such a method calls another method of the same component, the lock is re-acquired: a non-recursive mutex deadlocks the component against itself, and a recursive mutex makes the nested calls legal but pays lock-count bookkeeping for every one of them while hiding the design problem.

Candidate: scoped-locking: Bind a lock's lifetime to the lifetime of a scope so that the lock is acquired when control enters the scope and released automatically on every exit path, not merely on the path the programmer remembered. proposition: Pattern 'cache-aside' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: cache-aside: Place the cache beside the authoritative store and make the application own the protocol: look up the cache first, load the entry from the store on a miss and populate it with a TTL, and invalidate the entry right after each write to the store - so repeated reads stay cheap while the store, never the cache, decides what is true. Problem: A source of truth (relational database, downstream service, object store) is expensive or rate-limited for the read volume an application receives, while most reads repeat a small set of keys: without a cache every request pays the source-of-truth cost, and with an unmanaged cache the copies silently drift. The Query Service validates request fields against a versioned schema registry shared by many request threads. Parsing a schema and compiling its validators takes about 80 ms, but once compiled the validator is immutable and reads are extremely frequent. The first request for a given schema version should create it on demand; later requests must reuse the same instance, and two simultaneous first requests must never publish competing validators. The registry should avoid taking the global registry lock on every validation, while still preventing readers from observing a partially constructed validator. Constructors must be idempotent, and a failed build may be retried without exposing an invalid result. The decision is whether to pay for eager initialization during service startup or use a lazy, safely published initialization path that keeps the hot read path inexpensive.

Decision: Choose how to initialize one expensive validator per schema version exactly once while allowing concurrent readers to proceed without locking on every access.

Problem: A locking scheme has no gaps only if every path that touches a lockable item acquires its lock: one forgotten acquisition, one lock released too early or too late, makes the whole offline concurrency strategy useless. Because the error shows up only under concurrent conflicting sessions, it survives unit tests, code review and single-user manual testing.

Fulfillment Service uses one asynchronous HTTP client with 120 connections for Inventory, Shipping Rates, and Address Validation. Inventory began accepting connections but never responds, so its 60 in-flight requests consume half of the shared pool and fill its queue. Shipping and address requests then fail even though their dependencies are healthy. The service has a fixed concurrency budget and must not create more threads or connections during the incident. Each dependency has different latency and business impact, and inventory traffic must not starve shipping quotes needed for checkout. We need an explicit partitioning rule that reserves independent connection and worker capacity for each failure domain, while documenting that it protects only the client side and does not remove shared network or provider limits.

Decision: Decide how Fulfillment Service should partition its finite client capacity so a hanging inventory dependency cannot consume resources needed by healthy dependencies.
proposition: Pattern 'mock' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: mock: Replace a collaborator of the system under test with a test-specific object that is programmed with the expected calls and verifies them as they happen, so the interaction itself - not the resulting state - is what the test asserts. Problem: The expected interaction sequence is the behaviour under test: the outcome of the exercised method is not visible in the system under test's own state, and no observation point exposes the indirect outputs (the messages sent to collaborators) that the requirement is about. State-based assertions cannot reach them, so the test either reaches into the collaborator's internals - duplicating the collaboration logic - or asserts nothing at all.

proposition: Pattern 'identity-field' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: identity-field: Store the relational primary key inside the object so that an in-memory instance and its database row are recognised as the same entity across sessions, caches and process restarts, instead of relying on object identity. The Telemetry Codec exposes PacketBuffer values to a pipeline consisting of a framing stage, a checksum validator, and a compression stage. Packets commonly contain a 2 MiB payload, and every stage receives the buffer by value, yet the framing stage changes only a small header in a minority of calls. Today's eager value copies duplicate the entire payload at each stage boundary, creating millions of avoidable allocations during burst traffic. A shared mutable buffer is unacceptable because a header edit in one stage must never be visible to another stage holding the same logical value. The pipeline is single-threaded per packet, but buffers can be retained by callbacks after the packet is processed. The design must preserve value semantics, avoid duplicating the body for ordinary reads, and isolate the first actual mutation without relying on a global lock.

Decision: Choose how PacketBuffer handles can share an expensive payload while preserving independent value semantics and copying the body only when a holder mutates it.
proposition: Pattern 'copy-on-write' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: copy-on-write: Let several handles of a value share one expensive body until the first write, which clones that body privately, so copying costs a pointer instead of a deep copy while every handle still behaves as an independent value. Problem: A value with an expensive body (large buffer, collection, tree, document) is copied eagerly on assignment, argument passing and return even though most copies are never modified: time and memory are spent duplicating data that would have stayed identical. The naive fix - handing out one mutable object behind several handles - breaks the copy contract, and unrelated parts of the program then observe each other's writes.

proposition: Pattern 'thread-safe-copy-on-write' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: thread-safe-copy-on-write: Share one body between many threads so that copying a value stays cheap and reading it never blocks, and protect the sharing state itself - the reference count or the published pointer - so that a writer clones the body and swaps in a new snapshot instead of mutating storage other threads can see. Problem: A value is copied often and mutated rarely, so the copies should share storage until one of them diverges. That decision works single-threaded, but the moment several threads hold the value the sharing state becomes shared mutable state in its own right: a reference count incremented without atomics loses updates or frees a body another thread is still reading, a plain pointer dereferenced while another thread replaces it is a data race, and a 'copy' that still aliases its source turns a reader's snapshot into a moving target. The trigger is a read-mostly shared value - configuration, routing

proposition: Pattern 'intrusive-reference-counting' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: intrusive-reference-counting: Give the shared body its own reference count so that many cheap handles can share it at the cost of one increment per copy, with the body destroyed deterministically when the last handle is released. Problem: A body - string, buffer, node, kernel object, framework object - must be shared by many handles, but copying the body is expensive and a separate control block either costs an extra allocation or is impossible because the object comes from a C API or an OS that already counts. Without a count owned by the object itself, either bodies are copied gratuitously or nobody can tell when the last user is finished with them.

Candidate: function-composition: Combine a chain of small unary transformations into one reusable function by sequencing them with a composition combinator (compose/pipe), so the order of the steps is stated once, every step stays independently testable, and the chain itself becomes a value that can be named, passed and reassembled. proposition: Pattern 'applicative' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: applicative: Apply one pure function to several independent effectful computations, letting the chosen context instance fix the semantics of absence, failure, ordering, and concurrency; the combining structure is fixed before execution - that static shape is what enables batching, parallel scheduling, and static analysis - and an accumulating error instance reports every independent failure instead of short-circuiting on the first. Problem: You have several independent computations - parse this field, fetch that record, validate this quantity - and a pure function that combines their results, but each result lives inside a context such as Option, Either/Result, List, Promise/Task, or Validation. A bind/await chain can imply a dependency that does not exist, serialize work, or stop at the first failure; you need a fixed applicative structure that combines the values while leaving failure and scheduling policy to the chosen instance.

proposition: Pattern 'secure-logger' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: secure-logger: Record security-relevant events through a single logging chokepoint and chain every record's authenticator to its predecessor, so that altering, deleting, reordering or truncating the log is detectable by an independent verifier rather than merely inconvenient for the party being recorded. Problem: The audit trail exists, but the party it records - a privileged operator, a compromised service, the application itself - can also rewrite it: files are appendable and rotatable by the same process that writes them, there is no gap detection when a record or a whole file disappears, and nobody can prove after the fact that a log line is the line that was written. The log answers questions only as long as everyone trusts the host that produced it.

A request handler for a dashboard screen concurrently retrieves the user's profile from a database, recent orders from a billing service, and recommendations from a separate worker. The client may disconnect, the request may exceed its deadline, or one dependency may fail. In every case, the handler must stop waiting for unnecessary results, release database connections and sockets, and prevent abandoned child work from continuing in the background. The three dependencies support cooperative interruption but may perform cleanup before they stop, so immediate forced termination is unsafe. The handler also needs to distinguish an ordinary dependency failure from a request that was deliberately canceled, and it must not report success after the caller has gone away. The implementation should keep the stop signal separate from the returned business result, pass it through nested calls, and ensure that every component involved in the request observes it before the operation is considered finished.

Decision: How should the handler propagate one cooperative stop request through its dependent calls, clean up safely, and report cancellation separately from failure?
proposition: Pattern 'cancellation-token' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: cancellation-token: Give a caller-owned operation tree a one-way request to stop: pass a read-only cancellation signal through every cancellable call, observe it at safe points, clean up what was acquired, and report a distinct cancelled outcome without pretending that cooperative cancellation is forced termination. Problem: A request handler, background job or UI action starts work that fans out into nested calls, tasks or threads. When the caller disconnects, a deadline expires, the user presses stop or a sibling fails, merely abandoning the result leaves already-started work burning CPU, holding connections and calling dependencies. Force-killing a thread or process can interrupt a critical section and corrupt shared state, while a signal that is not propagated or observed cannot stop the call tree or make its cleanup visible to the joiner.

proposition: Pattern 'structured-concurrency' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: structured-concurrency: Confine the lifetimes of related concurrent subtasks to the dynamic extent of the operation that started them, so the parent cannot complete before its children do and failure or cancellation in either direction tears down the whole task tree in a controlled way. Problem: With raw spawn primitives (go, Thread.new, create_task, Task.Run, std::async, pthread_create) a child runs independently of the code that started it: when the parent fails, is cancelled or returns early, its children keep running, their failures are never observed, and shutdown must be coordinated by hand. The billing application already exposes a synchronous PaymentClient contract whose charge method accepts Money and an idempotency key, then returns a ChargeResult containing a provider-neutral reference and approved status. The only available payment vendor exposes a different API: amounts are decimal major units, currency is represented by vendor enums, submission is asynchronous and completes through a callback, and failures arrive as vendor-specific status objects. Business code must continue using the existing contract, and vendor types are forbidden from crossing the billing module. One implementation of PaymentClient must translate units and identifiers, reconcile the callback lifecycle, and map all documented failures into the target error contract. It must not add tax calculation, persistence, retries, or capabilities the vendor does not provide, and the vendor SDK cannot be changed. Integration tests must be able to exercise the application contract without loading the vendor library.

Decision: Choose where to preserve the billing application's existing synchronous charge contract while translating the vendor SDK's major-unit, callback-based protocol without leaking vendor types or adding unrelated behavior.
proposition: Pattern 'adapter' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: adapter: Present an existing component through the exact target contract its client already consumes, translating calls, results and boundary semantics without adding responsibilities or pretending a missing capability exists. Problem: An existing or foreign component has useful behaviour but speaks a different protocol: method names and signatures, data shapes, units, lifecycle, error model or sync/async contract do not satisfy the target. If every caller performs ad hoc conversion, semantics drift, vendor types leak and provider replacement becomes a cross-cutting rewrite; changing the adaptee or target may be impossible or too disruptive.

Candidate: copy-on-write: Let several handles of a value share one expensive body until the first write, which clones that body privately, so copying costs a pointer instead of a deep copy while every handle still behaves as an independent value. Candidate: version-number: Store a version token alongside each persistent record and make every write assert the token it read, so a write computed from stale data fails as a detectable conflict instead of silently overwriting a newer value. state:
A reporting platform must run recurring jobs through a reusable execution engine. The engine owns the complete lifecycle: it discovers enabled job definitions, prepares a tenant-specific context, starts a transaction, invokes the job, records the result, and decides whether to retry after a failure. Each customer supplies an operation that receives the prepared context and returns a report result; it must not call the engine's transaction, retry, or recording steps itself. The platform supports jobs written by several business teams, and a deployment may enable different jobs for different tenants. Job implementations must remain unaware of the engine internals, while the engine must be able to add tracing, timeout enforcement, and retry behavior without modifying every job. Registration is required because the engine discovers job definitions from configured modules, but the central decision being evaluated is who owns the execution sequence and when application behavior is invoked.

Decision: Choose whether the reporting engine or each customer job controls the run lifecycle, including setup, invocation, result recording, and retries.
proposition: Pattern 'inversion-of-control' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: inversion-of-control: Invert the direction of control between a reusable framework and application code: the framework owns the call flow and invokes the application's hooks at its extension points, so the generic sequence is reused while application code supplies only behaviour. Problem: A reusable component - framework, container, UI toolkit, event loop, test runner - must own the sequence of calls (main loop, request dispatch, component lifecycle), while the behaviour at each step is application-specific; if application code had to call the framework's steps itself, the generic flow could neither be reused as a whole nor be extended without modifying it.

proposition: Pattern 'producer-consumer' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: producer-consumer: Insert a bounded buffer between producers and consumers of work items so the two sides run concurrently at their own rates, the buffer absorbs bursts and slack, and its bound turns overload into backpressure, queueing or an explicit drop policy instead of unbounded growth. Problem: Production and consumption proceed at different rates: a fast producer outruns its consumer and either drops items or grows a backlog until memory runs out, a slow producer leaves consumers idle, and bursts arrive faster than they can be processed. The Order Service tracks fulfillment through Draft, Placed, Shipped, and Cancelled states. Today each order is a record with a status string, nullable payment reference, nullable shipping address, and nullable dispatch tracking number. Call sites construct these combinations directly, and validation happens only when an order is submitted or handed to the warehouse adapter. Consequently, a Draft can contain a payment reference, Shipped can lack tracking, and Cancelled can retain fulfillment data. The domain requires that each state expose only fields valid in that state, with no contradictory record constructible by application code. The Order API, Billing consumer, and Warehouse consumer must all consume the same state-specific representation. Decide how to encode the order lifecycle so construction rules are enforced centrally and downstream components can rely on the shape they receive without repeating validation.

Decision: Choose the representation that makes each order state carry only its valid fields and prevents callers from constructing contradictory lifecycle records.
proposition: Pattern 'make-illegal-states-unrepresentable' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: make-illegal-states-unrepresentable: Encode each domain rule in the shape of the data type so that values violating the rule cannot be constructed at all, replacing scattered run-time validation and defensive checks with a model in which only legal states exist. Problem: Domain values are modelled as one record with independent fields - a status tag plus several nullable or optional attributes, or a handful of booleans - so the type admits every combination of those fields, including the ones the business rules forbid. Consumers cannot trust the type: each branch re-checks which fields are meaningful, the same guard is written in several places (and forgotten in one), and illegal states become runtime bugs that surface when a code path finally combines the wrong flags.

The Grocer pricing service calculates basket totals in InvoicePricing, DiscountSchedule, and TaxRule. Today each component reads mutable configuration, a cached exchange rate, or counters hidden in the invoice while producing a result, so two identical baskets can receive different totals when requests are close together. The pricing rules must instead be predictable: given immutable basket lines, a snapshot of discount rules, the applicable tax jurisdictions, and currency conversion factors, the same inputs must always produce the same line totals, tax, and final amount. Each calculation must leave its inputs and any running total unchanged, while the application service remains responsible for loading snapshots and recording the resulting invoice. Tests must be able to exercise tax and rebate combinations without constructing repositories, clocks, or cached market data. The team also wants money arithmetic to remain valid at every combination boundary, including rejection of additions across different currencies. This decision concerns where pricing behavior lives and how it is evaluated, not how the invoice is persisted or how the web request is handled.

Decision: Move tax, rebate, and total calculations behind operations that derive results solely from explicit immutable inputs and never modify those inputs or shared state.
proposition: Pattern 'side-effect-free-function' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: side-effect-free-function: Put the model's logic into operations that compute a result from their inputs alone, so that a caller - and a test - can predict the result without knowing any state the operation might secretly touch. Problem: Reasoning about a design becomes guesswork when operations do more than return a result: the caller must read the implementation and every delegation to know which state a call changes, and no result can be reproduced in a test without recreating the state around it. As rules compose, the number of hidden interactions grows faster than the behaviour being built, so the model stops being safely predictable.
