Today each component reads mutable configuration, a cached exchange rate, or counters hidden in the invoice while producing a result, so two identical baskets can receive different totals when requests are close together. The pricing rules must instead be predictable: given immutable basket lines, a snapshot of discount rules, the applicable tax jurisdictions, and currency conversion factors, the same inputs must always produce the same line totals, tax, and final amount. Each calculation must leave its inputs and any running total unchanged, while the application service remains responsible for loading snapshots and recording the resulting invoice. Tests must be able to exercise tax and rebate combinations without constructing repositories, clocks, or cached market data. The team also wants money arithmetic to remain valid at every combination boundary, including rejection of additions across different currencies. This decision concerns where pricing behavior lives and how it is evaluated, not how the invoice is persisted or how the web request is handled.

Decision: Move tax, rebate, and total calculations behind operations that derive results solely from explicit immutable inputs and never modify those inputs or shared state.
proposition: Pattern 'iterator' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: iterator: Provide a way to access the elements of an aggregate object sequentially without exposing its underlying representation, by moving traversal state and the traversal algorithm out of the aggregate into a separate iterator object. Problem: Traversal leaks into every client: code that walks a collection has to know its storage layout (array indices, node links, hash buckets), the same loop is rewritten once per aggregate and once per client, and adding a new traversal order means changing the aggregate's interface — which is exactly what prevents algorithms from being written once and applied to any collection.

state:
The warehouse system accepts reservation commands for InventoryItem records. Each InventoryItem contains an on-hand quantity and a collection of Allocation records, where each Allocation names a Shipment by its ShipmentId and records a reserved quantity. The business rule is that the sum of active allocations for an item must never exceed its on-hand quantity. Two operators may reserve stock concurrently, and a failed command must not leave only some allocation changes persisted. Shipment records are maintained by another part of the system and are referenced by identity rather than modified during a reservation. The storage layer currently supports saving individual Allocation rows, which allows concurrent callers to interleave updates and violate the quantity rule. A command must load the relevant inventory record, apply the requested reservation to the records it owns, reject insufficient stock, and persist the complete change as one unit. The design must identify the narrowest boundary in which the quantity invariant can always be enforced.

Decision: Choose the ownership and transaction boundary that ensures active reservations for each inventory item can never exceed the available quantity under concurrent commands.
proposition: Pattern 'aggregate' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: aggregate: Define a transactional consistency boundary around domain objects: one root entity is the sole externally reachable entry point, owns internal entities and value objects, and is the only object application code modifies directly; each command loads and commits one root instance, while other roots are referenced by identity and coordinated separately. Problem: Business rules relate several objects at once - an order total that must stay within a credit limit, allocations that must never exceed stock - but if every object is writable on its own, no single place can enforce the rule at commit time. Concurrent callers interleave, persistence updates parts separately, and the invariant survives only while every caller remembers to check it; the model needs one owner and one atomic persistence boundary.

proposition: Pattern 'domain-service' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: domain-service: Model a significant domain operation - transfer, allocation, conversion - that is not a natural part of any single Entity or Value Object as a standalone, stateless service: declare its interface in the language of the model, make the operation name part of the ubiquitous language, and use it judiciously so services never strip entities and value objects of their behaviour. Problem: Some operations of the ubiquitous language - transferring funds, allocating cargo, pricing a basket, converting money - span several model elements and fit none of them: attaching the operation to an arbitrary entity turns that object into a script for someone else's job, and scattering it across callers leaves the rule unnamed and unowned. The recurring decision is whether to force the operation onto an object that does not really own it, or to model it explicitly as a service.

proposition: Pattern 'application-service' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: application-service: Give each externally callable business use case a thin, stateless application boundary that translates a request, loads the required aggregates, delegates every invariant to the domain model, commits one local unit of work, and returns a stable result without exposing domain objects. Problem: A business operation may need to load several aggregates, ask a domain service for a decision, persist the result, record an event and commit atomically. If an HTTP controller, CLI command, queue handler and scheduler each assemble that sequence, transaction scope, authorization, idempotency, error mapping and event handling drift. The application service gives that use case one explicit owner, while the domain model remains the owner of business truth.

proposition: Pattern 'copy-on-write' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: copy-on-write: Let several handles of a value share one expensive body until the first write, which clones that body privately, so copying costs a pointer instead of a deep copy while every handle still behaves as an independent value. Problem: A value with an expensive body (large buffer, collection, tree, document) is copied eagerly on assignment, argument passing and return even though most copies are never modified: time and memory are spent duplicating data that would have stayed identical. The naive fix - handing out one mutable object behind several handles - breaks the copy contract, and unrelated parts of the program then observe each other's writes.

proposition: Pattern 'event-aggregator' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: event-aggregator: Funnel the events of many source objects into one hub that owns the subscription wiring, so that subscribers register once with the aggregator instead of tracking down and registering with every publisher. Problem: Many components raise events and many components want to react: if every consumer registers directly with every producer, each consumer has to find the sources and subscribe to each event type separately, each producer accumulates knowledge of who listens, and both sides repeat the same registration and unsubscribe code at every pair. The trigger is a many-publisher / many-subscriber setting in which the wiring itself has become the maintenance problem.

proposition: Pattern 'table-data-gateway' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: table-data-gateway: Confine every SQL statement that touches one table or view inside a single gateway object whose methods take and return plain record structures, so that no other code contains SQL for that table and rows cross the boundary as data rather than as domain objects. Problem: Access to one table is spread across the codebase: SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE fragments are copied into every caller, nobody can say which queries a schema change will break, DBAs cannot find the SQL that needs tuning, and each caller has to know the dialect, the placeholders and the column order. The desired boundary is a single object that mediates all access to the whole table while the individual rows remain records (tuples, structs, hashes, DataRows) instead of becoming mapped objects.

proposition: Pattern 'dependency-injection' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: dependency-injection: Supply an object with the collaborators it needs from the outside — through its constructor, its setters/properties, or a dedicated injection interface — so it never constructs or looks a dependency up itself and every wiring decision is made once, in a composition root or container. Problem: An object that creates its own collaborators hard-wires a concrete class, a construction recipe and often a lifetime into itself: swapping the implementation for a test double, a second deployment or a new platform means editing the class, and the dependency graph stays invisible in the API. The recurring trigger is exactly the catalog's rule: an object should not create what it depends on — the caller, the framework or the composition root decides, and hands the dependency in.

proposition: Pattern 'composed-method' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: composed-method: Divide the work into methods that each perform one identifiable task, written as a short outline of invocations in which every operation sits at the same level of abstraction, so a reader grasps the task top-down and every change lands on one small, named step. Problem: A method accumulates several concerns at once: high-level policy ('validate the order, then charge it') interleaved with low-level detail (a loop index, a string concatenation, a counter), so the method grows long, needs comments to mark its sections, and changes for more than one reason. Readers must simulate the whole body to learn what it does, duplication hides inside similar-looking blocks, and anyone who must change one decision - a subclass in particular - ends up copying the method and editing it.

Candidate: poison-pill: Terminate queue consumers cooperatively by sending a reserved sentinel message that each consumer recognises as "no more work", so consumers drain the backlog and exit without a separate control channel or forced cancellation. Problem: A producer-consumer system must shut down, but its consumers block on an empty queue and the queue has no built-in "no more items" signal: callers either kill the workers mid-work and drop buffered items, or leave them blocked forever. Production has ended - how do the consumers learn that while still processing everything already queued?

proposition: Pattern 'either' is relevant to this decision. The warehouse system accepts reservation commands for InventoryItem records. Each InventoryItem contains an on-hand quantity and a collection of Allocation records, where each Allocation names a Shipment by its ShipmentId and records a reserved quantity. The business rule is that the sum of active allocations for an item must never exceed its on-hand quantity. Two operators may reserve stock concurrently, and a failed command must not leave only some allocation changes persisted. Shipment records are maintained by another part of the system and are referenced by identity rather than modified during a reservation. The storage layer currently supports saving individual Allocation rows, which allows concurrent callers to interleave updates and violate the quantity rule. A command must load the relevant inventory record, apply the requested reservation to the records it owns, reject insufficient stock, and persist the complete change as one unit. The design must identify the narrowest boundary in which the quantity invariant can always be enforced.

Decision: Choose the ownership and transaction boundary that ensures active reservations for each inventory item can never exceed the available quantity under concurrent commands.

A Fleet Telemetry service receives pressure readings from pressure sensors, temperature readings from refrigeration sensors, and cargo weights from scales. Each sensor supplies a numeric reading plus a unit code, while the Alerts component compares readings against threshold bands with lower and upper bounds and the Reporting component aggregates readings by hour. Readings can arrive in pascals, bar, or kilopascals; weights can arrive in kilograms, pounds, or tonnes. The Aggregation component stores readings in pascals and kilograms, but the Audit Export component must reproduce the original value and unit. The Threshold component must reject combinations whose dimensions do not match, and the API must accept input such as "2500 kg" without every endpoint implementing its own parser. Bare numeric fields are causing duplicate conversion factors, accidental addition of incompatible measurements, and inconsistent export formatting. The model must keep amount and unit together through ingestion, calculation, persistence, threshold evaluation, and display, while still allowing canonical-unit conversion at clear boundaries.

Decision: Choose the domain representation that keeps each measurement's amount and unit inseparable across ingestion, conversion, comparison, arithmetic, storage, and formatting.
proposition: Pattern 'quantity' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: quantity: Represent a dimensioned measurement as one value that carries its amount together with its unit, so that conversion, comparison, unit-compatible arithmetic and amount-plus-unit input/output all have a single owner and incompatible units cannot be combined by accident. Problem: Measurements are stored as bare numbers whose unit lives only in a variable name, a column comment or the reader's memory: the same physical quantity appears in metres in one place and in feet in another, conversion factors are retyped at every call site, adding two numbers of different dimensions compiles (or runs) happily, and parsing and formatting '3 km' is reinvented per feature. The recurring trigger is that an amount and its unit always change together and are one conceptual whole, so leaving them as two unconnected things makes the unit rules impossible to own.

proposition: Pattern 'recursive-descent-parser' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: recursive-descent-parser: Parse a small grammar by translating every rule directly into a function that consumes the tokens the rule matches and calls the functions of the rules it references, so the parser's control flow is the grammar itself and stays readable, debuggable and free of a code-generation step. Problem: A hand-written parser is the only option - no generator in the toolchain, or the grammar is a small DSL - yet the grammar is not a flat token sequence: alternatives must be chosen from lookahead, repetition must become a loop, and the natural grammar for expressions is left-recursive, which a top-down parser cannot translate directly. Candidate: applicative: Apply one pure function to several independent effectful computations, letting the chosen context instance fix the semantics of absence, failure, ordering, and concurrency; the combining structure is fixed before execution - that static shape is what enables batching, parallel scheduling, and static analysis - and an accumulating error instance reports every independent failure instead of short-circuiting on the first. Candidate: cancellation-token: Give a caller-owned operation tree a one-way request to stop: pass a read-only cancellation signal through every cancellable call, observe it at safe points, clean up what was acquired, and report a distinct cancelled outcome without pretending that cooperative cancellation is forced termination. DocumentPipeline, BlobStore, and Scanner expose one upload session object whose current stage is stored as a runtime field. The API allows callers to read bytes before the remote file has been opened, write after it has been committed, close it more than once, and acknowledge a checksum before scanning has completed. Existing validation reports these mistakes as runtime exceptions, and each caller implements a slightly different sequence of checks. The pipeline must support a fixed progression from creation through opening, writing, committing, scanning, and closing; each operation should be available only when its prerequisites are satisfied, and transitions should return the appropriately constrained session rather than mutating a boolean flag. Files abandoned mid-upload must remain harmless to close, while committed documents must not be modified. The application build must reject invalid operation sequences before deployment.

Decision: Should the upload session's lifecycle be represented in the API types so that only operations legal in the current stage can compile and each transition is checked?
proposition: Pattern 'typestate' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: typestate: Encode an object's state in its type - a type parameter or a distinct state type - so that only the operations legal in the current state exist and every transition is a checked, type-changing step. Problem: An object's methods are valid only in certain states (a closed file cannot be read, a client that has not connected cannot send), but the state lives in a runtime field: callers must remember the protocol, illegal calls still compile and fail at run time, and the legal sequences are documented rather than enforced.

proposition: Pattern 'protected-system' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: protected-system: Give a resource exactly one owning object whose published operations are the only way to touch it, so that every access is decided by an authorization check before the resource is used. Candidate: applicative: Apply one pure function to several independent effectful computations, letting the chosen context instance fix the semantics of absence, failure, ordering, and concurrency; the combining structure is fixed before execution - that static shape is what enables batching, parallel scheduling, and static analysis - and an accumulating error instance reports every independent failure instead of short-circuiting on the first. A Merchant Console asks a Pricing Service to calculate a promotion quote and must either receive a priced result or a business rejection before showing it to the customer. The Checkout service calls the external inventory system for each order line. CheckoutService depends on an ordinary StockLookup interface whose checkStock(sku) method returns a typed StockResult. The current integration uses a request-reply broker topic: each request must identify its destination, carry a correlation identifier and reply address, wait up to 800 ms, parse the response, and translate connection failures into an unavailable-stock result. An InventoryGateway implementation owns those details and invokes InventoryService for incoming replies. CheckoutService must not construct broker envelopes, select queues, inspect acknowledgements, or understand correlation metadata. A timeout must produce a deterministic local result, a retry must reuse the same correlation identifier, and malformed replies must be logged as integration errors without reaching the checkout business rules. The inventory system remains independently deployable and exposes no shared in-process interface.

state:
Meridian's desktop client currently performs separate remote requests to inventory availability, pricing, credit validation, and order persistence. A single checkout action therefore produces dozens of network calls, repeated authentication checks, and inconsistent partial results when a later request fails. The Merchandise service owns rich Order, SKU, Customer, and Pricing aggregates whose small methods must remain usable only inside that service. We need to expose one coarse SubmitOrder operation that gathers all required input, performs the existing use case locally, and returns one durable order identifier plus any rejection details. The network adapter may coordinate calls to internal collaborators but must not contain pricing, credit, or inventory rules. Its request and response need stable serializable shapes that do not expose the internal object graph, and the desktop client must be able to complete checkout in one remote round trip.

Decision: Decide where to place a coarse, domain-free remote interface that lets one client action complete checkout in a single round trip while the service's fine-grained domain objects remain internal.
proposition: Pattern 'remote-facade' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: remote-facade: Provide a single coarse-grained facade over a web of fine-grained objects so that a remote client can complete a unit of work in one round trip, while the fine-grained objects keep their local-only interfaces and the facade stays free of domain logic. Problem: An object model tuned for in-process use has small objects with small methods and heavy interaction. Across a process boundary every one of those interactions becomes a marshalling, security and routing event, so one user action turns into dozens of remote calls; the decision is whether, and at which seam, to replace that chatty protocol with a few coarse operations.

Maple CMS is a small public website with separate URLs for the home page, article pages, tag search, and a newsletter form. HomePageController, ArticlePageController, TagSearchController, and NewsletterController currently share one dispatching servlet, but each has different inputs, validation rules, repository calls, and response pages. ArticlePageController must read an article slug, reject malformed values, load the article and comments, and select either an article page or a not-found page. TagSearchController must combine a query, tag, and pagination cursor, while NewsletterController must validate an email address, execute a subscription workflow, and choose between confirmation and error output. The team wants each logical page or form to have a clear home for request-specific behavior rather than placing that behavior in HTML files or extending the shared servlet with branches for every screen. The public site has little common request processing beyond ordinary logging, so introducing a large infrastructure layer solely for routing would be undesirable. Domain services may be shared, but transport parsing and view selection must remain independently testable for each page.

Decision: Should each page or form have a dedicated component that owns input parsing, validation, domain invocation, and response selection, or should one shared component multiplex all of these behaviors?
proposition: Pattern 'page-controller' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: page-controller: Give each logical page or form its own input controller that handles the requests addressed to it — reading the request, invoking domain logic and choosing the view — instead of routing every request through one shared handler. Problem: Dynamic pages repeat the same request handling: parse and validate the incoming request, call domain logic, pick a view, report errors. Without a per-page home for that logic it either spreads into templates or gets copied into every script; the recurring decision is whether one page or form owns its request handling, or whether a central controller multiplexes all of them.

ProcurementCore manages purchase requests, approvals, and receipt status, but it must obtain supplier status from AcmeERP through Acme's SOAP SDK and proprietary database views. The external system calls an accepted purchase PO-1042, an in-progress PO-1043, and a rejected PO-1044; Acme reports rejection reasons using financial codes, while ProcurementCore distinguishes supplier rejection from internal approval failure. Amounts arrive in minor units, quantities use case-sensitive UOM codes, and an ERP outage may surface as a timeout, SOAP fault, or HTTP error. Acme also changes SDK field names during planned upgrades. ProcurementCore must not expose Acme types, status codes, units, or failure meanings in its domain or REST contracts. Create a Procurement-owned boundary component that calls Acme, translates requests, results, units, and failures into ProcurementCore concepts, and prevents Acme-specific details from entering purchase aggregates or other callers.

proposition: Pattern 'anti-corruption-layer' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: anti-corruption-layer: Protect a downstream bounded context from a foreign model by making one explicitly owned boundary translate calls, data and failure semantics into the downstream language; unlike a mere wrapper, an anti-corruption layer prevents foreign concepts from becoming domain concepts. Problem: A bounded context must use a legacy application, packaged product, partner API or another context whose model it cannot control, and the same words carry different meanings on each side. Reusing the foreign SDK types and status codes directly makes its names, optionality, units, errors and version churn load-bearing parts of the local domain; translation then drifts across callers and every upstream change becomes a core-model change. Without an explicit boundary, the contexts become accidental conformists and neither can evolve independently.

ProcurementCore manages purchase requests, approvals, and receipt status, but it must obtain supplier status from AcmeERP through Acme's SOAP SDK and proprietary database views. The external system calls an accepted purchase PO-1042, an in-progress PO-1043, and a rejected PO-1044; Acme reports rejection reasons using financial codes, while ProcurementCore distinguishes supplier rejection from internal approval failure. Amounts arrive in minor units, quantities use case-sensitive UOM codes, and an ERP outage may surface as a timeout, SOAP fault, or HTTP error. Acme also changes SDK field names during planned upgrades. ProcurementCore must not expose Acme types, status codes, units, or failure meanings in its domain or REST contracts. Create a Procurement-owned boundary component that calls Acme, translates requests, results, units, and failures into ProcurementCore concepts, and prevents Acme-specific details from entering purchase aggregates or other callers.

Decision: Should ProcurementCore place Acme-specific calls, data, and failure semantics behind its own translation boundary?
proposition: Pattern 'make-illegal-states-unrepresentable' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: make-illegal-states-unrepresentable: Encode each domain rule in the shape of the data type so that values violating the rule cannot be constructed at all, replacing scattered run-time validation and defensive checks with a model in which only legal states exist. Problem: Domain values are modelled as one record with independent fields - a status tag plus several nullable or optional attributes, or a handful of booleans - so the type admits every combination of those fields, including the ones the business rules forbid. Consumers cannot trust the type: each branch re-checks which fields are meaningful, the same guard is written in several places (and forgotten in one), and illegal states become runtime bugs that surface when a code path finally combines the wrong flags.

proposition: Pattern 'quantity' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: quantity: Represent a dimensioned measurement as one value that carries its amount together with its unit, so that conversion, comparison, unit-compatible arithmetic and amount-plus-unit input/output all have a single owner and incompatible units cannot be combined by accident. Problem: Measurements are stored as bare numbers whose unit lives only in a variable name, a column comment or the reader's memory: the same physical quantity appears in metres in one place and in feet in another, conversion factors are retyped at every call site, adding two numbers of different dimensions compiles (or runs) happily, and parsing and formatting '3 km' is reinvented per feature. The recurring trigger is that an amount and its unit always change together and are one conceptual whole, so leaving them as two unconnected things makes the unit rules impossible to own.

CustomerProfileService, RecommendationService, and PermissionService run inside the same WebRequestSession and all need the Customer, Address, and Subscription records touched by the request. The current data loader performs an independent SELECT for every lookup, so the profile path and permission path can each create a separate Customer instance for the same customer_id. The profile path renames the customer, while the permission path compares a locally cached address and later writes its older copy, silently replacing the new value. Repeated access also causes avoidable database traffic. The shared session must keep one authoritative in-memory instance per row for the duration of the request, including objects first reached through different queries, while still allowing the loader to retrieve related addresses only when a caller actually reads them. Session completion must discard the registry so the next request does not reuse stale state, and objects used by concurrent requests must never be shared across session boundaries.

Decision: Whether WebRequestSession should return the same in-memory customer, address, and subscription instances on repeated and cross-service lookups within one request.
proposition: Pattern 'identity-map' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: identity-map: Guarantee that within one session every database row is represented by exactly one in-memory object, by keeping a keyed registry of loaded objects that every load consults before hitting the database. Problem: Two code paths in the same session load the same row into two different objects: updates through one are invisible to the other, the last flush silently wins, and every load pays the remote-call cost again. The catalog states the invariant as: the same row must never be two different in-memory objects in one session.

proposition: Pattern 'unit-of-work' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: unit-of-work: Maintain a list of the objects affected by one business transaction and write their changes to the database in a single ordered flush, so that each business operation commits exactly once and in a consistent state. Problem: A business operation touches several objects, and writing each change as it happens produces many small database calls, keeps a transaction open for the whole interaction, and leaves the database inconsistent whenever a later step fails. Nobody can say which rows one operation will change, deletes and inserts arrive in an order the database rejects, and the same object is often written twice because two code paths each saved their own copy.

The Fulfillment Console reads and edits order lines from the legacy relational database. OrderSearchService currently embeds SELECT statements, OrderEntryService repeats INSERT statements, and OrderAdjustmentService contains UPDATE and DELETE statements for the same table. Each component knows placeholder syntax, column order, and date conversion rules. A schema change to the order_lines table therefore requires searching the entire repository, and the DBA cannot identify all statements that require tuning. Introduce one OrderLinesData component that owns every SQL operation for that table. Its methods accept and return simple record structures, while callers receive formatted rows or edited records. Keep transaction control in the services, keep formatting in the presentation layer, and prohibit direct table access from controllers and domain rules. Include read, insert, update, and delete operations in the component, with a small integration test that proves no SQL remains elsewhere.

proposition: Pattern 'state-colocation' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: state-colocation: Keep each piece of presentation state in the component closest to where it is used — down to the single component that owns and reads it — instead of hoisting it to a common ancestor or a global store, so that a change touches only the smallest part of the view that can observe it. Problem: State gets hoisted 'just in case': a value only one component reads is lifted to the screen or application root, or pushed into one global store, because someone may want it later. The consequences are components that receive props they never read, updates that invalidate far more of the UI than the value's actual consumers, an unclear owner for each value, and tests that must assemble the whole state container to exercise one field. The recurring decision is where a new piece of state should live: keep it at the smallest scope that actually needs it.

proposition: Pattern 'assertion' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: assertion: Express a model object's preconditions, postconditions and class invariants as executable, side-effect-free predicates at the operations that must uphold them, so a broken contract fails at its boundary instead of remaining a comment or surfacing later as corrupt state. This pattern is for design-by-contract correctness checks, not routine validation of untrusted input or test-only assertions. Problem: Model rules - a balance never below its floor, a period whose end follows its start, a status that cannot move backwards - are left in comments, documents and team memory while constructors and mutators check nothing. proposition: Pattern 'cursor-pagination' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: cursor-pagination: Bound what a read boundary returns for a large or changing ordered collection by sending one page plus an opaque continuation token that pins the filter and ordering, so clients advance deterministically without offsets and without watching rows move under them. Decision: Should all SQL for each database table be confined to one component whose methods exchange plain record structures, rather than leaving statements in transaction scripts?
proposition: Pattern 'aggregate' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: aggregate: Define a transactional consistency boundary around domain objects: one root entity is the sole externally reachable entry point, owns internal entities and value objects, and is the only object application code modifies directly; each command loads and commits one root instance, while other roots are referenced by identity and coordinated separately. Problem: Business rules relate several objects at once - an order total that must stay within a credit limit, allocations that must never exceed stock - but if every object is writable on its own, no single place can enforce the rule at commit time. Concurrent callers interleave, persistence updates parts separately, and the invariant survives only while every caller remembers to check it; the model needs one owner and one atomic persistence boundary.

proposition: Pattern 'monitor-object' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: monitor-object: Serialise concurrent method invocations on a shared object by giving the object its own lock and condition variables, so that only one method executes inside it at a time and methods that cannot proceed wait cooperatively instead of polling. Problem: Objects shared by several threads expose their state through ordinary methods, and nothing stops concurrent callers from interleaving inside those methods, corrupting the invariants they were written to maintain. proposition: Pattern 'producer-consumer' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: producer-consumer: Insert a bounded buffer between producers and consumers of work items so the two sides run concurrently at their own rates, the buffer absorbs bursts and slack, and its bound turns overload into backpressure, queueing or an explicit drop policy instead of unbounded growth. Problem: Production and consumption proceed at different rates: a fast producer outruns its consumer and either drops items or grows a backlog until memory runs out, a slow producer leaves consumers idle, and bursts arrive faster than they can be processed. The Order Service lets clients edit an order as one business unit. An Order owns its line items, shipment address, and payment allocations; removing a line must remove its persisted row, while adding a line and changing the shipping address must succeed or fail together. Clients never address lines or addresses directly, and the database exposes no endpoint that loads or saves them independently. The persistence layer must translate this object graph to the relational tables and coordinate the complete write, including deletions and optimistic version checks, without exposing the physical table layout to callers. A recent release persisted an address change while its new line failed, and support traced three similar partial writes to callers sequencing table operations by hand.

proposition: Pattern 'event-message' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: event-message: Announce that something has happened by publishing an immutable, self-describing event message - a past fact that expects no reply - on a channel, so that any number of interested receivers can react without the producer knowing who they are or what they do. Problem: A component has completed a state change that other parts of the system care about, but it must not - and usually cannot - know which ones care. Calling each interested party directly couples the producer to every consumer, to their availability and to their processing order, and every new consumer (search index, audit, notification, analytics) forces a change and a redeploy in the producer. The trigger is open-ended interest: something changed, and the set of parties wanting to know is neither closed nor known at compile time.

state:
The Orders application lets a planner revise an order for up to 45 minutes. One workspace can change the order header, line items, discounts, and shipping address, and those pieces must never be accepted as a partially updated cluster. The Order Service stores child records in separate tables, while clients may edit through the desktop app, a partner API, or a batch import. A revision stamp currently exists only on the header, so an address can change while an outdated line-item form is still open. Callers would have to discover and verify every affected child, which is error-prone and does not protect changes made by another workflow. The concurrency decision must cover the order and all of its members as one consistency boundary, without holding database locks for the full 45-minute editing period. A guard attached to the order root should therefore be checked whenever any member changes, while unrelated customer records remain independently editable.

Decision: Choose one shared concurrency guard for the order header and every line, discount, and address it contains, rather than requiring callers to coordinate each child separately.
proposition: Pattern 'coarse-grained-lock' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: coarse-grained-lock: Give a cluster of objects that must change together one shared lock — held on the cluster's root object, on a lock entry keyed by that root, or on a version token the root carries — so a caller locks one thing instead of discovering and locking every member. Problem: Changing one object really means changing a cluster: an edit that touches any member (a line item, an address, a child entity) has to be atomic with respect to the others, but a separate lock per member forces every caller to find and lock the whole set, makes the amount of locking grow with the object graph, and produces deadlocks whenever two callers acquire member locks in different orders.

proposition: Pattern 'pessimistic-offline-lock' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: pessimistic-offline-lock: Prevent conflicts between concurrent business transactions by making each one acquire an explicit, persisted lock on the data before it starts to use it, so that once work begins it is almost certain to complete without a concurrency conflict. proposition: Pattern 'optimistic-offline-lock' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: optimistic-offline-lock: Let a business transaction span several system transactions without holding a database lock by validating at commit that the records it read are still unchanged - and aborting or retrying the business transaction when they are not. Holding a database lock for the whole session is not acceptable because the session lasts minutes or hours while a conflict is unlikely.

Candidate: characterization-test: Pin the actual, currently deployed behaviour of existing code in committed reference artefacts (golden masters) so that a later edit can be distinguished from an accidental regression even when nobody can say what the code is supposed to do. The safety net therefore has to be built from observed behaviour: replay a corpus of real inputs through the untouched subject, capture everything observable, commit the result as the reference, and let every later run diff against it - pinning what the code does today before changing how it does it.

The Orders application lets a planner revise an order for up to 45 minutes. One workspace can change the order header, line items, discounts, and shipping address, and those pieces must never be accepted as a partially updated cluster. The Order Service stores child records in separate tables, while clients may edit through the desktop app, a partner API, or a batch import. A revision stamp currently exists only on the header, so an address can change while an outdated line-item form is still open. Callers would have to discover and verify every affected child, which is error-prone and does not protect changes made by another workflow. The concurrency decision must cover the order and all of its members as one consistency boundary, without holding database locks for the full 45-minute editing period. A guard attached to the order root should therefore be checked whenever any member changes, while unrelated customer records remain independently editable.

Decision: Choose one shared concurrency guard for the order header and every line, discount, and address it contains, rather than requiring callers to coordinate each child separately.
proposition: Pattern 'make-illegal-states-unrepresentable' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: make-illegal-states-unrepresentable: Encode each domain rule in the shape of the data type so that values violating the rule cannot be constructed at all, replacing scattered run-time validation and defensive checks with a model in which only legal states exist. Problem: Domain values are modelled as one record with independent fields - a status tag plus several nullable or optional attributes, or a handful of booleans - so the type admits every combination of those fields, including the ones the business rules forbid. Consumers cannot trust the type: each branch re-checks which fields are meaningful, the same guard is written in several places (and forgotten in one), and illegal states become runtime bugs that surface when a code path finally combines the wrong flags.

proposition: Pattern 'recursive-descent-parser' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: recursive-descent-parser: Parse a small grammar by translating every rule directly into a function that consumes the tokens the rule matches and calls the functions of the rules it references, so the parser's control flow is the grammar itself and stays readable, debuggable and free of a code-generation step. Problem: A hand-written parser is the only option - no generator in the toolchain, or the grammar is a small DSL - yet the grammar is not a flat token sequence: alternatives must be chosen from lookahead, repetition must become a loop, and the natural grammar for expressions is left-recursive, which a top-down parser cannot translate directly. Without a disciplined mapping from rules to functions the parser degenerates into ad-hoc index arithmetic and exception-driven backtracking, and errors end up without positions.

Candidate: function-composition: Combine a chain of small unary transformations into one reusable function by sequencing them with a composition combinator (compose/pipe), so the order of the steps is stated once, every step stays independently testable, and the chain itself becomes a value that can be named, passed and reassembled. The Billing application persists Invoice and Payment aggregates, while BillingService applies credit and cancellation rules and PaymentReminderJob repeatedly locates overdue invoices. Both components depend on an InvoiceStore contract that supports collection-like operations such as add, remove, getById, and overdueForDays, and returns domain objects rather than rows. The production implementation named PostgresInvoiceStore owns SQL, joins, ordering, and column conversion; a separate InMemoryInvoiceStore supports unit tests of BillingService without a database. Invoice and Payment classes must not contain table names, query strings, or persistence calls, and BillingService must never assemble SQL directly. The same logical operations are used by the interactive billing flow and the background job, so query behavior must be shared rather than reimplemented by each caller.

Decision: Should BillingService and PaymentReminderJob access persisted invoices through a domain-object collection contract, with all SQL isolated behind a replaceable implementation?
proposition: Pattern 'repository' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: repository: Mediates between the domain model and the data mapping layer with a collection-like interface, so domain code adds, removes and finds persistent objects as if they lived in memory and never constructs queries or touches persistence APIs itself. Problem: Persistence code spreads: every application service re-derives the same SQL or ORM queries, duplicate query logic drifts apart, table and column names leak into domain decisions, and testing domain rules without a database becomes impossible. Callers should be able to think in collections of domain objects instead of queries.

Shipping's persistence layer must handle Customer, Shipment, and Delivery records across multiple requests and worker processes. A customer may be loaded by the account service, cached by the rate service, and loaded again by the shipment service during the same session. Updates and cancellations must always affect the stored record, and a Shipment must retain a usable reference to its Customer even when the Customer object is not loaded. The current mapper creates a new in-memory object on every query and cannot reliably determine whether two copies refer to the same record. Define how each persistent entity carries a stable database handle so repeated loads, cache lookups, updates, deletions, and references all resolve to the same stored entity. Transient request-response payloads and immutable calculation results are out of scope and should not receive persistent identity semantics.

Decision: Decide where and how persistent entities retain their stable database identifier so repeated loads, references, cache entries, updates, and deletions resolve to the same stored record.
proposition: Pattern 'identity-field' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: identity-field: Store the relational primary key inside the object so that an in-memory instance and its database row are recognised as the same entity across sessions, caches and process restarts, instead of relying on object identity. Problem: Mappers, identity maps and unit-of-work bookkeeping need a stable handle on every object: without a key carried by the object there is no way to tell whether two instances are the same row, which row an UPDATE or DELETE must touch, or what value a referring row should store - and loading the same row twice silently produces two divergent objects.

Problem: A value object - a currency-aware money amount, a date range, an address, a coordinate - has no identity and no lifecycle of its own, so storing it as a row forces an invented key, an extra table and a join on every read. At the same time the object must not be flattened into loose primitives on the domain side: the cluster of attributes has to stay one typed concept with its invariants, and the mapper still has to write and read each of its fields. The decision is therefore where the fields go, not whether the object exists.

Shipping's persistence layer must handle Customer, Shipment, and Delivery records across multiple requests and worker processes. A customer may be loaded by the account service, cached by the rate service, and loaded again by the shipment service during the same session. Updates and cancellations must always affect the stored record, and a Shipment must retain a usable reference to its Customer even when the Customer object is not loaded. The current mapper creates a new in-memory object on every query and cannot reliably determine whether two copies refer to the same record. Define how each persistent entity carries a stable database handle so repeated loads, cache lookups, updates, deletions, and references all resolve to the same stored entity. Transient request-response payloads and immutable calculation results are out of scope and should not receive persistent identity semantics.

Decision: Decide where and how persistent entities retain their stable database identifier so repeated loads, references, cache entries, updates, and deletions resolve to the same stored record.
proposition: Pattern 'policy-based-design' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: policy-based-design: Assemble a class's behaviour, structure and defaults from small interchangeable policy units bound when the host type is instantiated, so that each orthogonal design decision can be varied independently instead of being frozen in the class's code. Problem: A reusable class hard-codes several independent design decisions - allocation, ownership, storage, threading, validation, error handling - inside its implementation, so a different combination is only reachable by editing or copying the class, while the runtime Strategy alternative costs a virtual call per use and gives up the guarantee that the choice is fixed, inlineable and checked before the program runs.

Candidate: strategy: Define a family of algorithms, encapsulate each one behind a common operation, and make them interchangeable, so the algorithm a context executes can vary independently of the context and its clients - including at run time. proposition: Pattern 'stub' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: stub: Replace a collaborator with a test-specific stand-in that returns canned answers, so the component under test can be driven down paths - success, empty, error, timeout - that the real collaborator cannot be made to produce on demand. Problem: The component under test receives indirect inputs through a collaborator, and the branch that must be exercised is selected by what that collaborator returns. The real collaborator will not produce the needed value on request: it is slow, remote, licensed, non-deterministic, or simply never returns the rare case - the empty result, the declined payment, the timeout - that the test exists for. Without a controllable replacement the test either cannot reach the path at all or has to provoke it through the production system, which is exactly what unit testing was supposed to avoid.

Candidate: anti-corruption-layer: Protect a downstream bounded context from a foreign model by making one explicitly owned boundary translate calls, data and failure semantics into the downstream language; unlike a mere wrapper, an anti-corruption layer prevents foreign concepts from becoming domain concepts. Problem: A bounded context must use a legacy application, packaged product, partner API or another context whose model it cannot control, and the same words carry different meanings on each side. Reusing the foreign SDK types and status codes directly makes its names, optionality, units, errors and version churn load-bearing parts of the local domain; translation then drifts across callers and every upstream change becomes a core-model change. Without an explicit boundary, the contexts become accidental conformists and neither can evolve independently.

Candidate: composed-method: Divide the work into methods that each perform one identifiable task, written as a short outline of invocations in which every operation sits at the same level of abstraction, so a reader grasps the task top-down and every change lands on one small, named step. proposition: Pattern 'copy-and-swap' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: copy-and-swap: Implement assignment (and any in-place state replacement) so that a failure while producing the new state leaves the target untouched: build the complete replacement off to the side, commit it with operations that cannot fail, and let the temporary's destructor or the garbage collector release the old state. Problem: A hand-written assignment has to tear down the old state and build a copy of the new one, but only the build can fail: destroying before allocating exposes a half-updated object when the allocation or the element copy throws, and the usual repair -- a self-assignment check plus manual rollback -- duplicates the per-member copying that already lives in the copy constructor. The trigger is an assignment (or, in a garbage-collected language, an in-place state replacement) that must satisfy the strong exception guarantee: either it completes, or the target still holds its previous value.

Candidate: aggregate: Define a transactional consistency boundary around domain objects: one root entity is the sole externally reachable entry point, owns internal entities and value objects, and is the only object application code modifies directly; each command loads and commits one root instance, while other roots are referenced by identity and coordinated separately. Candidate: deadline-propagation: Bound the total time and work of a logical request by carrying one deadline through its whole call tree: every hop forwards the remaining budget and the cancellation signal instead of inventing a fresh timeout, so work that can no longer succeed is abandoned at every level. The Catalog API serves product detail pages for a storefront. ProductService reads a product by tenant, SKU, and locale through ProductRepository, which queries PostgreSQL, while Redis stores previously read representations. Product detail traffic is heavily repeated, but each database read crosses a network boundary and consumes a connection. A miss should load the product from ProductRepository and populate Redis with a five-minute expiration; stored entries must be bounded by a maximum count and distinguished by tenant, SKU, locale, and schema version. When MerchandisingService updates a product, the database write commits first and the corresponding Redis entry must then be removed. Reads may remain stale for up to five minutes, but a stale entry must never be served after its expiration, and concurrent misses must not store incomplete or cross-tenant data. The Catalog API also publishes a small reference catalog that is loaded once and reused across requests. The implementation must choose where reads look, how misses populate the copy, how writes invalidate it, and how bounds are enforced without making Redis the authoritative source of product data.

Decision: Decide how the product read path should reuse prior results while PostgreSQL remains authoritative, including miss population, post-write invalidation, key completeness, and bounded expiration.
proposition: Pattern 'cache-aside' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: cache-aside: Place the cache beside the authoritative store and make the application own the protocol: look up the cache first, load the entry from the store on a miss and populate it with a TTL, and invalidate the entry right after each write to the store - so repeated reads stay cheap while the store, never the cache, decides what is true. Problem: A source of truth (relational database, downstream service, object store) is expensive or rate-limited for the read volume an application receives, while most reads repeat a small set of keys: without a cache every request pays the source-of-truth cost, and with an unmanaged cache the copies silently drift. The recurring decision is where the read path looks first, when a miss may populate the entry, and what a write must do so the cached copy stops lying.

Candidate: recursive-descent-parser: Parse a small grammar by translating every rule directly into a function that consumes the tokens the rule matches and calls the functions of the rules it references, so the parser's control flow is the grammar itself and stays readable, debuggable and free of a code-generation step. The Catalog API serves product detail pages for a storefront. ProductService reads a product by tenant, SKU, and locale through ProductRepository, which queries PostgreSQL, while Redis stores previously read representations. Product detail traffic is heavily repeated, but each database read crosses a network boundary and consumes a connection. A miss should load the product from ProductRepository and populate Redis with a five-minute expiration; stored entries must be bounded by a maximum count and distinguished by tenant, SKU, locale, and schema version. When MerchandisingService updates a product, the database write commits first and the corresponding Redis entry must then be removed. Reads may remain stale for up to five minutes, but a stale entry must never be served after its expiration, and concurrent misses must not store incomplete or cross-tenant data. The Catalog API also publishes a small reference catalog that is loaded once and reused across requests. The implementation must choose where reads look, how misses populate the copy, how writes invalidate it, and how bounds are enforced without making Redis the authoritative source of product data.

The Checkout API authenticates a customer and delegates card-funded order placement to the Funds API, which calls the Ledger Service and Payment Gateway. Security Operations requires a uniform record for every attempt, including requests rejected by authorization, calls that fail downstream, and successful transfers. Each event must identify the actor, action, target, correlation ID, attempt, and terminal result. Because the Ledger Service can roll back its database transaction, its audit record must not disappear with that rollback. The Funds API also needs a policy applied at one invocation boundary so engineers do not hand-code different schemas in Checkout, Ledger, and Payment Gateway. Events must be sent outside the business transaction to a separate integrity-protected destination, and the design must explicitly acknowledge that direct calls bypassing the Funds API are outside its coverage.

Decision: Choose where to enforce one consistent policy that captures attributable, outcome-aware security events around delegated payment operations without relying on each service to emit its own records.
proposition: Pattern 'audit-interceptor' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: audit-interceptor: Declare an audit policy at an invocation seam that records the actor, action, target, correlation id and both attempt and terminal outcome around a delegated operation, then sends the structured event to a dedicated integrity-protected sink, so security accountability is consistent without inline logging in every service. Problem: Security-relevant operations (privileged actions, state changes and access to sensitive data) must be attributable, but inline logging misses denied and failed attempts, varies in schema, can leak raw arguments and disappears with a rolled-back transaction. Teams also need to cover components they cannot modify without pretending that a proxy sees calls that bypass it.

proposition: Pattern 'secure-logger' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: secure-logger: Record security-relevant events through a single logging chokepoint and chain every record's authenticator to its predecessor, so that altering, deleting, reordering or truncating the log is detectable by an independent verifier rather than merely inconvenient for the party being recorded. Problem: The audit trail exists, but the party it records - a privileged operator, a compromised service, the application itself - can also rewrite it: files are appendable and rotatable by the same process that writes them, there is no gap detection when a record or a whole file disappears, and nobody can prove after the fact that a log line is the line that was written. The log answers questions only as long as everyone trusts the host that produced it.

Candidate: version-number: Store a version token alongside each persistent record and make every write assert the token it read, so a write computed from stale data fails as a detectable conflict instead of silently overwriting a newer value. The Account Server keeps user sessions alive inside a long-running process, while the Session Handler receives an object representing the signed-in user's preferences, active device list, and messaging service. On logout, the Account Server must invalidate the handler's ability to use that session immediately, even if the handler continues running or has copied the object reference elsewhere. Active administrative sessions and the underlying user account must not be destroyed, and a later login must receive a fresh session rather than a resurrected one. Logout is issued by a separate session-control service and must not depend on the handler acknowledging a message. Calls already in progress may complete, but any call started after logout must be rejected, including calls through related objects returned from the original session.

Decision: Select the approach that lets an independent control service invalidate future session use after logout without destroying the account or requiring the handler's cooperation.

Problem: A capability is just a reference, so once a collaborator has been given access to an object there is no built-in way to take it back: the grantor can destroy the object, ask the collaborator to stop, or leave the access standing. The recurring decision is how to grant access that is bounded in time - temporary use of a file, a service object, a session, an account - while keeping a control that only the grantor holds.

A graph database supplies a custom forward iterator over immutable node records. Its dereference, increment, and advancement operations intentionally remain implementation details so that only the iterator facade controls traversal, reference lifetime, and boundary behavior. A reusable iterator adapter library needs to invoke those core operations while implementing the standard iterator operations and allowing only the adapter's traversal hooks, not the complete private surface of the iterator, to be reached. Establish a named internal access gateway that the custom iterator alone authorizes, and let the adapter call through that gateway to perform dereference and movement. The adapter must not obtain direct access to the stored node pointer, the iterator's comparison internals, or unrelated state. The result must continue to compile with the standard facade and must prevent arbitrary user code from invoking the core hooks directly.

Decision: Choose how to give the iterator adapter compile-time access to the custom iterator's core hooks without exposing its storage or unrelated private operations.
proposition: Pattern 'aggregate' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: aggregate: Define a transactional consistency boundary around domain objects: one root entity is the sole externally reachable entry point, owns internal entities and value objects, and is the only object application code modifies directly; each command loads and commits one root instance, while other roots are referenced by identity and coordinated separately. Problem: Business rules relate several objects at once - an order total that must stay within a credit limit, allocations that must never exceed stock - but if every object is writable on its own, no single place can enforce the rule at commit time. Concurrent callers interleave, persistence updates parts separately, and the invariant survives only while every caller remembers to check it; the model needs one owner and one atomic persistence boundary.

proposition: Pattern 'request-reply' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: request-reply: Let a sender obtain a result or a domain error from an asynchronous or remote receiver by pairing each request with a correlated reply, and give the missing reply a defined outcome: timeout, cancellation and disposal of late replies. Problem: Messaging is one-way, but the sender frequently needs a return value or a domain error from the receiver before it can continue. Without an agreed reply destination, a way to match replies to requests, and a rule for what happens when no reply arrives, the caller either blocks forever, mis-associates the next reply with the wrong request, or accumulates pending state it never cleans up.

proposition: Pattern 'entity' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: entity: Give a domain concept a stable identity that survives attribute changes, representation changes and time, and define its equality, lifecycle and lookup in terms of that identity instead of in terms of its attributes. Problem: A model that compares objects by their attributes cannot answer whether two instances are the same thing: a customer whose e-mail and plan changed looks like a different customer, while two distinct people who share a name look like one. References held by other objects, caches and audit records break silently, and every state change forces callers to re-identify the object.

Northstar Health needs a shared credential vault used by the billing service, the reporting service, and several scheduled jobs. Today each caller retrieves a signing key, decrypts the value itself, and performs its own role check, so authorization logic is duplicated and the batch exporter can bypass checks introduced elsewhere. The Vault API team will create a KeyStore component that retains all key material and connection handles internally. Its published operations will include Sign, Decrypt, and Rotate only; no method will return raw bytes, key identifiers with embedded secrets, or the underlying provider client. Callers will provide the subject, requested operation, and resource scope, and the component will consult the existing AccessRules service before acting. Revocation and tenant changes must take effect on the next operation, including calls from retries and recovery workers. The migration may wrap legacy provider clients, but direct provider credentials must never be distributed to application code or retained in process memory beyond the vault boundary.

Decision: Decide whether all credential use should be confined behind a single owning KeyStore component instead of exposing key material and distributing authorization checks across callers.
proposition: Pattern 'protected-system' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: protected-system: Give a resource exactly one owning object whose published operations are the only way to touch it, so that every access is decided by an authorization check before the resource is used. Problem: A resource - a credential store, a file tree, a socket, a connection pool, a device handle - is referenced from many places. When each use site performs its own permission check, the checks drift, new code paths forget them, and the resource remains reachable as a raw handle, so a missing check cannot even be detected. The recurring trigger: one object can own the resource and clients can be made to hold only that object, so ownership itself can carry the enforcement.

proposition: Pattern 'complete-mediation' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: complete-mediation: Route every access to a protected object through a single decision point that re-checks authority at the point of use, so that no later access — on any path, including retry, batch, recovery and maintenance paths — can rely on an earlier check. Problem: Authority is verified where access is first obtained (login, connection setup, first call) and every later path to the object then trusts that context: internal callers, cached handles, background jobs, admin and recovery code reach the object unchecked, and a revocation does not take effect because the earlier decision is remembered. Between checking an access right and performing the access there is also a window in which the checked facts can change.

proposition: Pattern 'composite-entity' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: composite-entity: Represent a cluster of related, dependent objects through one coarse-grained entity that owns them and persists and synchronises the whole graph as a single unit of work, so clients never reference, sequence, or save the parts themselves. Coined for coarse-grained EJB business objects; its modern form is the aggregate root with cascading or owned mappings. Problem: A business concept clients treat as one thing (an order with its lines, a customer with addresses) is really a cluster of dependent objects, and persisting each part separately forces callers to know the parts, save them in the right order in the right transaction, delete the ones that left the relationship, and absorb a leaking physical schema. The catalog trigger: a cluster of related objects must persist and synchronise as one unit.

proposition: Pattern 'copy-on-write' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: copy-on-write: Let several handles of a value share one expensive body until the first write, which clones that body privately, so copying costs a pointer instead of a deep copy while every handle still behaves as an independent value. Problem: A value with an expensive body (large buffer, collection, tree, document) is copied eagerly on assignment, argument passing and return even though most copies are never modified: time and memory are spent duplicating data that would have stayed identical. The naive fix - handing out one mutable object behind several handles - breaks the copy contract, and unrelated parts of the program then observe each other's writes.

proposition: Pattern 'version-number' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: version-number: Store a version token alongside each persistent record and make every write assert the token it read, so a write computed from stale data fails as a detectable conflict instead of silently overwriting a newer value. Problem: Two sessions read the same record, both edit it, and the later write wins: the earlier update vanishes without any error (the lost update). Once the read-modify-write spans more than one system transaction the database cannot tell 'this is the record I read' from 'this record changed under me', so no code path can notice in time - unless the record itself carries a per-row token that changes on every write and the write tests that token before committing.

Problem: A source of truth (relational database, downstream service, object store) is expensive or rate-limited for the read volume an application receives, while most reads repeat a small set of keys: without a cache every request pays the source-of-truth cost, and with an unmanaged cache the copies silently drift. The recurring decision is where the read path looks first, when a miss may populate the entry, and what a write must do so the cached copy stops lying.

Northstar Health needs a shared credential vault used by the billing service, the reporting service, and several scheduled jobs. Today each caller retrieves a signing key, decrypts the value itself, and performs its own role check, so authorization logic is duplicated and the batch exporter can bypass checks introduced elsewhere. The Vault API team will create a KeyStore component that retains all key material and connection handles internally. Its published operations will include Sign, Decrypt, and Rotate only; no method will return raw bytes, key identifiers with embedded secrets, or the underlying provider client. Callers will provide the subject, requested operation, and resource scope, and the component will consult the existing AccessRules service before acting. Revocation and tenant changes must take effect on the next operation, including calls from retries and recovery workers. The migration may wrap legacy provider clients, but direct provider credentials must never be distributed to application code or retained in process memory beyond the vault boundary.

proposition: Pattern 'table-data-gateway' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: table-data-gateway: Confine every SQL statement that touches one table or view inside a single gateway object whose methods take and return plain record structures, so that no other code contains SQL for that table and rows cross the boundary as data rather than as domain objects. Problem: Access to one table is spread across the codebase: SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE fragments are copied into every caller, nobody can say which queries a schema change will break, DBAs cannot find the SQL that needs tuning, and each caller has to know the dialect, the placeholders and the column order. The desired boundary is a single object that mediates all access to the whole table while the individual rows remain records (tuples, structs, hashes, DataRows) instead of becoming mapped objects.

proposition: Pattern 'monitor-object' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: monitor-object: Serialise concurrent method invocations on a shared object by giving the object its own lock and condition variables, so that only one method executes inside it at a time and methods that cannot proceed wait cooperatively instead of polling. Problem: Objects shared by several threads expose their state through ordinary methods, and nothing stops concurrent callers from interleaving inside those methods, corrupting the invariants they were written to maintain. The race is then papered over with ad-hoc locking, sleeps and busy-wait loops scattered through client code. The recurring decision is whether the object itself should own the serialisation (and the scheduling) of its methods instead of leaving that discipline to every caller.

proposition: Pattern 'composed-method' is relevant to this decision. proposition: Pattern 'copy-and-swap' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: copy-and-swap: Implement assignment (and any in-place state replacement) so that a failure while producing the new state leaves the target untouched: build the complete replacement off to the side, commit it with operations that cannot fail, and let the temporary's destructor or the garbage collector release the old state. Problem: A hand-written assignment has to tear down the old state and build a copy of the new one, but only the build can fail: destroying before allocating exposes a half-updated object when the allocation or the element copy throws, and the usual repair -- a self-assignment check plus manual rollback -- duplicates the per-member copying that already lives in the copy constructor. The trigger is an assignment (or, in a garbage-collected language, an in-place state replacement) that must satisfy the strong exception guarantee: either it completes, or the target still holds its previous value.

Candidate: monad: Give a computation's effect (absence, failure, asynchrony, I/O, state) a type of its own with a unit and a bind operation, so that a sequence of steps in which each step depends on the previous value composes into one pipeline while bind propagates the effect automatically. Contoso deploys the same Tenant Portal at several sites. One site uses LDAP with password authentication, another uses Kerberos tickets, and a cloud region accepts OIDC tokens; a local emergency deployment uses a database-backed password check. The Login Controller currently branches among these checks and different callers also duplicate lockout, error translation, and audit behavior. The new design needs a deployment-configured component registry that selects a verifier by tenant and channel without changing the controller or domain code. Each verifier must report either one normalized successful identity, including the directory identity and verified attributes, or an explicit reason such as expired evidence, unavailable provider, or rejected credential. Password-specific throttling must remain inside the password verification path and must not disable Kerberos or federated logins. The Login Controller must not import LDAP, Kerberos, OIDC, or database-verification APIs, and adding a fourth mechanism must require only a new implementation plus deployment configuration. Verification failures must be audited without logging secrets or complete tokens.

Decision: Decide whether to isolate mechanism-specific credential checks behind a deployment-selected verification boundary that returns a uniform success or explicit failure to the login workflow.
proposition: Pattern 'authenticator' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: authenticator: Verify the identity a subject claims from mechanism-specific credentials and return one normalized principal or an explicit failure, so callers can select or replace password, certificate, token, Kerberos or passkey verification without coupling login, session, audit or authorization code to a credential format. Problem: A request must decide whether presented evidence proves a subject's identity, but password, client-certificate, OIDC/JWT, Kerberos and passkey checks differ by deployment, tenant and channel. If one mechanism is hard-wired into the request path, every caller learns its credential format; adding OIDC, migrating from LDAP or accepting service tokens becomes a cross-cutting change, while comparison, retry/lockout and verifier-failure handling drift between endpoints.

proposition: Pattern 'poison-pill' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: poison-pill: Terminate queue consumers cooperatively by sending a reserved sentinel message that each consumer recognises as "no more work", so consumers drain the backlog and exit without a separate control channel or forced cancellation. Problem: A producer-consumer system must shut down, but its consumers block on an empty queue and the queue has no built-in "no more items" signal: callers either kill the workers mid-work and drop buffered items, or leave them blocked forever. Production has ended - how do the consumers learn that while still processing everything already queued?

The naive fix - handing out one mutable object behind several handles - breaks the copy contract, and unrelated parts of the program then observe each other's writes.
