The tax-reporting platform is replacing the untested ReportingEngine that reads monthly CSV exports from the TreasuryGateway and emits formatted PDF summaries. Production behavior is known mainly from support investigations: blank account codes sometimes remain blank, currency symbols vary by locale, and rows with malformed dates are skipped. The nightly ReportingJob must continue producing byte-identical PDFs while the engine is split into parser, calculation, and rendering components. There is no authoritative specification, and the team cannot interview the original author. Before refactoring, engineers need to replay a representative corpus of stored TreasuryGateway exports through the untouched engine and commit every observable result, including report text, row ordering, skipped records, and logged warnings. The new components must be checked against those committed reference artifacts on every build, even when a deliberate business change later makes the old behavior undesirable.

Decision: Decide whether to preserve the ReportingEngine's undocumented production behavior with committed reference artifacts before changing its internals, rather than write assertions from a guessed specification.
proposition: Pattern 'request-reply' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: request-reply: Let a sender obtain a result or a domain error from an asynchronous or remote receiver by pairing each request with a correlated reply, and give the missing reply a defined outcome: timeout, cancellation and disposal of late replies. Problem: Messaging is one-way, but the sender frequently needs a return value or a domain error from the receiver before it can continue. Without an agreed reply destination, a way to match replies to requests, and a rule for what happens when no reply arrives, the caller either blocks forever, mis-associates the next reply with the wrong request, or accumulates pending state it never cleans up.

ParcelHub consumes shipping events from several regional queues. Events may be JSON or Avro, and each carries a schema version, parcel identifier, weight, destination code, and optional declared value. Today QueueConsumer passes each message to RouteParcelHandler, CalculateChargeHandler, or ExceptionHandler before any validation, causing those handlers to repeat range checks and handle malformed payloads differently. A small number of events with negative weight, oversized strings, unknown versions, or invalid destination codes have reached downstream domain code. The platform team needs a single ingress component that checks payload shape, encoding, size, and permitted ranges for every message before dispatching to any handler, using versioned schemas supplied by SchemaRegistry. Validation failures must produce a dead-letter event with a reason code and must not invoke business components. The decision is whether to place these checks in the queue-consumer ingress path or in a shared handler hierarchy, given that every inbound message must pass through the checks exactly once before domain processing.

Decision: Choose where every inbound queue message receives schema, size, encoding, and range validation so malformed events cannot reach any business handler.
proposition: Pattern 'intercepting-validator' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: intercepting-validator: Insert one interception layer on the ingress path that validates every inbound message before any handler runs, so that input checking is uniform, central and impossible to forget per endpoint. Problem: Inbound data - HTTP requests, RPC messages, queue events, protocol frames - is validated inside each handler: every new endpoint re-implements parsing, range and encoding checks, rules drift between handlers, and some paths end up with no validation at all. The recurring decision is where to put validation so that all inbound data passes through it exactly once, before application logic.

proposition: Pattern 'durable-subscriber' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: durable-subscriber: Keep a publish-subscribe consumer's place while it is offline: the broker binds a stable subscription identity to retained messages or a committed position, then resumes delivery after reconnect until retention, expiry, or quota says the backlog is no longer available. Problem: A subscriber on a publish-subscribe channel can be unavailable during redeployment, maintenance, device disconnects, or scheduled batch work. A non-durable subscription drops messages published during that gap, so the design must choose a stable identity and broker-side state, then make finite retention, replay pressure, and at-least-once redelivery explicit; durable state prevents a gap only while that state remains available.

proposition: Pattern 'applicative' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: applicative: Apply one pure function to several independent effectful computations, letting the chosen context instance fix the semantics of absence, failure, ordering, and concurrency; the combining structure is fixed before execution - that static shape is what enables batching, parallel scheduling, and static analysis - and an accumulating error instance reports every independent failure instead of short-circuiting on the first. Problem: You have several independent computations - parse this field, fetch that record, validate this quantity - and a pure function that combines their results, but each result lives inside a context such as Option, Either/Result, List, Promise/Task, or Validation. The Meridian application gateway fronts three APIs: orders, invoices, and customer profiles. Each request must carry an authenticated principal, and the Policy Service must return a rule that permits the requested method, route, and tenant before the gateway forwards it. Recently added endpoints have been exposed when no matching rule was found, so the new requirement is that any route without an explicit grant, including unknown methods and newly introduced resources, receives no upstream access. A missing identity, an unavailable Policy Service, an unsupported token format, or an exception while evaluating a rule must also produce a rejection rather than forwarding the request. Public product documentation is served by a separate listener whose small set of routes is explicitly listed, while customer and invoice traffic never uses that listener. The gateway must record the reason for each rejection without logging credentials or sensitive invoice fields.

Decision: Should the gateway reject every request that lacks an explicit matching grant, including unmatched routes, invalid identities, and policy-evaluation failures?
proposition: Pattern 'fail-safe-defaults' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: fail-safe-defaults: Make denial the default outcome of every access decision, so that access exists only where it has been explicitly granted and no missing rule, missing identity or failed check can silently permit an operation. Problem: Authorisation written as exclusion: code asks 'is this forbidden?' and everything the deny rules do not cover - a route added last sprint, a new operation, an unknown role, an object-level case, a request the parser cannot classify - is permitted by omission. The failure modes compound it: a missing principal, an unreachable policy source or an exception inside the check falls through to the permissive branch, so the code paths that look most careful are the ones that open the system.

The Meridian application gateway fronts three APIs: orders, invoices, and customer profiles. Each request must carry an authenticated principal, and the Policy Service must return a rule that permits the requested method, route, and tenant before the gateway forwards it. Recently added endpoints have been exposed when no matching rule was found, so the new requirement is that any route without an explicit grant, including unknown methods and newly introduced resources, receives no upstream access. A missing identity, an unavailable Policy Service, an unsupported token format, or an exception while evaluating a rule must also produce a rejection rather than forwarding the request. Public product documentation is served by a separate listener whose small set of routes is explicitly listed, while customer and invoice traffic never uses that listener. The gateway must record the reason for each rejection without logging credentials or sensitive invoice fields.

PolicyDecisionService evaluates access requests by reading tenant claims and asking ClassificationClient.classify(documentId) for a document classification. proposition: Pattern 'cache-aside' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: cache-aside: Place the cache beside the authoritative store and make the application own the protocol: look up the cache first, load the entry from the store on a miss and populate it with a TTL, and invalidate the entry right after each write to the store - so repeated reads stay cheap while the store, never the cache, decides what is true. Problem: A source of truth (relational database, downstream service, object store) is expensive or rate-limited for the read volume an application receives, while most reads repeat a small set of keys: without a cache every request pays the source-of-truth cost, and with an unmanaged cache the copies silently drift. proposition: Pattern 'quantity' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: quantity: Represent a dimensioned measurement as one value that carries its amount together with its unit, so that conversion, comparison, unit-compatible arithmetic and amount-plus-unit input/output all have a single owner and incompatible units cannot be combined by accident. The merchant checkout application has a PaymentScreen implemented with the company UI framework. The framework constructs this screen, supplies its window, and invokes callbacks for field changes and the Pay button. The screen currently decides whether the card number, billing address, and purchase limit are acceptable, and it decides whether the user may advance to confirmation. Unit tests cannot construct PaymentScreen without starting a window server and dispatching framework events, so these rules are checked only through a slow browser suite. The required change is to make every checkout eligibility decision verifiable in a fast, synchronous test while preserving the framework behavior that renders fields, forwards user events, and starts navigation. The team must choose where the eligibility and progression rules should reside without changing the externally visible checkout flow, adding network calls to the fast tests, or duplicating the rules between the screen and the tests.

Decision: Decide where the payment validation and navigation rules should live so they can be verified synchronously outside the framework-controlled screen.
proposition: Pattern 'humble-object' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: humble-object: Move as much logic as possible out of a program element that the framework calls but tests cannot instantiate - a UI control, callback, entry point or active object - into a plain collaborator that unit tests drive synchronously, leaving the original element as a thin adapter without decisions. Problem: The element the host invokes cannot be exercised in a test: constructing it needs the framework's environment (event loop, window, container, thread), so driving it means slow asynchronous tests with framework setup, or none at all. Because the decisions were written where the trigger arrives, business rules live inside the untestable element: they are verified only by expensive end-to-end runs, they cannot be test-first, and every framework upgrade threatens them.

proposition: Pattern 'copy-and-swap' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: copy-and-swap: Implement assignment (and any in-place state replacement) so that a failure while producing the new state leaves the target untouched: build the complete replacement off to the side, commit it with operations that cannot fail, and let the temporary's destructor or the garbage collector release the old state. Problem: A hand-written assignment has to tear down the old state and build a copy of the new one, but only the build can fail: destroying before allocating exposes a half-updated object when the allocation or the element copy throws, and the usual repair -- a self-assignment check plus manual rollback -- duplicates the per-member copying that already lives in the copy constructor. The trigger is an assignment (or, in a garbage-collected language, an in-place state replacement) that must satisfy the strong exception guarantee: either it completes, or the target still holds its previous value.

Candidate: poison-pill: Terminate queue consumers cooperatively by sending a reserved sentinel message that each consumer recognises as "no more work", so consumers drain the backlog and exit without a separate control channel or forced cancellation. The Feature Registry resolves a feature name to an immutable configuration record. The Registry Index checks its in-memory map, and the Remote Overlay Store may contain a newer revision for the same name. A lookup may legitimately find nothing: a feature can be disabled, not yet deployed, or intentionally absent from the overlay. The Feature Resolver needs to distinguish that ordinary absence from a malformed remote document, a timeout, and an authorization failure, since only the last three require diagnostics and retry behavior. When no record exists, the caller may apply a documented default and continue rendering the application. The current implementation returns null, which caused the Notification Center to dereference it and the Metrics Collector to count the absence as a successful zero-valued setting. Define the contract across Registry Index, Remote Overlay Store, Feature Resolver, Notification Center, and Metrics Collector so absence is explicit at every call site, while failures that require investigation still expose their reason and cannot be mistaken for a missing feature.

Decision: Choose the contract for a registry miss so callers must recognize ordinary absence without discarding or confusing actionable lookup failures.
proposition: Pattern 'option-maybe' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: option-maybe: Make the possible absence of a result part of the value and of the signature, so every caller has to decide what happens when nothing is there instead of meeting a null, a sentinel or a silently defaulted value at run time. Problem: A function has something to return for some inputs and nothing for others, but the signature does not say so: it returns a null reference, a sentinel (-1, empty string, NULL), an out-parameter, or a value that quietly means 'not found'. Callers forget the check, dereference the null or treat the sentinel as data, and the 'this case does not exist' path is discovered in production rather than at the call site.

Problem: A value with an expensive body (large buffer, collection, tree, document) is copied eagerly on assignment, argument passing and return even though most copies are never modified: time and memory are spent duplicating data that would have stayed identical. The naive fix - handing out one mutable object behind several handles - breaks the copy contract, and unrelated parts of the program then observe each other's writes.

The Feature Registry resolves a feature name to an immutable configuration record. The Registry Index checks its in-memory map, and the Remote Overlay Store may contain a newer revision for the same name. A lookup may legitimately find nothing: a feature can be disabled, not yet deployed, or intentionally absent from the overlay. The Feature Resolver needs to distinguish that ordinary absence from a malformed remote document, a timeout, and an authorization failure, since only the last three require diagnostics and retry behavior. When no record exists, the caller may apply a documented default and continue rendering the application. The current implementation returns null, which caused the Notification Center to dereference it and the Metrics Collector to count the absence as a successful zero-valued setting. Define the contract across Registry Index, Remote Overlay Store, Feature Resolver, Notification Center, and Metrics Collector so absence is explicit at every call site, while failures that require investigation still expose their reason and cannot be mistaken for a missing feature.

Decision: Choose the contract for a registry miss so callers must recognize ordinary absence without discarding or confusing actionable lookup failures.
proposition: Pattern 'compound-components' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: compound-components: Give a family of cooperating components one owner — the parent — that holds the shared state and publishes it implicitly to every child, so consumers compose the family declaratively while the parent alone enforces its invariants and behaviour. Problem: A widget only works when a parent and its children agree on one piece of state (which option is selected, which panel is open, whether a field is invalid), but the call site is the only place that knows the children. Holding the state at the call site means threading the value and its update callbacks into every child (prop drilling), and holding it in the children means the parent cannot enforce the family's invariants — exclusivity, ordering, keyboard behaviour — nor react to a child's change in one place. proposition: Pattern 'applicative' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: applicative: Apply one pure function to several independent effectful computations, letting the chosen context instance fix the semantics of absence, failure, ordering, and concurrency; the combining structure is fixed before execution - that static shape is what enables batching, parallel scheduling, and static analysis - and an accumulating error instance reports every independent failure instead of short-circuiting on the first. Problem: You have several independent computations - parse this field, fetch that record, validate this quantity - and a pure function that combines their results, but each result lives inside a context such as Option, Either/Result, List, Promise/Task, or Validation. A bind/await chain can imply a dependency that does not exist, serialize work, or stop at the first failure; you need a fixed applicative structure that combines the values while leaving failure and scheduling policy to the chosen instance.

proposition: Pattern 'version-number' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: version-number: Store a version token alongside each persistent record and make every write assert the token it read, so a write computed from stale data fails as a detectable conflict instead of silently overwriting a newer value. Problem: Two sessions read the same record, both edit it, and the later write wins: the earlier update vanishes without any error (the lost update). Once the read-modify-write spans more than one system transaction the database cannot tell 'this is the record I read' from 'this record changed under me', so no code path can notice in time - unless the record itself carries a per-row token that changes on every write and the write tests that token before committing.

proposition: Pattern 'side-effect-free-function' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: side-effect-free-function: Put the model's logic into operations that compute a result from their inputs alone, so that a caller - and a test - can predict the result without knowing any state the operation might secretly touch. As rules compose, the number of hidden interactions grows faster than the behaviour being built, so the model stops being safely predictable.

Candidate: coarse-grained-lock: Give a cluster of objects that must change together one shared lock — held on the cluster's root object, on a lock entry keyed by that root, or on a version token the root carries — so a caller locks one thing instead of discovering and locking every member. proposition: Pattern 'active-record' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: active-record: Make a domain object the record for one database row: keep the row's state, row-local behavior, and the methods that find and persist it together, so a small domain does not pay for a separate mapping layer. Problem: A simple relational domain still needs a choice about where persistence lives. A Data Mapper or gateway separates table I/O from the object but adds mapping code and a second place to navigate, while direct SQL leaks schema knowledge into callers; the recurring question is whether one row object can own its data and CRUD without hiding transaction boundaries or pretending to model cross-row rules.

proposition: Pattern 'producer-consumer' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: producer-consumer: Insert a bounded buffer between producers and consumers of work items so the two sides run concurrently at their own rates, the buffer absorbs bursts and slack, and its bound turns overload into backpressure, queueing or an explicit drop policy instead of unbounded growth. Problem: Production and consumption proceed at different rates: a fast producer outruns its consumer and either drops items or grows a backlog until memory runs out, a slow producer leaves consumers idle, and bursts arrive faster than they can be processed. Wiring the two sides together directly also couples their lifetimes and schedules - a synchronous hand-off makes the faster side wait for the slower - so neither side can be scaled, restarted or tested on its own.

proposition: Pattern 'dependency-injection' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: dependency-injection: Supply an object with the collaborators it needs from the outside — through its constructor, its setters/properties, or a dedicated injection interface — so it never constructs or looks a dependency up itself and every wiring decision is made once, in a composition root or container. Problem: An object that creates its own collaborators hard-wires a concrete class, a construction recipe and often a lifetime into itself: swapping the implementation for a test double, a second deployment or a new platform means editing the class, and the dependency graph stays invisible in the API. The recurring trigger is exactly the catalog's rule: an object should not create what it depends on — the caller, the framework or the composition root decides, and hands the dependency in.

proposition: Pattern 'quantity' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: quantity: Represent a dimensioned measurement as one value that carries its amount together with its unit, so that conversion, comparison, unit-compatible arithmetic and amount-plus-unit input/output all have a single owner and incompatible units cannot be combined by accident. The recurring trigger is that an amount and its unit always change together and are one conceptual whole, so leaving them as two unconnected things makes the unit rules impossible to own.

state:
The RuleKit service lets operations teams write policies such as "permit if tenant.acl contains owner and request.amount < limit". Its Lexer emits tokens, the PolicyParser builds a syntax tree, and PolicyEvaluator executes that tree. The grammar has ordered alternatives, repetitions, nested parenthesized terms, and left-recursive expression forms such as amount < limit and limit <= amount. The team forbids generated parser artifacts because policy syntax changes weekly and the production build has no code-generation stage. It also requires clear stack traces that identify the exact grammar production and input token, and the parser must make one forward pass without speculative rescanning. Engineering must decide how to organize parsing so that alternatives are selected with the available lookahead, repetitions become loops, and the expression grammar can still be represented without recursive calls that never return. The resulting tree remains consumed only by PolicyEvaluator and the policy formatter.

Decision: Choose the control-flow structure for a hand-written, generator-free parser that handles alternatives, repetition, and left-recursive expression forms while producing precise diagnostics.
proposition: Pattern 'recursive-descent-parser' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: recursive-descent-parser: Parse a small grammar by translating every rule directly into a function that consumes the tokens the rule matches and calls the functions of the rules it references, so the parser's control flow is the grammar itself and stays readable, debuggable and free of a code-generation step. Problem: A hand-written parser is the only option - no generator in the toolchain, or the grammar is a small DSL - yet the grammar is not a flat token sequence: alternatives must be chosen from lookahead, repetition must become a loop, and the natural grammar for expressions is left-recursive, which a top-down parser cannot translate directly. Without a disciplined mapping from rules to functions the parser degenerates into ad-hoc index arithmetic and exception-driven backtracking, and errors end up without positions.

A cooperative harbor game contains patrolling guards, animated statues, homing projectiles, and crowd agents. Each actor type has its own recurring behavior: GuardPatrol chooses a route, StatueCharge accumulates energy, ProjectileMotion steers toward a target, and CrowdAgent selects a local goal. The central FrameDriver currently contains type checks and inline blocks for all four behaviors, making it difficult to add an actor without editing the driver. Each live participant must advance exactly once per simulation tick, in a deterministic registry order, and newly spawned actors must not be advanced twice in the same tick. A behavior must also be able to request removal without invalidating the current traversal. Input polling and presentation must continue while actors advance, and no actor may run an unbounded private loop that prevents other actors from progressing. The design must establish a clear home for actor-specific recurring behavior and a uniform way for the driver to invoke it across heterogeneous object types.

Decision: Choose where recurring actor-specific behavior resides and define the uniform contract by which the frame driver advances every live participant exactly once.
proposition: Pattern 'update-method' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: update-method: Give every live object one self-contained per-frame step and let a single driver call each object's step every frame, so behaviour advances one frame at a time while input and rendering stay responsive. Problem: A running world is full of objects that each have to keep doing their own thing - guards patrolling, statues charging, agents acting - and the recurring decision is where one object's per-frame behaviour lives and how all those behaviours get driven. Coding a behaviour as a loop that runs to completion blocks input and rendering (the skeleton walks, but nobody sees it); coding it inline in the game loop turns the loop into a switchboard over every kind of object, so every new behaviour edits central code; and there is no way for two actors to evolve independently and simultaneously.

Each actor type has its own recurring behavior: GuardPatrol chooses a route, StatueCharge accumulates energy, ProjectileMotion steers toward a target, and CrowdAgent selects a local goal. The central FrameDriver currently contains type checks and inline blocks for all four behaviors, making it difficult to add an actor without editing the driver. Each live participant must advance exactly once per simulation tick, in a deterministic registry order, and newly spawned actors must not be advanced twice in the same tick. A behavior must also be able to request removal without invalidating the current traversal. Input polling and presentation must continue while actors advance, and no actor may run an unbounded private loop that prevents other actors from progressing. The design must establish a clear home for actor-specific recurring behavior and a uniform way for the driver to invoke it across heterogeneous object types.

Decision: Choose where recurring actor-specific behavior resides and define the uniform contract by which the frame driver advances every live participant exactly once.
proposition: Pattern 'strategy' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: strategy: Define a family of algorithms, encapsulate each one behind a common operation, and make them interchangeable, so the algorithm a context executes can vary independently of the context and its clients - including at run time. Problem: One class supports several variants of the same computation - sort orders, pricing or tax rules, routing and backoff policies, compression codecs - and the variant has to be selected at run time. Hard-wiring the variants into the class (or into one subclass per variant) mixes algorithm detail with the class's own logic, forces recompilation for every new variant, and turns selection into a growing conditional that runs on every call.

proposition: Pattern 'bulkhead' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: bulkhead: Partition finite shared capacity at the failure domain (dependency, tenant, priority class, or cell) into independently bounded pools or permits, with an explicit queue and saturation policy, so one slow, saturated, or failing participant cannot consume capacity reserved for others. Problem: Several dependencies or tenants share thread, connection, worker, or permit pools. When one becomes slow, leaky, or overloaded, its calls hold shared slots and fill shared queues, so unrelated work queues and fails behind it; the design needs a boundary that contains resource exhaustion without pretending to isolate CPU, network, or server-side limits that remain shared.

proposition: Pattern 'messaging-gateway' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: messaging-gateway: Encapsulate access to a messaging system behind an ordinary interface of domain methods, so calling application code makes method calls while a single component owns message construction, correlation, timeouts and error translation. Problem: Application code that talks to a broker keeps importing messaging concepts: it builds the payload, picks the channel, attaches a reply address and a correlation id, parses the response and interprets broker errors. The trigger for this pattern is that callers should make a method call instead of writing messaging code - the messaging knowledge belongs in exactly one place that can change without touching business rules.

proposition: Pattern 'pipeline' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: pipeline: Decompose a transformation into an ordered sequence of named stages that each consume the previous stage's output and produce the next stage's input, so the workflow reads top to bottom and every step can be tested, instrumented, reordered or replaced on its own. Problem: A multi-step transformation is written as one long function or a tangle of nested calls: the steps are unnamed, their order is implicit in statement order, intermediate values need throwaway names, there is no seam at which a single step can be logged, tested or replaced, and the same sequence is retyped at every call site that needs it.

proposition: Pattern 'lazy-acquisition' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: lazy-acquisition: Defer acquiring an expensive or scarce resource until it is first used, so the acquisition cost is paid only by the holders that actually use it, while clients keep seeing an ordinary interface. Problem: A resource is costly to acquire, scarce, and on many execution paths never needed at all, yet the code that holds it acquires it during construction, at start-up or on a hot entry path: the process pays for resources it never dereferences, start-up time grows with every optional subsystem, and scarce capacity (descriptors, connections, licenses, memory) is consumed by holders that never use it.

proposition: Pattern 'poison-pill' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: poison-pill: Terminate queue consumers cooperatively by sending a reserved sentinel message that each consumer recognises as "no more work", so consumers drain the backlog and exit without a separate control channel or forced cancellation. Problem: A producer-consumer system must shut down, but its consumers block on an empty queue and the queue has no built-in "no more items" signal: callers either kill the workers mid-work and drop buffered items, or leave them blocked forever. Production has ended - how do the consumers learn that while still processing everything already queued?

proposition: Pattern 'function-composition' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: function-composition: Combine a chain of small unary transformations into one reusable function by sequencing them with a composition combinator (compose/pipe), so the order of the steps is stated once, every step stays independently testable, and the chain itself becomes a value that can be named, passed and reassembled. Problem: A transformation that is naturally a sequence of small pure steps gets written as nested calls or as repeated imperative assignment (`h(g(f(x)))`, or `y = f(x); y = g(y); ...; return y`) at every call site. The order is duplicated wherever the chain is used, the intermediate values need throwaway names, steps cannot be reused in a different order, and changing one stage means editing every copy.

Candidate: inversion-of-control: Invert the direction of control between a reusable framework and application code: the framework owns the call flow and invokes the application's hooks at its extension points, so the generic sequence is reused while application code supplies only behaviour. proposition: Pattern 'protected-system' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: protected-system: Give a resource exactly one owning object whose published operations are the only way to touch it, so that every access is decided by an authorization check before the resource is used. Problem: A resource - a credential store, a file tree, a socket, a connection pool, a device handle - is referenced from many places. When each use site performs its own permission check, the checks drift, new code paths forget them, and the resource remains reachable as a raw handle, so a missing check cannot even be detected. The recurring trigger: one object can own the resource and clients can be made to hold only that object, so ownership itself can carry the enforcement.

proposition: Pattern 'composite-entity' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: composite-entity: Represent a cluster of related, dependent objects through one coarse-grained entity that owns them and persists and synchronises the whole graph as a single unit of work, so clients never reference, sequence, or save the parts themselves. Coined for coarse-grained EJB business objects; its modern form is the aggregate root with cascading or owned mappings. Problem: A business concept clients treat as one thing (an order with its lines, a customer with addresses) is really a cluster of dependent objects, and persisting each part separately forces callers to know the parts, save them in the right order in the right transaction, delete the ones that left the relationship, and absorb a leaking physical schema. The catalog trigger: a cluster of related objects must persist and synchronise as one unit.

proposition: Pattern 'version-number' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: version-number: Store a version token alongside each persistent record and make every write assert the token it read, so a write computed from stale data fails as a detectable conflict instead of silently overwriting a newer value. Problem: Two sessions read the same record, both edit it, and the later write wins: the earlier update vanishes without any error (the lost update). Once the read-modify-write spans more than one system transaction the database cannot tell 'this is the record I read' from 'this record changed under me', so no code path can notice in time - unless the record itself carries a per-row token that changes on every write and the write tests that token before committing.

Candidate: copy-on-write: Let several handles of a value share one expensive body until the first write, which clones that body privately, so copying costs a pointer instead of a deep copy while every handle still behaves as an independent value. Candidate: cancellation-token: Give a caller-owned operation tree a one-way request to stop: pass a read-only cancellation signal through every cancellable call, observe it at safe points, clean up what was acquired, and report a distinct cancelled outcome without pretending that cooperative cancellation is forced termination. Candidate: request-reply: Let a sender obtain a result or a domain error from an asynchronous or remote receiver by pairing each request with a correlated reply, and give the missing reply a defined outcome: timeout, cancellation and disposal of late replies. Problem: Messaging is one-way, but the sender frequently needs a return value or a domain error from the receiver before it can continue. Without an agreed reply destination, a way to match replies to requests, and a rule for what happens when no reply arrives, the caller either blocks forever, mis-associates the next reply with the wrong request, or accumulates pending state it never cleans up.

proposition: Pattern 'producer-consumer' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: producer-consumer: Insert a bounded buffer between producers and consumers of work items so the two sides run concurrently at their own rates, the buffer absorbs bursts and slack, and its bound turns overload into backpressure, queueing or an explicit drop policy instead of unbounded growth. Problem: Production and consumption proceed at different rates: a fast producer outruns its consumer and either drops items or grows a backlog until memory runs out, a slow producer leaves consumers idle, and bursts arrive faster than they can be processed. Wiring the two sides together directly also couples their lifetimes and schedules - a synchronous hand-off makes the faster side wait for the slower - so neither side can be scaled, restarted or tested on its own.

proposition: Pattern 'composite-entity' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: composite-entity: Represent a cluster of related, dependent objects through one coarse-grained entity that owns them and persists and synchronises the whole graph as a single unit of work, so clients never reference, sequence, or save the parts themselves. Coined for coarse-grained EJB business objects; its modern form is the aggregate root with cascading or owned mappings. Problem: A business concept clients treat as one thing (an order with its lines, a customer with addresses) is really a cluster of dependent objects, and persisting each part separately forces callers to know the parts, save them in the right order in the right transaction, delete the ones that left the relationship, and absorb a leaking physical schema. The catalog trigger: a cluster of related objects must persist and synchronise as one unit.

proposition: Pattern 'bulkhead' is relevant to this decision. Candidate: bulkhead: Partition finite shared capacity at the failure domain (dependency, tenant, priority class, or cell) into independently bounded pools or permits, with an explicit queue and saturation policy, so one slow, saturated, or failing participant cannot consume capacity reserved for others. Problem: Several dependencies or tenants share thread, connection, worker, or permit pools. When one becomes slow, leaky, or overloaded, its calls hold shared slots and fill shared queues, so unrelated work queues and fails behind it; the design needs a boundary that contains resource exhaustion without pretending to isolate CPU, network, or server-side limits that remain shared.
